A test asserting that `bulk_export` raises `Forbidden` (or filters out) reports not owned by `user.tenant_id` is needed to make this kind of regression detectable.

findings.title: Unknown report IDs now surface as AttributeError instead of Forbidden
findings.body: If `Report.get(rid)` returns `None` for an unknown ID, the deleted loop previously dereferenced `report.tenant_id` inside `require_owner`, which at minimum failed before serialisation. Now the `None` flows to `r.to_dict()` on line 7 and raises `AttributeError`, producing a 500 for what is a client input error. Validate the fetched list (drop or reject missing IDs) as part of reinstating the ownership filter.

findings.title: SQL injection: f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates `term` and `status` into the SQL text via an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Both values land inside single-quoted literals, so any caller-supplied apostrophe terminates the literal and the rest of the input is parsed as SQL (e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer; `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` depending on whether the driver permits multi-statement execution).

Fix by passing the values as bind parameters, matching `get_customer` on line 5 and the contract in `billing/db.py` ("`params` must carry every caller value"):

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the *parameter value*, not the SQL text.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract and breaks on quoted input
findings.body:
`billing/db.execute` documents "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with `params=None`.

Beyond the contract breach, this is wrong for reachable, entirely legitimate inputs:
- `term="O'Brien"` or `status="don't know"` closes the quoted literal and the statement fails to parse — a plain syntax error on a normal customer name.
- `term` values containing `%` or `_` are treated as LIKE wildcards rather than literal characters, so the search silently returns wrong rows.
- `term=None` or `status=None` stringifies to the literal `None` instead of raising or matching NULL.

Fix by parameterising, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, which also removes the need for the surrounding quotes. If literal `%`/`_` matching is required, escape them in the pattern before binding.

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers, missing SQL injection detection
findings.body: search_customers builds a query via f-string interpolation instead of parameterised placeholders (unlike get_customer above it, and unlike the convention documented in billing/db.py that params must carry every caller value). No test in this diff calls search_customers with a value like `term="'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` or asserts that placeholders are used, so this behavior change is currently uncatchable by any test.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary URL with no scheme/host check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight to `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it parses the host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before posting, so the control exists in this module and is simply not applied on this path.

An attacker who can register or test a webhook target can make the server issue GET requests to internal addresses (`http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...`, `http://127.0.0.1:6379/`, internal admin panels) and learn the outcome — the status code is returned to the caller, so this is a probing oracle, not just a blind request. Non-HTTP schemes are also accepted by the caller's URL string: `file://` is handled by requests only with an adapter, but `http+unix`-style adapters or a redirect to another scheme are worth ruling out. `requests.get` also follows redirects by default, so even if a host check were added at call time, an allowed host could 302 to an internal address.

Suggested fix: reuse the same host parse + `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check used at lines 8-9, require the scheme to be `https` (or `http`/`https`), resolve the hostname and reject private/loopback/link-local/reserved IPs, and pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop).

I cannot see the caller of `verify_endpoint` in this diff or in retrieved context; the assessment that `url` is attacker-influenced rests on the PR description ("caller-supplied URL") and on the function's name and placement next to a customer-facing webhook sender.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sibling function enforces

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new function that performs a server-side HTTP GET against a caller-supplied URL, unlike the sibling function above it which validates against ALLOWED_HOSTS. No test exists for this function in the diff, so there is nothing to catch a regression, an incorrect status code return, or a fix that later adds/removes host validation. Add a test that exercises verify_endpoint's behavior (e.g. with allowed/disallowed hosts, or mocked requests.get) so behavioral changes are caught.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is exported at module level with no docstring. A caller cannot determine from the signature alone whether the URL is validated (it is not—there is no allowlist check like the adjacent `send_payload` function performs), what exceptions it may raise, or what the return value semantics are (HTTP status codes can span 100–599 with different meanings). A competent caller could easily misuse this—for example, assuming it validates the target against an allowlist before issuing a request, when it does not.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on non-public invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false`, which is an exact copy of the block written for the intentionally-public `assets` bucket above. For a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices` this switches off the account-level safety net entirely: any ACL or bucket policy that grants `AllUsers`/`AuthenticatedUsers` will take effect, and a single mis-set ACL exposes customer invoices publicly.

Unless this bucket is genuinely meant to serve public content, set all four attributes to `true`, or simply delete this resource and rely on the S3 defaults (which block public access) plus any account-level block. Worth also confirming that nothing else in the module attaches a permissive policy to `aws_s3_bucket.invoices`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Public access block disabled on customer-invoices bucket

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC hexdigest as `verify_stripe` one line above, but returns `expected == header`. `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte across repeated requests. Use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` exactly as `verify_stripe` does on line 7.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay signature check has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay uses a plain == comparison instead of hmac.compare_digest (used by the sibling verify_stripe). No test file is part of this diff, so nothing would catch a timing side-channel regression or even a basic correctness regression (e.g. wrong header format) in this new function. Add a test asserting correct/incorrect signature behavior, and ideally one that would fail if compare_digest were swapped for ==.

findings.title: Divergent behaviour from verify_stripe when header is None or bytes
findings.body: Beyond the timing issue, `==` and `hmac.compare_digest` differ on edge inputs: `compare_digest(str, None)` or a `bytes` header raises `TypeError`, while `expected == header` quietly returns `False`. A caller that wraps `verify_stripe` in a `try/except TypeError` (or relies on the exception to distinguish "malformed request" from "bad signature") will see a silently different result from `verify_acmepay`. Switching line 12 to `hmac.compare_digest` resolves this along with the timing problem.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` is the generic 500 error path and now serialises `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response body. A stack trace discloses file system paths, module and function names, framework and library versions, and the source line structure of the application; exception messages frequently embed the offending input, SQL fragments, connection strings or internal hostnames. An unauthenticated caller who can provoke an error — malformed input, an unexpected content type, a missing record — gets a free map of the internals, which meaningfully lowers the cost of finding the next bug.

Keep the client-facing payload opaque and leave the detail in the log, which line 8 already captures. If developers need the detail in a response, gate it on an explicit debug/development configuration flag that is off by default, and consider returning a correlation id the client can quote instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    log.exception("request failed")
    return {"error": "internal error"}, 500
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and depends on ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape changed: new key and non-constant `error` value

findings.title: Public error handler return contract is now undocumented
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler whose return value is part of the API contract. The diff changes it from returning `{"error": "internal error"}` to `{"error": str(exc), "traceback": traceback.format_exc()}`. This is a breaking change to the response structure and content that callers need to know about. The function has no docstring explaining what it returns, so callers cannot discover this contract change except by reading the code. Add a docstring documenting the new return structure, or document this change in the API specification if one exists.

findings.title: No test guards against leaking exception details in error responses
findings.body: The handle() function now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the client-facing response body, a behavior change from the previous generic 'internal error' message. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts the shape/content of the response returned by handle(), so this leak could be introduced, removed, or altered again without any test failing either way.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`) and callers must be verifying it with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest for the same conceptual value (a stored user password). Storing that in the same column means verification after a reset either fails outright or, with bcrypt's parsing, raises `ValueError: invalid salt` — the user is locked out. Separately, an unsalted single-round MD5 is not an acceptable password hash at all: it is trivially reversed via rainbow tables. The reset path should call `hash_password` (bcrypt) so both writers and the single reader agree on one format; if a distinct value is genuinely needed, it should be a random one-time reset *token*, not a hash of the user's password.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives the stored value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5()` pass, while `hash_password` on line 7 correctly uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no per-user salt here, so any password written through the reset path is recoverable from a leaked database at rainbow-table/brute-force speed, and identical passwords across users produce identical digests. It also means reset-set passwords are stored in a format incompatible with the bcrypt verifier, which suggests the two paths disagree about the stored format.

Fix: delete `hash_reset_password` and call `hash_password` (bcrypt) from the reset flow. If a distinct function is needed for readability, have it delegate to `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`.

Entry point note: the caller that feeds `raw` (presumably a reset-token-authenticated form submission) is not in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot name the exact HTTP handler; the defect is in the storage primitive itself regardless of caller.

findings.title: New hash_reset_password function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password uses MD5 to hash a password for reset purposes, but there is no test file in this diff exercising it. Nothing would fail if this function were changed, removed, or if its weak-hash behavior regressed further. Since this is a change to authentication-critical code, at minimum a test asserting the function's contract (or documenting expected hashing scheme) should exist.

findings.title: Public function hash_reset_password lacks docstring
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` is a public function in the auth module. Its name suggests it hashes a password for reset purposes, but callers cannot determine from signature alone whether this is a temporary token hash, a validation step, or something else. A docstring explaining the intended use and any limitations would help callers use it correctly.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled script with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: the job gets the repository's secrets and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions, and it runs without the approval gate that fork PRs get under `pull_request`. Line 12 then deliberately checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the fork's code — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on line 15.

Entry point: any unprivileged user opens a pull request from a fork and edits `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources/invokes, e.g. `package.json` lifecycle scripts, a lockfile pointing at a malicious package). Sink: the `run` step on line 13, which executes that attacker-authored code on a runner holding `NPM_TOKEN` and the base-repo `GITHUB_TOKEN`. The attacker can exfiltrate `NPM_TOKEN`, read every other secret available to the job, and use the write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` to push commits or alter releases.

Remediations, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `on: pull_request`. If the only reason for the change was that fork PRs did not get a token, reconsider whether `measure.sh` needs `NPM_TOKEN` at all — a size measurement usually does not.
2. If `pull_request_target` is genuinely required, do **not** check out and execute the head SHA in the same job. Split it: an untrusted job on `pull_request` that builds and uploads an artifact, and a privileged job on `workflow_run` that only consumes the artifact and never executes fork code.
3. At minimum, if any privileged job remains, add an explicit `permissions:` block reducing `GITHUB_TOKEN` to `contents: read` and never pass secrets to a step that runs fork-authored code.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-supplied script with NPM_TOKEN in scope

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ No permissions block: GITHUB_TOKEN is write-scoped under pull_request_target

findings.title: Measurement now covers the PR head, not the merge result
findings.body: With the previous `pull_request` trigger, `actions/checkout` defaults to `refs/pull/N/merge` — the simulated merge of the PR into the base branch — so the reported size reflected what the repository would look like after merging. Pinning `ref` to `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` measures the fork's branch tip in isolation, which diverges whenever the base branch has moved since the PR was created. Size numbers and any threshold comparison derived from them will no longer match the post-merge reality. If this check gates merges on a size budget, the gate is now measuring the wrong tree.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values from hashable to JSON-serialisable
findings.body:
The previous key, `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, worked for any context whose values were hashable — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `Path`, model instances, frozensets, enum members. `json.dumps` accepts a much smaller set and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of the above. Any existing caller passing a non-primitive context value will now get an exception from what used to be a working call, and the failure happens before `_render` is ever reached, so it is not a cache miss but a hard break.

If the digest form is wanted, pass a fallback: `json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True, default=repr)` (accepting that `repr` may not be stable across processes), or keep the tuple key and only hash its `repr`.

findings.title: JSON-serialization requirement for context values is untested
findings.body: The old key was built from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which only required context values to be hashable/sortable. The new key uses `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which requires every value in context to be JSON-serializable (and will raise or silently misbehave for things like sets, custom objects, or dicts with non-string keys under sort_keys). None of the added tests exercise a context with a non-JSON-serializable value, so this behavior change — from 'must be hashable' to 'must be JSON-serializable' — is not covered.

findings.title: Shell-safety test only checks `shell=False`, not the argv list
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` asserts only `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects the actual command that was passed to `subprocess.run` (e.g. `spy.last_call.args[0]`). Because `spy` is a stand-in for `subprocess.run` and never actually executes anything, a regression where the implementation sets `shell=False` but reverts to building a single interpolated string (e.g. `subprocess.run(f"tar -czf /exports/{name}.tar.gz {directory}", shell=False)`) — which would silently fail or misbehave at runtime, and reintroduces exactly the kind of unsafe construction this PR is fixing — would still pass this test. The whole point of the change (argv list instead of a shell string) is left unverified.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test pins `shell=False` but not the list argv that is the actual fix

findings.title: Dropping the shell removes word-splitting/globbing for `directory`
findings.body: Previously the command was interpolated into a shell string, so a `directory` value such as `/srv/a /srv/b` or `/srv/data/*` was word-split and glob-expanded by `/bin/sh` and tar received multiple paths. With a list argv the whole value is passed as one literal path argument, so any such caller now gets `tar: /srv/a /srv/b: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and, because `check=True`, a `CalledProcessError` at runtime rather than a working archive. If callers only ever pass a single concrete directory this is a no-op, but that needs confirming — no callers were retrieved. If multi-path input is a real use case, take a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv instead of relying on the shell.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; may allow arbitrary-path archiving
findings.body:
`name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight from the caller into the tar argv on line 12 with no validation or containment check. Passing it as a list element plus `--` correctly prevents shell injection and option injection, so this is not a command-execution issue. It does mean that if any caller derives `directory` from request data, a caller can ask for `/etc`, `/root`, or `../../` relative paths and the contents land in a readable tarball under `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` — an arbitrary-file-read primitive if that directory is ever served or downloadable.

If callers only pass trusted constants, this is nothing. If not, resolve the path and assert it stays under an allowed root before invoking tar, e.g. `root = Path('/srv/data').resolve(); p = (root / directory).resolve(); if not p.is_relative_to(root): raise ValueError(...)`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result, so the only failure mode it can detect is an exception. If `render` returns `None`, an empty string, a stray header/footer, or a mis-formatted zero total for the empty case, the test still passes. Assert the expected output for an empty invoice explicitly, e.g. the rendered string equals the expected header/total-only form (mirroring the style of `test_renders_total` on line 2).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: test_renders_line_items asserts on a mock, not on output
findings.body:
This test patches out format_line and only checks that it was called twice via fmt.call_count. It never checks the rendered output produced by render(). If render() mishandles the formatted line items (wrong order, wrong joining, dropped lines), this test would still pass. Assert on the actual string returned by render() instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on a mock's call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Deleted test leaves round_cents half-to-even behavior uncovered
findings.body:
The test `test_rounds_half_to_even` (which asserted `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.34")`) was removed along with the fix it was presumably validating. No replacement test was added, so if the rounding fix is wrong or regresses in the future, nothing in this suite would catch it.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Tie-breaking test deleted, removing the only .5 boundary assertion

findings.title: PR claims a rounding fix but only the test file changed
findings.body:
The PR is titled "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test", yet the change set is a single file (`tests/test_rounding.py`) containing only a deletion. There is no implementation change to `round_cents` anywhere in this diff. Either the fix was omitted from the commit — in which case the failing test was simply removed and the underlying defect remains in production — or the behaviour was already changed in an earlier commit and this is a retroactive silencing of the guard.

Please either include the implementation change in this PR so the pair can be reviewed together, or restore the test with the updated expectation and point at the commit that changed the behaviour.

findings.title: Patch targets the definition module, so the mock is never used
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` into the `notify.sender` namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. The test therefore exercises the real `deliver` — it will hit whatever the real transport does (network I/O, flakiness), and the `is False` assertion passes or fails for reasons unrelated to the retry logic it claims to cover. Use `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`, matching the existing test on line 2. Consider also asserting the mock was called exactly `attempts` times, since that is the actual behaviour under test.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; test proves nothing about retries

findings.title: Test patch target contradicts documented behavior
findings.body: The test on line 7 patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the module docstring in sender.py (lines 4–5) explicitly documents that `deliver` is bound into the sender module's namespace at import time, so patching the original location does not affect it. This test will not validate the retry logic as intended—the real function will still execute. The patch should target `notify.sender.deliver` (as the passing test on line 2 correctly does).

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins stringified field values with `","` directly, so a value such as `Smith, John` or `he said "hi"` injects an extra delimiter / unbalanced quote and shifts every subsequent column for that row. The escaping helper needed to prevent exactly this is added two functions below (`csv_escape`), but it is never called. Wrap each field: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note also that `csv_escape` does `"," in value`, which raises `TypeError` on non-string input, so the `str(...)` conversion must happen before the escape call (as written above) rather than after. `csv_header` has the same exposure for column names containing commas.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values unescaped; csv_escape ignores newlines
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each cell directly into a comma-joined string and never calls the `csv_escape` helper added two functions below. Any cell value containing `,`, `"`, `\n` or `\r` therefore changes the structure of the emitted CSV: a comma splits one field into two, and a newline injects an entire extra record that downstream parsers (or a spreadsheet) will read as real data. `csv_escape` would only partly fix this as written, because its condition checks for comma and quote but not for CR/LF, so a newline-bearing value is returned unquoted.

Suggested fix: route every cell through an escaper (`str(r.get(c, ""))`) and extend the escape condition to `any(ch in value for ch in ',"\n\r')`, or simply use the stdlib `csv` module (`csv.writer`), which handles quoting, embedded newlines and doubling correctly. If the exported cells can ever be opened in a spreadsheet, also consider neutralising leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` to avoid formula injection.

I cannot see the caller that supplies `rows`, so I cannot name the entry point; if those values are report data derived from user input (names, free-text fields), this is directly attacker-influenced output.

findings.title: New exporter functions lack tests, unlike existing csv_header
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (in csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (in json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (in pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with no accompanying tests. The repo already has a test for csv_header (test_csv.py), establishing the convention that exporter functions get direct tests. If any of these had a bug — e.g. csv_escape failing to quote a leading/trailing space, dump_streaming producing overlapping chunks off-by-one, or margins_for miscalculating for an unsupported page size — nothing in the current test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Flaky test: relies on real-time midnight boundary
findings.body:
test_token_issued_today_is_valid() calls issue_token() and datetime.now(timezone.utc) separately and compares .date(). If issue_token() is invoked just before midnight UTC and the assertion's datetime.now() call executes just after midnight, token.issued_at.date() will differ from datetime.now().date(), causing a spurious failure. The sibling test on line 4-6 correctly injects a fixed 'now' via the `now=` parameter to is_expired, but this new test does not use any time injection for issue_token or the date comparison, making it non-deterministic and unable to reliably catch real expiry-window bugs.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date-granularity clock comparison is flaky across UTC midnight

findings.title: Test name promises determinism but exhibits time-dependent behavior
findings.body: The test function `test_token_issued_today_is_valid` has a misleading name and contract. The name suggests a stable, deterministic test, but the implementation depends on the system clock and will fail intermittently at midnight boundaries. Line 11 compares `token.issued_at.date()` with `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()`, and line 12 calls `is_expired()` with no explicit `now` parameter, likely using the current real time internally. If a token is issued just before midnight and the assertion runs after midnight, the date comparison fails. The function's public contract — what a reader infers from its name — does not warn of this time-dependent behavior, making it a trap for future maintainers.

findings.title: New CouponExpired branch is untested
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test in this PR updates the happy-path test to pass a future expiry date, avoiding the new branch entirely. If the expiry check were inverted, off-by-one, or silently removed, no test would fail.

findings.title: `expires_at` None or naive datetime raises TypeError, not CouponExpired
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes `expires_at` is always a non-None, timezone-aware datetime. If a coupon has no expiry (`None`) the comparison raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime'`; if it was stored/parsed as a naive datetime it raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. Either way the caller sees an opaque TypeError instead of a coupon being applied or a `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def`, so callers will `await` it expecting the coroutine to yield control while the network round-trip is in flight. `requests.get` is synchronous: it holds the thread for the whole duration of the call, up to the `timeout=5`, during which no other task on the event loop can run. Under any concurrency this serialises all requests behind this one call and can produce multi-second latency spikes across unrelated handlers.

The file already imports `httpx` and the sibling `fetch_plan` takes an `httpx.AsyncClient`. Use the same approach here, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or create one in an `async with`) and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If the synchronous client must stay, wrap it in `asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the loop is not blocked. Note also that the new `import requests` on line 2 becomes unnecessary once this is converted.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function blocks on synchronous HTTP call

findings.title: New async function with blocking I/O has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that performs a blocking `requests.get` call inside an async def. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so nothing would fail if this blocking call stalls the event loop or if the function's behavior regresses (e.g. wrong URL, missing timeout handling, wrong JSON parsing). Since fetch_plan above appears to follow an async-client pattern, a test for fetch_plan_limits (even a basic one mocking requests.get) would at least catch behavioral changes, though it would need to be async-aware to catch the blocking-call defect itself.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. If `tenant_id` reaches this function from request data without validation, a value such as `../admin` or `..%2fadmin` lets the caller address arbitrary paths on the internal `billing.internal` host — requests/urllib3 resolve dot-segments before sending, so the traversal is not blocked at the HTTP layer. A value containing `?` or `#` can likewise inject query parameters or truncate the path.

Fix by encoding and constraining the value rather than interpolating it: pass it as a path parameter through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, or validate it against the expected shape (e.g. integer or UUID) before building the URL. The same treatment applies to the pre-existing `client.get(f"/plans/{tenant_id}")` on line 6, though that one is outside this change.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. If `_client.send` blocks on a socket and an operator sends SIGINT, or if shutdown code raises `SystemExit` while this frame is on the stack, the interrupt is silently converted into `return None` and the process keeps running. Narrow this to `except Exception:` so control-flow exceptions propagate. If the intent is specifically network failure, narrowing further to the client's transport error type would be better still.

findings.title: No test covers the new bare-except fallback behavior
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions (including KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit) and returns None instead of raising. There is no test in this diff verifying that a failing _client.send call results in push_metrics returning None rather than propagating. If this behavior were reverted or broken (e.g. exception re-raised, or wrong return value), nothing would fail.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await` on line 18, and only then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all outside `_lock`. Two concurrent calls for the same tenant can both read the same `current`, both pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and both write, so the effective total can reach up to `LIMIT + cost - 1` (or more with N concurrent callers): the limit this function exists to enforce does not hold.

The write is also an absolute assignment rather than a read-modify-write increment, so any `consume()` call that interleaves during the `await` has its increment silently clobbered — the two functions do not agree on how `_counters` is mutated even though they share it.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write inside the existing lock, and by incrementing rather than overwriting:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 is standing in for real I/O that must not be held under the lock, then the post-await write must re-check the counter under the lock rather than trusting `current`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act outside the lock in try_consume

findings.title: New racy try_consume has no test exercising concurrent callers
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters (line 15), awaits (line 18), then writes (line 19) without holding _lock, unlike consume which does hold the lock for the whole read-modify-write. This is a textbook check-then-act race: two concurrent calls can both pass the LIMIT check before either writes, allowing the tenant's counter to exceed LIMIT. No test file is present in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if this race were triggered or if the limit-enforcement logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one on the LIMIT comparison, or the race allowing over-limit consumption under concurrency).

findings.title: Docstring describes old tuple return type, not new dict
findings.body:
The docstring states "Return (name, email) for a user." but the function now returns a dict with keys "name", "email", and "tier". A caller reading this docstring would expect to unpack a tuple and would break. The repository context shows `reports/weekly.py` already does exactly this: `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)` will fail with the new dict return type. Update the docstring to describe the actual return shape.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple return

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of `(name, email)`. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:6` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a 3-key dict into two names raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack`; even if the dict had exactly two keys it would bind the key strings, not the values, silently producing `"name" <"email">`. Either update every caller (e.g. `u = lookup_user(id); u["name"], u["email"]`) or keep the tuple contract and expose the tier via a separate function / `NamedTuple` that remains unpack-compatible.

findings.title: No test catches the tuple→dict contract break for lookup_user callers
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple, but reports/weekly.py still does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise at runtime (unpacking a dict yields keys, not the expected two values in that order). There is no test in this diff—or apparently elsewhere—that calls lookup_user and checks its return shape, nor one that exercises render_row in reports/weekly.py. Because nothing exercises either function, this breaking change would ship silently and only surface when weekly.py is actually invoked in production.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
WriteSettlement has no test covering its error path
findings.body: WriteSettlement is new and untested. In particular, the DB-insert-error branch never propagates the error (a fresh `var err error` shadows it and always returns nil), but no test exercises db.Exec failing, so this defect would pass silently. Add a test that forces db.Exec to return an error and asserts WriteSettlement returns a non-nil error.

findings.title: Public function WriteSettlement has no docstring
findings.body: The new exported function `WriteSettlement` has no documentation describing what it does, what its parameters mean, or what errors (if any) it may return. For a function whose behavior is non-obvious — it logs errors but does not propagate them — a docstring would help callers understand the intended contract.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` accumulates across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to that shared list and line 11 returns it, meaning the second call reports the failures from the first call as well, and callers that hold the returned list see it mutate underneath them on the next call.

Use the same pattern already applied on line 2 for `extra_headers`: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted or [])` (or `if attempted is None: attempted = []` if the caller is meant to be mutated in place).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients across calls and grows unboundedly

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function with mutable default argument and no documentation

findings.title: No test exercises send_with_retries or its mutable default arg bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument (attempted=[]) which will persist and accumulate across calls when the caller doesn't pass its own list, silently corrupting results on subsequent invocations. There is no test in this diff that calls the function twice without an explicit `attempted` list, so this behavior change (and the bug) would go undetected — a test would pass today and continue to pass even if this bug ships or regresses further.

findings.title: compute_rounding flips >= 0.5 to > 0.5, changing half-cent rounding
findings.body:
The rename commit also changed the comparison in the rounding calculator from `>= 0.5` to `> 0.5`. For the exact boundary value `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1 — i.e. exact half-cents round down instead of up. This is a silent money-value behaviour change buried in an otherwise mechanical rename, and half-cent remainders are common in tax/percentage splits, so it is reachable in normal operation. If the rounding rule was genuinely meant to change, it belongs in its own commit with a test; otherwise restore `>= 0.5`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rounding comparison flipped from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 inside a rename

findings.title: Rounding boundary change (>= to >) has no test coverage in this diff
findings.body: compute_rounding changed the comparison operator from `>=` to `>` while ostensibly just renaming calc_rounding. At the boundary value remainder_cents == 0.5, the old function returned 1 and the new one returns 0 — a real behavior change. No test file is present in this diff, so there is nothing that would catch this regression at the 0.5 boundary.

findings.title: page_of_sorted drops one record per page (off-by-one slice)
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` computes `start = page * PAGE_SIZE` but slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, yielding only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. Because the offset advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` on the next call, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — so a full paginated export silently loses one record per page rather than merely returning short pages. The existing `page_of` on line 6 uses the correct bound `start + PAGE_SIZE`; the new function should match it. Edge case: if `PAGE_SIZE` were ever 1, every page returns an empty list and the caller's "empty page means done" loop terminates immediately with zero records.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns fewer items than page_of

findings.title: New paginated-sort function is untested and has an off-by-one bug
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, which returns only PAGE_SIZE-1 records per page instead of PAGE_SIZE, silently dropping the last record of every page. No test accompanies this change, so nothing would catch a regression or confirm the intended page size is returned.

findings.title: AttributeError when purchase_order is None (the common case)
findings.body: `invoice.purchase_order` is declared `str | None` and the model docstring states it is only set for customers on invoicing terms (~1 account in 20). The removed guard was the only thing preventing `None.upper()`. As written, `header_lines` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for roughly 95% of invoices — every render path through this function breaks. Restore the conditional append (or use `if invoice.purchase_order:` / a default) so the PO line is only emitted when the field is set.

findings.title: Function now breaks on optional field it documents handles
findings.body: The function `header_lines` previously guarded against `None` values in `invoice.purchase_order`. The refactored code unconditionally calls `.upper()` on this field, which will crash when the field is `None`. The Invoice model documents that `purchase_order` is optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms"), so the function's contract with its caller has changed without being documented. Either the guard must be restored, or the docstring must state that the field is now required.

findings.title: No test exercises header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: header_lines was changed to always call invoice.purchase_order.upper() unconditionally, but per models/invoice.py this field is optional and unset for ~19/20 accounts. No test in this diff (or apparently in the repo) calls header_lines with an invoice whose purchase_order is None, so a regression that raises AttributeError on the common case would go undetected.

findings.title: File handle leaks when the header check fails
findings.body: `fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on the success path (line 16). When `header != expected_header`, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open, so the descriptor is only reclaimed whenever GC happens to collect it (and never, on implementations without refcounting). For an importer that may be called per-file in a loop over a directory, this accumulates descriptors and can hit the process limit. Wrap the body in `with open(path) as fh:` as `read_rows` (lines 5-6) already does, and drop the explicit `close()`.

findings.title: No test covers read_validated's early-return leak path
findings.body: read_validated returns None on header mismatch without closing fh (line 14), but no test in this diff calls read_validated with a mismatched header. A test asserting file handles are properly closed (or not leaked) on validation failure would catch this regression; currently nothing would fail if this behavior were wrong.

findings.title: Public function `read_validated` lacks docstring for return contract
findings.body: The function `read_validated` is a new public API without a docstring. A caller needs to understand that it returns `None` on header mismatch (line 14) but returns rows on success (line 17). This contract is not self-evident from the signature alone — a competent caller could reasonably expect an exception on validation failure, or might not realize that `None` is a possible return value. Document the return behavior, especially the validation-failure path.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in billing/gateway.py as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge — and its docstring points at the gateway's `Idempotency-Key` header as the way to make retries safe. `@retry(attempts=3)` here will re-issue the POST on any failure that the decorator considers retryable, including timeouts and 5xx responses where the first charge may well have been created server-side. The result is a customer charged up to three times for one logical purchase, with no way for this layer to detect it.

Fix by threading an idempotency key through: generate one key per logical charge in the caller (or at the top of `charge_card`, before the retry boundary, so it is stable across attempts) and pass it to `charge()`. Note that generating it *inside* the retried function body would not help, since each attempt would produce a fresh key. If `charge()` cannot yet accept a key, drop the retry from this path until it can.

Contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5–7, which wraps `get_charge` — documented "Safe to repeat" — and is a correct use of the same decorator.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge can double-bill without Idempotency-Key

findings.title: charge_card lacks required idempotency documentation
findings.body: The new `charge_card` function applies `@retry` to a non-idempotent gateway call. The underlying `charge()` function's docstring explicitly states it is NOT idempotent and requires an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. The wrapper either needs a docstring that documents this requirement and confirms the key is being passed, or the implementation must be corrected to actually pass an Idempotency-Key header. As written, callers have no reason to believe retries here are unsafe — but they are.

findings.title: No test guards against duplicate charges on retry
findings.body: charge_card wraps the non-idempotent charge() call with @retry(attempts=3) and passes no idempotency key. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises retry behavior against a failing/flaky charge() call to verify it doesn't produce multiple real charges. A test that mocks charge() to fail once then succeed, and asserts it was only invoked in a way that avoids duplicate side effects (or that an idempotency key is passed), would catch this; currently nothing would fail if retries caused duplicate charges.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, but `invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC (see `models/invite.py`). Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every input rather than returning a boolean. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. (`timezone` is already imported, since line 5 uses it.)

findings.title: Naive datetime compared against aware datetime
findings.body: The new `expires_within` function creates a naive datetime via `datetime.now()` on line 9 and subtracts it from `invite.expires_at`, which is documented in `models/invite.py` as "always tz-aware, set from datetime.now(timezone.utc)". In Python, subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises TypeError at runtime. The function signature does not document this contract violation, and callers could be misled into using it.

findings.title: expires_within has no test exercising the naive/aware datetime bug
findings.body: expires_within subtracts a naive datetime.now() from invite.expires_at, which per the Invite model docstring is always tz-aware. This raises TypeError at runtime. Nothing in this diff (no test file) calls expires_within, so this defect would ship silently.

findings.title: expires_within returns True for already-expired invites
findings.body: Once the tz bug is fixed, `delta.total_seconds()` is negative for invites whose `expires_at` is in the past, so `expires_within` reports `True` for invites that have already expired. If the intent is "expiring soon but still valid" (the usual use for a reminder/renewal check), the condition needs a lower bound, e.g. `0 <= delta.total_seconds() < hours * 3600`. Worth confirming which semantics callers expect.

findings.title: contactEmail throws when billingContact is absent
findings.body: `Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so any pre-onboarding account produces `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. The sibling function `bannerFor` on line 4 handles exactly this case with `?.` plus a `??` default. Mirror it, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or change the return type to `string | undefined` and let callers decide the fallback. (If this compiles today, `strictNullChecks` is likely off, which means the compiler will not catch it for you.)

findings.title: No test covers contactEmail with missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail dereferences account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, despite billingContact being declared optional in Account. No test exercises the case where billingContact is undefined, so a runtime TypeError on this path would not be caught by any test in this change.

findings.title: Public function `contactEmail` lacks documentation of required precondition
findings.body: The function `contactEmail` is public and calls `.email.toLowerCase()` directly on `account.billingContact` without optional chaining. However, the `Account` interface defines `billingContact` as optional (`billingContact?`), meaning it can be undefined. A caller could pass an account without a billing contact and receive a runtime error. The function needs documentation clarifying that it requires `billingContact` to be defined, or the code should handle the optional case.

findings.title: Default retry count change breaks documented caller contract
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's default `retries` parameter has been reduced from 5 to 1. However, documented code in `sync/nightly.py` relies on the old default of 5 retries to handle a known flaky partner API that returns 503 errors. The docstring in `sync_partner_catalogue()` explicitly states: "We rely on fetch()'s default retry count to get through it; this is deliberate and was the fix for INC-4471." This change breaks that documented contract without updating the caller or the documentation. Either restore the default to 5, update `sync_partner_catalogue()` to explicitly pass `retries=5`, or update its docstring to reflect the new behavior.

findings.title: Lowered default retries regresses INC-4471 for nightly catalogue sync
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s default `retries` drops from 5 to 1. `sync/nightly.py:sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch("https://partner.example.com/catalogue")` with no `retries` argument and its docstring states explicitly that it relies on the default retry count because the partner API returns 503 for roughly one call in three during the nightly window, and that this was the fix for INC-4471.

With the old default the chance of exhausting all attempts on a 1-in-3 failure rate was very small; with `retries=1` the sync will fail regularly, reintroducing the incident. Either pass the required count explicitly at the call site (`fetch(url, retries=5)`) as part of this change, or leave the default alone and lower it only for the callers that want less aggressive behaviour.

findings.title: No test guards fetch()'s default retry count against regressions
findings.body: The default for `retries` was lowered from 5 to 1. There is no test in the diff or evident in the repository that exercises `fetch()`'s default retry behavior or `sync_partner_catalogue()`'s reliance on it. Per the comment in sync/nightly.py, this default was deliberately chosen to survive a known flaky dependency (INC-4471); nothing would fail if this default silently regresses again. A test asserting that `fetch()` retries at least N times by default (or a test around `sync_partner_catalogue()` simulating transient 503s) would catch this class of change.

findings.title: Index duplicates invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, column list and sort direction as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, already created in migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql and applied 2025-11-02. The planner will never prefer one over the other; the only effects are an extra index to maintain on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE of `invoices`, extra disk, and a build that takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on a presumably large table during deploy. Drop these lines and rely on the existing index. If the intent was actually a different shape (e.g. including `status`, or `created_at ASC`), state that explicitly — as written it is not different.

findings.title: Auth token in Referer header is now logged verbatim
findings.body:
The previous code special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it in the `headers` dict that is serialised by `log_method(json.dumps(headers, indent=2))`. The new code assigns `request.headers[header]` directly for every header, including `Referer`, so the scrubbing is no longer applied.

Per the retrieved `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, which means the browser attaches that token in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. Any request that reaches this logging path (e.g. a 5xx) will therefore write a live session token into the server log, where it is readable by anyone with log access, by log-shipping pipelines, or by support bundles attached to bug reports. A token recovered from a log grants the holder full authenticated access to the server.

Restore the `Referer` branch that routes the value through `_scrub_uri` (and consider applying the same scrub to any other header that can carry a URL) rather than logging the raw header.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Referer is logged verbatim, leaking the auth token into logs

findings.title: No test guards against unscrubbed Referer token leaking to logs
findings.body: The change removes the _scrub_uri call that stripped tokens from the Referer header before logging. If a test existed asserting that a Referer containing a token query parameter is scrubbed in the logged output, this regression would have failed it. No such test appears to exist or was updated/added in this diff, so nothing catches the reintroduction of the token-in-log vulnerability.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` is now accepted but ignored
findings.body: `extra_param_keys` was consumed only by the deleted `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` call. After this change the function still takes the argument (callers presumably still pass their deployment-specific secret query keys) but it has no effect, so callers silently get behaviour they did not ask for. Either restore the scrubbing call or remove the parameter and update its callers, but do not leave a live-looking knob wired to nothing.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer scheme-checked, reintroducing SVG XSS
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` no longer matches the condition on line 6, so it falls through to whatever the function's trailing default is — evidently a permissive `return true`, since every attribute that needs checking is enumerated explicitly here. The file header states rendered attributes come from end-user-submitted markdown and that `validateProp` is the only barrier to the DOM, so `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` becomes executable again. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` to the condition unless a replacement check exists elsewhere on the xlink path (none is visible in the retrieved context).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, reintroducing SVG XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation, allowing silent regression
findings.body: The removal of the 'xlinkhref' check from validateProp reopens the SVG xlink:href XSS vector this code was previously fixed for. There is no test in this diff (or evidenced elsewhere) that exercises validateProp with attribute === 'xlinkhref' and an unsafe value (e.g. 'javascript:...') to assert it is rejected. Since no such test exists, this behavior change would pass CI silently even though it reintroduces a known vulnerability.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches filesystem path construction
Removed validation contradicts buildPath's documented contract
findings.body: The `buildPath` function in file.go has explicit documentation stating: 'It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point.' By removing the `ValidateID` check on `projectQueryParameter` before it flows through to filesystem operations, this code now violates that documented contract. The next caller to use this `projectQueryParameter` value in a path operation will be operating under the assumption that validation has already occurred, creating a path traversal vulnerability. The documentation of buildPath's precondition is no longer satisfied by this calling code.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of project ID validation
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) check that previously rejected malformed/path-traversal project names before they reach buildPath (which joins project into a filesystem path with no validation of its own, per file.go's doc comment). No test in this change (or referenced) exercises list() with a malicious projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '../') to confirm it is rejected. If this regression is real, nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Buffer sized from client-declared contentLength before body is read
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory based on a value the client asserts in the request (the part's `Content-Length`), and it does so *before* a single byte of `body` is consumed on line 8. A client can send `Content-Length: 10737418240` with a one-byte body and the server allocates regardless; a handful of concurrent `UploadPart` calls will OOM the process. The previous code let the pool-backed RW grow as bytes actually arrived, so peak memory tracked real data rather than a claim.

If the pre-sizing is wanted for throughput, clamp it to a bounded maximum (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartChunk)`) and only ever treat it as a hint — the RW still has to grow on demand, so a small reservation costs nothing but a large one must never be honoured verbatim.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-allocated from client-declared Content-Length (memory exhaustion)

findings.title: No test exercises Reserve(contentLength) with an oversized/mismatched length
findings.body: The change adds `.Reserve(contentLength)` which pre-allocates memory based on a value that (per the PR description) is attacker/client-controlled, before the body is actually read. There is no test in this diff that calls uploadPart with a large declared contentLength and a small or mismatched actual body to verify memory is not over-allocated, nor a test asserting behavior when contentLength is wrong. As written, any regression here (including the one this PR appears to introduce) would go undetected by the existing test suite.

findings.title: Negative/unknown contentLength (-1) is passed to Reserve unchecked
findings.body:
HTTP requests with chunked transfer encoding or no `Content-Length` yield `-1` for the declared length, and that value reaches `Reserve` unguarded. Depending on `Reserve`'s implementation this either panics (`make([]byte, -1)` / slice bounds) or silently produces a nonsense capacity. The old `NewRW()` call had no such dependency on the header being present.

Guard the value before using it: only reserve when `contentLength > 0`, and cap it at a maximum part size.

findings.title: Stale comment about dynamic buffer growth
findings.body: The comment states the RW 'grows a page at a time as the body is read', but this is no longer accurate after pre-reservation via `Reserve(contentLength)`. The buffer now has pre-allocated capacity and will grow differently (if at all) compared to the previous dynamic growth pattern. Update the comment to reflect that the buffer is now pre-reserved to the declared content length.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to HTTP on an *explicit* `is_secure=False`; every other case — including the overwhelmingly common case where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` at all and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats missing/`None` as falsy, so the default flips to `http`.

This URL is used to build the request that carries the AWS signature (and, depending on the auth mode, session tokens) to `s3.amazonaws.com`, so the signed request now travels unencrypted by default and is exposed to interception and replay by anyone on the path. Restore the fail-secure form, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so only an explicit opt-out downgrades the scheme.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP, exposing signed credentials

findings.title: No test covers the default scheme selection behavior
findings.body: The scheme selection logic changed from defaulting to https (when is_secure is absent/None) to defaulting to http. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression or verify the new default behavior for the case where request.meta.get('is_secure') is unset. Add a test asserting that when 'is_secure' is not set in request.meta, the resulting URL uses the expected scheme, and another for is_secure=True/False explicitly.

findings.title: DELETE now authorized by "push" action, dropping the delete check
findings.body:
The removed switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct action `"delete"`. The replacement condition treats every method other than GET/HEAD as `"push"`, so a DELETE request is now authorized against the push permission. Any account granted push on a repository can delete existing tags/manifests without holding delete. Restore the explicit DELETE arm (e.g. keep the switch, or add `if m == http.MethodDelete { action = "delete" }`) so `requestedAccess.Action` on line 9 carries "delete" for DELETE requests.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised as "push", allowing push tokens to delete

findings.title: ActionDelete removed but documented as distinct action
findings.body: The config documentation in pkg/api/config/config.go explicitly states that 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' The three documented actions are pull, push, and delete. This diff removes the delete action mapping entirely, making DELETE requests map to 'push' instead. This makes the code behavior inconsistent with its documented contract, which would cause callers to misunderstand what permissions are actually required.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE-to-action mapping regression
findings.body: The change collapses the action mapping so any non-GET/HEAD method (including DELETE) now maps to "push" instead of "delete". Per the repo's own documented invariant (config.go: pull/push/delete are 'distinct on purpose' so an account can push without being able to delete), this silently grants delete capability to push-only tokens. No test in this diff exercises a DELETE request and asserts the resulting action/authorization outcome, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Unknown methods (e.g. OPTIONS) default to "push" instead of "pull"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set to `"pull"`. The new negated condition sends OPTIONS, TRACE and any other unlisted verb down the `"push"` branch, so requests that previously needed only pull access now require push. If OPTIONS is used for CORS preflight or capability probes, pull-only clients will start receiving authorization failures. Either enumerate the write methods explicitly or keep an explicit fallback to "pull".

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh's mutation and cache-eviction logic is untested
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches fresh data, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is covered by any test in the diff: a bug that skipped the cache write, inverted the eviction condition (e.g. `<` instead of `>`), or cleared on every call would still pass with no visible failure. Add tests asserting that (1) the cache is populated with the fetched value after a call, and (2) the cache is cleared once the size threshold is exceeded but not before.

findings.title: Misleading function name: get_* should not mutate
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh()` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which signals a read-only operation in most codebases. However, the function mutates the cache (line 10), and conditionally clears it (line 12). A caller expecting read-only semantics could be surprised by side effects. Rename to `fetch_tenant_fresh()` or `load_tenant_fresh()` to accurately signal that this performs a network fetch and cache mutation.

findings.title: Eviction clears the entry just inserted, defeating the write
findings.body: On the request that pushes the cache past 1000 entries, `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` is immediately undone by `_CACHE.clear()`. The caller still gets the right value back, but a following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though the tenant was just fetched, and every other tenant loses its entry at once (a cliff that sends the full working set back to `_fetch`). If a size bound is the goal, evict a bounded number of entries (e.g. pop the oldest via `OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache`) and check the bound before inserting, so the fresh entry survives.

findings.title: README documents renamed CLI flag by old name
findings.body: The README at line 7 documents the flag as `--workers`, but the code now uses `--concurrency`. A user reading the documentation will attempt to use the wrong flag name and fail. Update the README to match the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename also renames the Namespace attribute args.workers
findings.body:
`add_argument("--concurrency", ...)` makes argparse store the value as `args.concurrency` instead of `args.workers`. Every call site that does `args.workers` (or `getattr(ns, "workers")`) after `parser().parse_args()` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than failing at import, so it will not be caught by a smoke import. Either update all consumers, or preserve the attribute with `p.add_argument("--concurrency", dest="workers", type=int, default=4)`, and if the old CLI spelling is public, keep it accepted via an alias: `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="workers", ...)`.

The README block this diff touches still lists `--workers` (line 7), which is consistent with the old name still being expected somewhere.

findings.title: No test verifies the renamed --concurrency flag
findings.body: The flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency, but no test asserts that parser() now accepts --concurrency (or rejects --workers). If this rename were reverted or misspelled, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring no longer matches return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dict mapping day to count. Any caller relying on the docstring will pass an integer to code expecting a dict, causing immediate runtime failures.

findings.title: Return shape changed from int to dict, breaking existing callers
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a single integer via `_db.scalar(...)`; it now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller that does arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (`usage > limit`, `f"{usage} calls"`, `total += monthly_usage(...)`) will now silently operate on a dict or raise a `TypeError`. The empty case also changes meaning: previously `0`, now `{}`, which is falsy but not numerically usable.

If per-day breakdown is the goal, either add a new function (e.g. `daily_usage`) and keep `monthly_usage` returning the total, or update every caller in the same change. The docstring on line 2 still states "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer", which no longer describes the value returned and must be updated either way.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day breakdown behavior
findings.body: monthly_usage's behavior changed from returning a single integer total to returning a dict keyed by day. If the GROUP BY query, key naming (row["day"]/row["count"]), or dict construction were wrong, nothing in this diff would catch it. Add a test that calls monthly_usage against a fixture/mock DB returning multiple day rows and asserts the resulting dict has the expected day->count mapping.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body:
`list_invoices` previously accepted `page_size`; it now accepts `limit`. Any existing call site written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. Positional callers are unaffected, so the failure will only show up on the keyword call paths, which makes it easy to miss in a quick smoke test.

Either grep for `page_size=` at every call site (including tests and any external consumers of this module) and update them in this PR, or keep backwards compatibility for a deprecation window, e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a legacy alias and map it onto `limit` with a warning.

findings.title: Docstring parameter name does not match function signature
findings.body: The docstring documents the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 renames it to `limit`. Update the docstring to reflect the new parameter name so callers reading the documentation get the correct argument name.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will raise ImportError
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so on Python 3 (and on Python 2 for anyone whose CWD isn't `requests/`) importing `requests.sessions` raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` — i.e. `import requests` fails outright. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: New request() accepts verify/cert but never applies them to the send
findings.body:
The rewritten `Session.request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature, but neither value is ever written onto `req`, nor passed to `self.send(prep)` / `adapter.send(request)`. A caller that explicitly asks for TLS verification (`verify=True`, or a CA bundle path) or supplies a client certificate now gets those arguments silently discarded, and the connection is made with whatever the freshly constructed `HTTPAdapter()` defaults to. Callers cannot detect this — the parameter is accepted without error. Either thread `verify`/`cert` through to the adapter (`self.send(prep, verify=verify, cert=cert)`) or remove them from the signature so the failure is loud rather than silent. The same applies to `prefetch`/`timeout`, which are also accepted and dropped.

I cannot see `adapters.HTTPAdapter` in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm what its default verification behaviour is; if it defaults to not verifying, this is a straightforward MITM exposure for any caller that asked for verification.

findings.title: `old_request` calls `_send_request`, which this diff deletes
findings.body: `_send_request` is removed (the hunk at line 293), but the surviving `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches `old_request` now dies with `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or inline `r.send(prefetch=...); return r.response` at the call site.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, config
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only transfers method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `return_response` and `config` are accepted and then dropped on the floor, and `self.send(prep)` takes no way to pass them through. Existing callers doing `session.get(url, timeout=1, verify=False)` will now hang indefinitely and perform full certificate verification with no error — a silent behaviour change, which is worse than a failure. Either thread these through to `send()`/the adapter or raise on the unsupported ones while the refactor is in flight.

findings.title: `close()` no longer releases connections; `self.poolmanager` is never set
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and its call from `__init__` are gone, and `close()` is now `pass`. Two consequences: (1) `Session.poolmanager` no longer exists, so any remaining code path that reaches for it (including `old_request`'s eventual `r.send()`, which historically used the session's pool manager) raises `AttributeError`; (2) `close()` / `__exit__` no longer dispose of pooled sockets, so `with requests.session() as s:` silently leaks connections. If pooling is moving to the adapter, `close()` should delegate to the adapter rather than become a no-op.

findings.title: Top-level `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is resolvable from sys.path
findings.body:
Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`), but this one is absolute. Under Python 3 — and under Python 2 with `absolute_import` in effect — `adapters` is looked up on `sys.path`, not inside the `requests` package. `sys.path[0]` is the invoking script's directory (or the CWD for `-c`/interactive use), so any file named `adapters.py` sitting next to an application that imports `requests` is imported and executed instead of the library's own module, and its `HTTPAdapter.send` then handles every outbound request, URL, header and credential the session produces. In a shared or writable working directory that is a code-execution and credential-interception foothold; in the ordinary case it is simply an ImportError at `import requests`.

Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Refactored send/close/request paths have no test coverage
findings.body: This diff changes real runtime behavior in three places with no accompanying test changes: close() now does `pass` instead of clearing the poolmanager (line 132), send() now instantiates HTTPAdapter and delegates to it instead of calling request.send() (lines 365-367), and a new request() method builds and sends a Request via req.prepare()/self.send() while the old implementation is kept alongside as old_request (lines 134-172). If HTTPAdapter.send() returns the wrong object, if close() silently drops connections, or if the new request() path diverges from old_request's behavior, nothing in the suite would catch it — these are exactly the kind of behavior changes that need a session-level test (e.g. verifying a real request round-trips through send() and that close() actually releases the pool).

findings.title: Removed docstring misleads about close() behavior
findings.body: The `close()` method previously documented that it disposes internal state and closes pooled connections via the PoolManager. The docstring was removed (lines 131-135 in original), but callers relying on the documented contract will now have their connections remain open. The method now does nothing (`pass`), making the old documentation actively false if referenced elsewhere.

findings.title: `send()` constructs a fresh HTTPAdapter per request, defeating pooling
