Two reachable inputs escape the export directory: `name="../../etc/passwd"` (join does no normalisation, and `open` resolves the `..` segments), and any absolute `name` such as `"/etc/passwd"`, which makes `os.path.join` discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and return the absolute path. The result is an arbitrary-file read limited only by `limit` bytes. Call `_confined(name)` here exactly as line 14 does, rather than joining directly.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks safety contract for untrusted input
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview()` function has no docstring and does not restrict the input `name` parameter, unlike the existing `read_export()` immediately above it which applies `_confined()`. A caller seeing two side-by-side public functions with similar names would reasonably assume they have similar safety properties. This docstring-less function invites misuse by callers who may pass untrusted path components expecting confinement.

findings.title: New unconfined path-join function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without the _confined() normalization used by the neighboring read_export handler (line 14). There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a path-traversal-capable name (e.g. '../secret') reaching this function would not be caught by any existing test, and no test asserts the output is confined to EXPORT_ROOT.

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export returns other tenants' reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it directly, with no check that the objects belong to the caller's tenant. The documented invariant on `require_owner` is that "every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this"; after this change nothing does. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and read cross-tenant data. The now-unused `user = current_user(request)` on line 5 is the tell that the only consumer of the identity was the deleted loop.

If the goal is to avoid N validation calls, keep the control and make it cheap: filter at the query level, e.g. fetch with `Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and treat a short result set as a 403/404, rather than dropping the check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (IDOR)

findings.title: No test exists to catch removal of ownership check
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report `require_owner` call from `bulk_export`, eliminating tenant isolation on this endpoint. There is no test file in this change (or referenced) that exercises `bulk_export` with reports belonging to a different tenant than `user`. If this regression is real, nothing in the test suite would fail — the function would simply return cross-tenant data silently. A test asserting that `bulk_export` raises `Forbidden` (or filters out) reports not owned by `user.tenant_id` is needed to make this kind of regression detectable.

findings.title: Unknown report IDs now surface as AttributeError instead of Forbidden
findings.body: If `Report.get(rid)` returns `None` for an unknown ID, the deleted loop previously dereferenced `report.tenant_id` inside `require_owner`, which at minimum failed before serialisation. Now the `None` flows to `r.to_dict()` on line 7 and raises `AttributeError`, producing a 500 for what is a client input error. Validate the fetched list (drop or reject missing IDs) as part of reinstating the ownership filter.

findings.title: SQL injection: f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates `term` and `status` into the SQL text via an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Both values land inside single-quoted literals, so any caller-supplied apostrophe terminates the literal and the rest of the input is parsed as SQL (e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer; `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` depending on whether the driver permits multi-statement execution).

Fix by passing the values as bind parameters, matching `get_customer` on line 5 and the contract in `billing/db.py` ("`params` must carry every caller value"):

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the *parameter value*, not the SQL text.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract and breaks on quoted input
findings.body:
`billing/db.execute` documents "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with `params=None`.

Beyond the contract breach, this is wrong for reachable, entirely legitimate inputs:
- `term="O'Brien"` or `status="don't know"` closes the quoted literal and the statement fails to parse — a plain syntax error on a normal customer name.
- `term` values containing `%` or `_` are treated as LIKE wildcards rather than literal characters, so the search silently returns wrong rows.
- `term=None` or `status=None` stringifies to the literal `None` instead of raising or matching NULL.

Fix by parameterising, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, which also removes the need for the surrounding quotes. If literal `%`/`_` matching is required, escape them in the pattern before binding.

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers, missing SQL injection detection
findings.body: search_customers builds a query via f-string interpolation instead of parameterised placeholders (unlike get_customer above it, and unlike the convention documented in billing/db.py that params must carry every caller value). No test in this diff calls search_customers with a value like `term="'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` or asserts that placeholders are used, so this behavior change is currently uncatchable by any test.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary URL with no scheme/host check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight to `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it parses the host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before posting, so the control exists in this module and is simply not applied on this path.

An attacker who can register or test a webhook target can make the server issue GET requests to internal addresses (`http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...`, `http://127.0.0.1:6379/`, internal admin panels) and learn the outcome — the status code is returned to the caller, so this is a probing oracle, not just a blind request. Non-HTTP schemes are also accepted by the caller's URL string: `file://` is handled by requests only with an adapter, but `http+unix`-style adapters or a redirect to another scheme are worth ruling out. `requests.get` also follows redirects by default, so even if a host check were added at call time, an allowed host could 302 to an internal address.

Suggested fix: reuse the same host parse + `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check used at lines 8-9, require the scheme to be `https` (or `http`/`https`), resolve the hostname and reject private/loopback/link-local/reserved IPs, and pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop).

I cannot see the caller of `verify_endpoint` in this diff or in retrieved context; the assessment that `url` is attacker-influenced rests on the PR description ("caller-supplied URL") and on the function's name and placement next to a customer-facing webhook sender.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sibling function enforces

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new function that performs a server-side HTTP GET against a caller-supplied URL, unlike the sibling function above it which validates against ALLOWED_HOSTS. No test exists for this function in the diff, so there is nothing to catch a regression, an incorrect status code return, or a fix that later adds/removes host validation. Add a test that exercises verify_endpoint's behavior (e.g. with allowed/disallowed hosts, or mocked requests.get) so behavioral changes are caught.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is exported at module level with no docstring. A caller cannot determine from the signature alone whether the URL is validated (it is not—there is no allowlist check like the adjacent `send_payload` function performs), what exceptions it may raise, or what the return value semantics are (HTTP status codes can span 100–599 with different meanings). A competent caller could easily misuse this—for example, assuming it validates the target against an allowlist before issuing a request, when it does not.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on non-public invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false`, which is an exact copy of the block written for the intentionally-public `assets` bucket above. For a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices` this switches off the account-level safety net entirely: any ACL or bucket policy that grants `AllUsers`/`AuthenticatedUsers` will take effect, and a single mis-set ACL exposes customer invoices publicly.

Unless this bucket is genuinely meant to serve public content, set all four attributes to `true`, or simply delete this resource and rely on the S3 defaults (which block public access) plus any account-level block. Worth also confirming that nothing else in the module attaches a permissive policy to `aws_s3_bucket.invoices`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Public access block disabled on customer-invoices bucket

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC hexdigest as `verify_stripe` one line above, but returns `expected == header`. `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte across repeated requests. Use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` exactly as `verify_stripe` does on line 7.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay signature check has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay uses a plain == comparison instead of hmac.compare_digest (used by the sibling verify_stripe). No test file is part of this diff, so nothing would catch a timing side-channel regression or even a basic correctness regression (e.g. wrong header format) in this new function. Add a test asserting correct/incorrect signature behavior, and ideally one that would fail if compare_digest were swapped for ==.

findings.title: Divergent behaviour from verify_stripe when header is None or bytes
findings.body: Beyond the timing issue, `==` and `hmac.compare_digest` differ on edge inputs: `compare_digest(str, None)` or a `bytes` header raises `TypeError`, while `expected == header` quietly returns `False`. A caller that wraps `verify_stripe` in a `try/except TypeError` (or relies on the exception to distinguish "malformed request" from "bad signature") will see a silently different result from `verify_acmepay`. Switching line 12 to `hmac.compare_digest` resolves this along with the timing problem.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` is the generic 500 error path and now serialises `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response body. A stack trace discloses file system paths, module and function names, framework and library versions, and the source line structure of the application; exception messages frequently embed the offending input, SQL fragments, connection strings or internal hostnames. An unauthenticated caller who can provoke an error — malformed input, an unexpected content type, a missing record — gets a free map of the internals, which meaningfully lowers the cost of finding the next bug.

Keep the client-facing payload opaque and leave the detail in the log, which line 8 already captures. If developers need the detail in a response, gate it on an explicit debug/development configuration flag that is off by default, and consider returning a correlation id the client can quote instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    log.exception("request failed")
    return {"error": "internal error"}, 500
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and depends on ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape changed: new key and non-constant `error` value

findings.title: Public error handler return contract is now undocumented
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler whose return value is part of the API contract. The diff changes it from returning `{"error": "internal error"}` to `{"error": str(exc), "traceback": traceback.format_exc()}`. This is a breaking change to the response structure and content that callers need to know about. The function has no docstring explaining what it returns, so callers cannot discover this contract change except by reading the code. Add a docstring documenting the new return structure, or document this change in the API specification if one exists.

findings.title: No test guards against leaking exception details in error responses
findings.body: The handle() function now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the client-facing response body, a behavior change from the previous generic 'internal error' message. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts the shape/content of the response returned by handle(), so this leak could be introduced, removed, or altered again without any test failing either way.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`) and callers must be verifying it with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest for the same conceptual value (a stored user password). Storing that in the same column means verification after a reset either fails outright or, with bcrypt's parsing, raises `ValueError: invalid salt` — the user is locked out. Separately, an unsalted single-round MD5 is not an acceptable password hash at all: it is trivially reversed via rainbow tables. The reset path should call `hash_password` (bcrypt) so both writers and the single reader agree on one format; if a distinct value is genuinely needed, it should be a random one-time reset *token*, not a hash of the user's password.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives the stored value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5()` pass, while `hash_password` on line 7 correctly uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no per-user salt here, so any password written through the reset path is recoverable from a leaked database at rainbow-table/brute-force speed, and identical passwords across users produce identical digests. It also means reset-set passwords are stored in a format incompatible with the bcrypt verifier, which suggests the two paths disagree about the stored format.

Fix: delete `hash_reset_password` and call `hash_password` (bcrypt) from the reset flow. If a distinct function is needed for readability, have it delegate to `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`.

Entry point note: the caller that feeds `raw` (presumably a reset-token-authenticated form submission) is not in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot name the exact HTTP handler; the defect is in the storage primitive itself regardless of caller.

findings.title: New hash_reset_password function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password uses MD5 to hash a password for reset purposes, but there is no test file in this diff exercising it. Nothing would fail if this function were changed, removed, or if its weak-hash behavior regressed further. Since this is a change to authentication-critical code, at minimum a test asserting the function's contract (or documenting expected hashing scheme) should exist.

findings.title: Public function hash_reset_password lacks docstring
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` is a public function in the auth module. Its name suggests it hashes a password for reset purposes, but callers cannot determine from signature alone whether this is a temporary token hash, a validation step, or something else. A docstring explaining the intended use and any limitations would help callers use it correctly.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled script with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: the job gets the repository's secrets and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions, and it runs without the approval gate that fork PRs get under `pull_request`. Line 12 then deliberately checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the fork's code — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on line 15.

Entry point: any unprivileged user opens a pull request from a fork and edits `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources/invokes, e.g. `package.json` lifecycle scripts, a lockfile pointing at a malicious package). Sink: the `run` step on line 13, which executes that attacker-authored code on a runner holding `NPM_TOKEN` and the base-repo `GITHUB_TOKEN`. The attacker can exfiltrate `NPM_TOKEN`, read every other secret available to the job, and use the write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` to push commits or alter releases.

Remediations, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `on: pull_request`. If the only reason for the change was that fork PRs did not get a token, reconsider whether `measure.sh` needs `NPM_TOKEN` at all — a size measurement usually does not.
2. If `pull_request_target` is genuinely required, do **not** check out and execute the head SHA in the same job. Split it: an untrusted job on `pull_request` that builds and uploads an artifact, and a privileged job on `workflow_run` that only consumes the artifact and never executes fork code.
3. At minimum, if any privileged job remains, add an explicit `permissions:` block reducing `GITHUB_TOKEN` to `contents: read` and never pass secrets to a step that runs fork-authored code.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-supplied script with NPM_TOKEN in scope

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ No permissions block: GITHUB_TOKEN is write-scoped under pull_request_target

findings.title: Measurement now covers the PR head, not the merge result
findings.body: With the previous `pull_request` trigger, `actions/checkout` defaults to `refs/pull/N/merge` — the simulated merge of the PR into the base branch — so the reported size reflected what the repository would look like after merging. Pinning `ref` to `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` measures the fork's branch tip in isolation, which diverges whenever the base branch has moved since the PR was created. Size numbers and any threshold comparison derived from them will no longer match the post-merge reality. If this check gates merges on a size budget, the gate is now measuring the wrong tree.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values from hashable to JSON-serialisable
findings.body:
The previous key, `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, worked for any context whose values were hashable — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `Path`, model instances, frozensets, enum members. `json.dumps` accepts a much smaller set and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of the above. Any existing caller passing a non-primitive context value will now get an exception from what used to be a working call, and the failure happens before `_render` is ever reached, so it is not a cache miss but a hard break.

If the digest form is wanted, pass a fallback: `json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True, default=repr)` (accepting that `repr` may not be stable across processes), or keep the tuple key and only hash its `repr`.

findings.title: JSON-serialization requirement for context values is untested
findings.body: The old key was built from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which only required context values to be hashable/sortable. The new key uses `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which requires every value in context to be JSON-serializable (and will raise or silently misbehave for things like sets, custom objects, or dicts with non-string keys under sort_keys). None of the added tests exercise a context with a non-JSON-serializable value, so this behavior change — from 'must be hashable' to 'must be JSON-serializable' — is not covered.

findings.title: Shell-safety test only checks `shell=False`, not the argv list
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` asserts only `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects the actual command that was passed to `subprocess.run` (e.g. `spy.last_call.args[0]`). Because `spy` is a stand-in for `subprocess.run` and never actually executes anything, a regression where the implementation sets `shell=False` but reverts to building a single interpolated string (e.g. `subprocess.run(f"tar -czf /exports/{name}.tar.gz {directory}", shell=False)`) — which would silently fail or misbehave at runtime, and reintroduces exactly the kind of unsafe construction this PR is fixing — would still pass this test. The whole point of the change (argv list instead of a shell string) is left unverified.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test pins `shell=False` but not the list argv that is the actual fix

findings.title: Dropping the shell removes word-splitting/globbing for `directory`
findings.body: Previously the command was interpolated into a shell string, so a `directory` value such as `/srv/a /srv/b` or `/srv/data/*` was word-split and glob-expanded by `/bin/sh` and tar received multiple paths. With a list argv the whole value is passed as one literal path argument, so any such caller now gets `tar: /srv/a /srv/b: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and, because `check=True`, a `CalledProcessError` at runtime rather than a working archive. If callers only ever pass a single concrete directory this is a no-op, but that needs confirming — no callers were retrieved. If multi-path input is a real use case, take a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv instead of relying on the shell.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; may allow arbitrary-path archiving
findings.body:
`name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight from the caller into the tar argv on line 12 with no validation or containment check. Passing it as a list element plus `--` correctly prevents shell injection and option injection, so this is not a command-execution issue. It does mean that if any caller derives `directory` from request data, a caller can ask for `/etc`, `/root`, or `../../` relative paths and the contents land in a readable tarball under `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` — an arbitrary-file-read primitive if that directory is ever served or downloadable.

If callers only pass trusted constants, this is nothing. If not, resolve the path and assert it stays under an allowed root before invoking tar, e.g. `root = Path('/srv/data').resolve(); p = (root / directory).resolve(); if not p.is_relative_to(root): raise ValueError(...)`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result, so the only failure mode it can detect is an exception. If `render` returns `None`, an empty string, a stray header/footer, or a mis-formatted zero total for the empty case, the test still passes. Assert the expected output for an empty invoice explicitly, e.g. the rendered string equals the expected header/total-only form (mirroring the style of `test_renders_total` on line 2).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: test_renders_line_items asserts on a mock, not on output
findings.body:
This test patches out format_line and only checks that it was called twice via fmt.call_count. It never checks the rendered output produced by render(). If render() mishandles the formatted line items (wrong order, wrong joining, dropped lines), this test would still pass. Assert on the actual string returned by render() instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on a mock's call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Deleted test leaves round_cents half-to-even behavior uncovered
findings.body:
The test `test_rounds_half_to_even` (which asserted `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.34")`) was removed along with the fix it was presumably validating. No replacement test was added, so if the rounding fix is wrong or regresses in the future, nothing in this suite would catch it.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Tie-breaking test deleted, removing the only .5 boundary assertion

findings.title: PR claims a rounding fix but only the test file changed
findings.body:
The PR is titled "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test", yet the change set is a single file (`tests/test_rounding.py`) containing only a deletion. There is no implementation change to `round_cents` anywhere in this diff. Either the fix was omitted from the commit — in which case the failing test was simply removed and the underlying defect remains in production — or the behaviour was already changed in an earlier commit and this is a retroactive silencing of the guard.

Please either include the implementation change in this PR so the pair can be reviewed together, or restore the test with the updated expectation and point at the commit that changed the behaviour.

findings.title: Patch targets the definition module, so the mock is never used
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` into the `notify.sender` namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. The test therefore exercises the real `deliver` — it will hit whatever the real transport does (network I/O, flakiness), and the `is False` assertion passes or fails for reasons unrelated to the retry logic it claims to cover. Use `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`, matching the existing test on line 2. Consider also asserting the mock was called exactly `attempts` times, since that is the actual behaviour under test.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; test proves nothing about retries

findings.title: Test patch target contradicts documented behavior
findings.body: The test on line 7 patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the module docstring in sender.py (lines 4–5) explicitly documents that `deliver` is bound into the sender module's namespace at import time, so patching the original location does not affect it. This test will not validate the retry logic as intended—the real function will still execute. The patch should target `notify.sender.deliver` (as the passing test on line 2 correctly does).

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins stringified field values with `","` directly, so a value such as `Smith, John` or `he said "hi"` injects an extra delimiter / unbalanced quote and shifts every subsequent column for that row. The escaping helper needed to prevent exactly this is added two functions below (`csv_escape`), but it is never called. Wrap each field: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note also that `csv_escape` does `"," in value`, which raises `TypeError` on non-string input, so the `str(...)` conversion must happen before the escape call (as written above) rather than after. `csv_header` has the same exposure for column names containing commas.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values unescaped; csv_escape ignores newlines
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each cell directly into a comma-joined string and never calls the `csv_escape` helper added two functions below. Any cell value containing `,`, `"`, `\n` or `\r` therefore changes the structure of the emitted CSV: a comma splits one field into two, and a newline injects an entire extra record that downstream parsers (or a spreadsheet) will read as real data. `csv_escape` would only partly fix this as written, because its condition checks for comma and quote but not for CR/LF, so a newline-bearing value is returned unquoted.

Suggested fix: route every cell through an escaper (`str(r.get(c, ""))`) and extend the escape condition to `any(ch in value for ch in ',"\n\r')`, or simply use the stdlib `csv` module (`csv.writer`), which handles quoting, embedded newlines and doubling correctly. If the exported cells can ever be opened in a spreadsheet, also consider neutralising leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` to avoid formula injection.

I cannot see the caller that supplies `rows`, so I cannot name the entry point; if those values are report data derived from user input (names, free-text fields), this is directly attacker-influenced output.

findings.title: New exporter functions lack tests, unlike existing csv_header
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (in csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (in json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (in pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with no accompanying tests. The repo already has a test for csv_header (test_csv.py), establishing the convention that exporter functions get direct tests. If any of these had a bug — e.g. csv_escape failing to quote a leading/trailing space, dump_streaming producing overlapping chunks off-by-one, or margins_for miscalculating for an unsupported page size — nothing in the current test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Flaky test: relies on real-time midnight boundary
findings.body:
test_token_issued_today_is_valid() calls issue_token() and datetime.now(timezone.utc) separately and compares .date(). If issue_token() is invoked just before midnight UTC and the assertion's datetime.now() call executes just after midnight, token.issued_at.date() will differ from datetime.now().date(), causing a spurious failure. The sibling test on line 4-6 correctly injects a fixed 'now' via the `now=` parameter to is_expired, but this new test does not use any time injection for issue_token or the date comparison, making it non-deterministic and unable to reliably catch real expiry-window bugs.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date-granularity clock comparison is flaky across UTC midnight

findings.title: Test name promises determinism but exhibits time-dependent behavior
findings.body: The test function `test_token_issued_today_is_valid` has a misleading name and contract. The name suggests a stable, deterministic test, but the implementation depends on the system clock and will fail intermittently at midnight boundaries. Line 11 compares `token.issued_at.date()` with `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()`, and line 12 calls `is_expired()` with no explicit `now` parameter, likely using the current real time internally. If a token is issued just before midnight and the assertion runs after midnight, the date comparison fails. The function's public contract — what a reader infers from its name — does not warn of this time-dependent behavior, making it a trap for future maintainers.

findings.title: New CouponExpired branch is untested
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test in this PR updates the happy-path test to pass a future expiry date, avoiding the new branch entirely. If the expiry check were inverted, off-by-one, or silently removed, no test would fail.

findings.title: `expires_at` None or naive datetime raises TypeError, not CouponExpired
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes `expires_at` is always a non-None, timezone-aware datetime. If a coupon has no expiry (`None`) the comparison raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime'`; if it was stored/parsed as a naive datetime it raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. Either way the caller sees an opaque TypeError instead of a coupon being applied or a `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.
